*"start IM-4c please Claude"* (he pushed IM-4b first). Three read-only searches mapped the placement paths,
the payment paths and Tier A, each reporting file and line; I checked the facts the recommendation turns on.
IM-4's decision 10 does not fit the code in four places, so the build is held:

  change every collapse in a lake and a pinned test. Recommended: a lake read of its own.

  millijoule budget, priced at arm's reach too, paid through `Pack.Pay` (lead-acid or window, no new
  `PowerExact` term).

  flooded-room door as it is today, printed, with a pre-count as a named lever.
- **"Refused `Wet`"**: `Unpowered` already means "couldn't pay". Recommended.

Also: machines, rubble and the debug writers stay piers; part-litres ride a session carry per lake; the top
voxel of a band is charged its fraction. The price in lead-acid terms: a full pack fills 3.6 m³ of lake, and
67 minutes of recharge buys each further cubic metre.

**A live bug found alongside:** Ctrl+Z does not drop the pending fills, so an undo in the half second before
the boundary is redone by the replay, dry voxels and all. It is fixed in 4c whichever way the decisions go.

## 2026-09-29 (night) — IM-3's r6 control, and IM-3b's code-level pass: seven decisions handed back

*"IM-3b, next please Claude thanks!"*. First, the check IM-3 owed: the r6 control on its build read `2601 / 325
/ 3446 at 411`, 0 `ERROR`, with the game closed and his log copied aside first.

IM-3b is a new part (his vault's own energy, taken mid-build), so it got its pass: the paragraph read against
`MachineTick`'s pool, `VaultState`, `ChargeOf` and the vault half of the set. Five facts; two of them change
what was taken.

- **IM-3's fuse is put out by any cell, measured.** The unpaid pool is written back into the cells, builds up,
  and pays the whole bill one boundary in N. One paid boundary puts the fuse out, and a broke channel's fuse is
  10–15 s. So a throwaway test (reverted) held a vault for 4,000 boundaries on 5% of its bill; at 3% it
  dumped in 25. The demo's storm is 25% of its vault's bill, so decision 12's "the weather finishes it" never
  happens. Nothing a player can reach (no vault ships before IM-6). An own charge refilled from the spare is
  the same store as the cell, so it would not close this by itself.
- **A minute of the *full* bill is a capacity, not a time.** The demo's vault is 5% full, and 2.4 MJ against a
  1.5 kW deficit lasts about 27 minutes, through every storm. The varying parameter is the fill.
- The own charge needs **no `PowerExact` term**: `ChargeOf` already carries a row's stored energy into the
  identity. TODO said it would need one.
- `MoveAtPick`'s fresh `VaultContents()` is the one write that would drop the charge out of the books.
- The pool's "spare" includes the cells.

The seven recommendations are in the plan ("IM-3b — the code-level pass"). The two forks:
- **A minute of its bill as it stands** (capacity recomputed each boundary, the excess back to the pool),
  against the fixed minute of the full bill he took.
- **A paid boundary pauses a lit fuse and only a full own charge puts it out**, amending 28.

Nothing is built.

## 2026-09-29 (late) — IM-2 built: the quantum backpack is a window, and consumers are paid by priority

*"start on IM-2 please Claude"*. Decisions 7, 8, 9 and 41 were read against the pack, the tick and the tool
call sites first, and they fit, so no pass was handed back. The deciding fact: the tools pay only through
`EquippedPack.VoxelsAffordable` and `Pay`, so a window answering both from its channel's cells changes no
call site. The plan's "IM-2 — built" has the file-by-file account.

- **The draw** is behind an internal `IChannelBank` that `MachineTick` implements explicitly. It takes the
  last-filled cell first (the write-back read backwards), writes `StorageState` directly, and throws inside
  `Run`. The pack counts what it takes as `taken`, so `PowerExact` needed no new term: 1,000 random
  operations of every door into the pool, exact after each.
- **Priority**: the relay pump ships `priority` 0–9 at 5, and a pump without the extra reads 5, so every
  existing test passed unchanged. That was the "equal priorities are position order" check, for free.
  Played worlds' pumps take the port at its default on open.
- **Shipped**: `quantum_backpack.json` with a cyan swatch on layer 13. `P` does not seed it until IM-6's bank
  line; `--pack=overburden:quantum_backpack` wears one.
- **The prints name the bank** for a window, and the power line prints `pack initial` with the full formula.
  The first oracle run printed `the pack at 0 mJ of 0 mJ` for a window, which would have misled the next
  person reading a log.

**Checks:**
- Suite **2,088**.
- **Ten mutations**: nine red on their own tests, one green as predicted (a window's zero capacity already
  refuses the fill).
- The r6 control to the digit.
- M10a-3's loaded arm exact.
- The window's own oracle: `306,650,000 by the tool`, the same on two runs. Its 26 unpowered swings are the
  ones before `--pump` places the cell, as the log's order shows. `--port=pump:priority=9` sets and 42
  clamps to 9, checked headless before COMMANDS.md claimed it.

## 2026-09-29 (late) — IM-1 built: the strict loader, format, the extras and their table, programmer

*"as recommended please Claude"* took the pass's eight decisions, and IM-1 was built the same session.
Suite **2,076** (+70). The plan's "IM-1 — built" has the file-by-file account.

- **The strict walk** (`StrictJson`) reads the loader's own classes by reflection, so it and the binding
  cannot disagree. It reports every unknown key with its path and nearest name (`machine.links.charge.carrys
  — did you mean 'carries'?`), refuses a key given twice, and drops `$` notes at every level, maps included.
  It hands the serialiser the original text when nothing was dropped, so type errors keep their line numbers.
- **The existing 2,006 passed under it unchanged.** No fixture or shipped file used a key the loader does not
  bind.
- **`format`** is read alone, before the manifest's keys. A newer mod fails in one line with none of its files
  read, and a mod depending on it is told "skipped", not "not installed".
- **The extras.** Six bits and six quantum forms. The base game's `extras.json` ships the quantum row. Media
  are checked by the `via` rule, with a did-you-mean for `channel`. One (extra, medium) pair has one owner.
  Every extra is refused on a machine, naming its slice, until that slice switches it on in
  `MachineExtras.Served`.
- **The three-mod fixture** loads identically in all 24 listing orders. It has three conflicts, one between
  two third-party mods.
- **`programmer`** keys the computer's verb in `PlaceController`; any other item's click does nothing.

**The mutation battery: twelve rules, twelve red**, each on its own test, and files restored byte-identical
(hash-checked). My first draft of the three-mod fixture asserted two conflicts where it built three; I caught
it by recounting the fixture before the first run.

**He was playing through the build.** `start.cmd` launched at 7:17 PM on `TajMahal2`, and his log's `Content:`
line has no extras term and 0 `ERROR`, so his binary predates the loader change. The Game DLL on disk is IM-1's
now, and his next launch rebuilds anyway. **The r6 control is owed.** It waits for the game to close, per the
probing rule (a headless run beside him steals CPU and rotates his log).

## 2026-09-28 — The water was slow because Core was built unoptimised

*"profile it please Claude"*. The sampler, attached to the game process (not the console wrapper,
whose 5 threads hold no managed frames), on a copy of TajMahal (18.7 ML, 1.2 M cells). Under
`FluidSimulation.Advance`, 22.6 s on the CPU:
- `Record` → `Wake` → `WakeNeighboursOf` took 47%;
- `CanHold` through `LakeBoundedTerrain` → `FluidFieldView` took 40%;
- `VoxelPos.get_Chunk` alone was 12% self, `get_Local` 10%, `ChunkPos.Equals` 6%.

**One-line getters as real call frames mean the JIT did not optimise them.**
- `DOTNET_TieredCompilation=0` changed nothing (0.84 / 1.00 Hz against 0.91 / 0.89 tiered,
  interleaved).
- The Core DLL the game loads carried `DebuggableAttribute(263)`, which is DisableOptimizations.
- `dotnet msbuild -getProperty:Optimize` read `true` for the Game and `false` for Core.

**The mechanism:** `Directory.Build.props` is imported before the SDK defaults Configuration. So a
project given no configuration sees `''` at the 2026-09-15 condition `'$(Configuration)' ==
'Debug'` and is not optimised. The Game's own SDK sets Configuration first, which is why the
2026-09-15 fix looked whole. Core and Persistence, built as the Game's references by `dotnet build
Overburden.Game` (start.cmd's build), were not optimised. A `dotnet test` or solution build in
between (Configuration global) optimised them. **So which build a play ran on depended on the last
build command.**

**The fix:** `'$(Configuration)' == 'Debug' or '$(Configuration)' == ''`. All four projects read
`Optimize true`, and the game's Core DLL carries 2.

**Measured, alternating old and fixed four times on fresh copies, 45 s each:**

| | old | fixed |
|---|---|---|
| tick wall | 1,021 / 922 ms | **185 / 184 ms** |
| tick rate | 0.89 / 0.96 Hz | **2.00 / 2.00 Hz** |
| visits | 778 / 679 ms | **118 / 119 ms** |
| sheet solve | 238 / 235 ms | **63 / 62 ms** |
| visits a second | 269 k / 278 k | **676 k / 672 k** |
| boundary on the main thread | 79 / 73 ms | **20 / 20 ms** |

Also: the r6 control holds (2601 / 325 / 3446 at 411), and the suite passes at 1,996.

**So the water on his quarry runs at full speed.** Yesterday's levers (colour waves, bodies) are
re-read against the fixed build before any is taken. *Possibly related, not claimed:* some of this
machine's "two speeds" readings may have been an unoptimised Core; any figure taken through
`dotnet build Overburden.Game` since 2026-09-15 is suspect.

|---|---|---|

**The tick is 6× on the branch, and it is the water, not the code.** The branch with

the machine control: every run landed in one speed phase.

**The pond code's own cost is small, and it saves the enclosure most of its work.** Observing the
box costs 4.8 ms a second and the grid 9.7. The enclosure falls from 13.3 ms a second to 3.3,
because it is asked only on a raised sample (2,905 calls against 391,273). So the net is about +1
ms a second, plus 94.5 ms once at open and ~130 ms a re-analysis on a worker. **One call read
past the plan's 5 ms bar, the worst grid build at 4.0–6.0 ms, and a probe the same morning
showed it is the first build of a launch** (the JIT: build #1 at 5.4 ms on a light column, one at
1.3 ms, the other 1,040 under a millisecond). So no cap was built, and POND-PLAN's criterion 5 is
met.

**The sampler, and its trap.** `dotnet-trace collect -- <godot>` cannot launch the game: the
hosted runtime never connects to the reversed port. Attaching by PID works (`dotnet-trace ps`,
then `collect -p`). **The trace needs `--duration` shorter than the run**, or the game exits
before the rundown and every managed frame reads `?!?`. **And samples ending in `PollGCWorker`
are threads parked at a safepoint**, by a GC or by the sampler's own suspension. They pile onto
whatever loop polled: the per-frame raise loop read 3.7 s of CPU, and 0.9 s even with the raise
off, where it returns at its first line. The stopwatch said 0.16 s. With those samples set apart,
the CPU shares agree with the stopwatch: tick 2.7% → 19.5%, solve 2.2% → 8.8%, raise ~0.2%. Inside
the flood the leaders are the same on both branches: `FluidGrid.AmountAt` 12–14%, `Pop` 10–12%,
`VoxelPos.Chunk` / `Local` 13–15% together, `FloodIndex.TryGet` 4–6%.

## 2026-09-26 — The sheet flood on flat arrays: 0.76× the flood, the same water

Matthew, after reading his CSharp-Lookuptables repo against the sheet solve: *"maybe a lookup
cache would be better"*, then *"install dotnet-trace and profile it"*, then *"build the three flat
array fixes"*. dotnet-trace (10.0, sampled thread time, Speedscope) on `--solve` put the flood's
time in: neighbour reads ~65% (inlined), `Find` ~13%, copying cell lists in `Union` ~10%, the
index ~6%, interface casts ~5%, and the index's `Dictionary<long,int>` 1.6%. Three changes, one
per finding that was a data structure:

- **Union-find on a flat `int[] _parent`**, `Find` walking the array — no object per sheet on the
  path.
- **A sheet's cells as a chain** (`Head` / `Tail` / `Count`, an `int[] _cellNext` over the
  records) — `Union` splices the smaller chain after the larger's tail in O(1) where it copied a
  list. `CellsOf` materialises one list for the three readers that index it.
- **`FloodIndex`'s first layer flat** — his `FlatTableBuckets`: a 64 × 64 window of chunk columns
  anchored on the flood's first, the dictionary kept past it, so the window is a speed and never
  a limit. Stamped like the leaves.

**Measured old against new, alternated three rounds (A B A B A B, machine control 1.05–1.07× on
every run), `--solve` Release:** the two-layer arm's flood **73.3 → 55.6 ms** a pass (0.76×), the
solve **137.5 → 116.4 ms** (0.85×), 102–108 → 78–83 ns an item; the dictionary arm, which has the
first two changes and not the window, 73.4 → 59.7 ms — so the flat parents and the chain are most
of it and the window the rest. **Every run landed checksum `699103278A0A470B`, counts
`57/4/0/53/0/270700/126448`**, the old code's.

**The trap, and the test for it.** Levelling hands its remainder to the first cells in flood order
and packing breaks ties by it, so **the order a merge splices the chains in is physics** — a
splice of the smaller sheet on the front lands different water with every count the same. The
battery (8 recipes, 8 caught) found the suite blind to it: the arm test compares two indexes over
one solve and cannot see a change both share; only the bench's fingerprint caught it.
`TheSolveLandsTheSameWaterItLandedBeforeTheFlatArrays` pins the old code's checksums on three
seeds and catches it (3 fail). A second fuzz spreads floods over ±40 chunk columns so both sides
of the window's edge answer as a dictionary does. Suite 1,897; r6 control 2601 / 325 / 3446 at
411 to the digit. `--solve` prints the last round's checksum always now.

## 2026-09-24 — Planned: the front advance's slice 2

Matthew tried `--frontadvance=8` on `Regions13`: *"very little difference to the 4, look overall its
better"*. His log says why: the session's settle line reads 39,735 levelled against **184,380 left
alone as still being fed**, so four sheets in five never met the advance. Reading `NoteInflow` found
the cause is broader than streams: **"fed" is chunk-granular and volume-blind** — every `Add`,
`Emit`, disturbance and re-pour stamps its 8 m chunk, so a rain drop or a litre sweated from a wall
makes every sheet in that chunk "a stream" for a second, and a seeping mine is fed permanently. The
plan ("Slice 2" in FRONT-ADVANCE-PLAN) counts the inflow as a share of each fed sheet first, then
calls a sheet fed only above a share of it (`--fedshare=`, 0 the old rule), and only then — if the
play still wants it — advances real streams pro rata, scaling the sheet so its gradient keeps its
shape.

## 2026-09-23 — A power switch on the vacuum cell

Matthew, starting a world to build useful things in: *"can we add a power toggle to the quantum
vacuum cell, will make debugging some of it easier"*. Built as a port rather than a verb, because
the computer's panel already draws one box per declared port — `vacuum_cell.json` declares
`"enabled": { default 1, min 0, max 1 }` and the panel has a switch with no UI code at all.

**Off means out of the pool, not empty.** `MachineTick.Rebuild` leaves an off storage row out of
its channel's list, so it is never summed into what the pumps may draw and never written back
into — its charge stands still. `StoredMillijoules` still sums every row, so the pool identity
sees the frozen charge on both sides and stays exact; nothing new is a term. A row whose material
declares no `enabled` port is on, and a cell saved before today is restored with the default, so
no world changes. `SetPort` moves the set's version, so the switch lands at the next boundary.

Two tests (an off cell neither charges from a panel nor pays a pump, and resumes from where it
stood; a pump on a channel whose only cell is off stalls `unpowered`), both watched failing with
`IsEnabled` forced true. The panel's status line reads `OFF — holding …, out of channel N's
pool`, and the `power:` term counts `N cell(s) (+M off)` — the first headless run read `0 cell(s)
hold 5,000.0 MJ` with the cell switched off, which is true of the pool and reads as a lost cell.
Headless wire: `--pump=100 --openpanel=cell --panelset=enabled=0` reads `enabled := 0: set to 0`,
the pump `4 unpowered`, the cell still at 5,000 MJ, identity exact. Suite 1,813.

## 2026-09-23 — Where you are and which way you face

Matthew, handed a bearing to a mountain: *"even if you find a mountain i have no compass and could
not locate it"* — and he was right about more than the compass. The HUD had a hotbar, a crosshair,
a status line and the seed banner, and **nothing at all saying where you are or which way you are
pointing**; M5c-2 took the directional light away, so there is not even a sun to steer by. A play
check that says "the hills are north-east" was not a check anybody could carry out, which makes it
my error rather than a gap in the feature.

The status line gained a line above it: `x 108  y 11  z 6 · facing 315° NW · relief 8.1 m`. The
relief term is the surface amplitude where you stand, in metres — the thing `--reliefbase` and
`--relief` set the ends of — because **that is how you tell a plain from a highland without being
able to see 2 km**, which is the whole difficulty with a feature whose regions are larger than the
view distance by a factor of forty.

**The bearing comes from the camera's forward vector, not from its yaw, and that is the only
interesting decision here.** A yaw needs a sign convention and a zero point to mean anything, and
reasoning about those is wrong half the time and *invisible*: a compass pointing consistently the
wrong way looks exactly like a compass. `Overburden.Core/Navigation/Compass.cs` takes a direction
and returns a bearing, with the convention — **north is −Z, east is +X** — written down in Core
with tests on the four cardinals, the four diagonals, the wrap at 360°, every one of the sixteen
points being reachable, and a player looking straight down having no bearing at all. Confirmed in
the real renderer too: the scene's own 45° camera yaw reads `315° NW`, which is what +45° about Y
means when forward is −Z.

It also gives the map that follows a convention to share rather than to re-derive.

Suite 1,761 → 1,772.

## 2026-09-23 — Every world was identical at the one place you stand in it

Matthew, after building several worlds with the new shape: *"I tried a few worlds do i need to hand
in a command line parameter?"* — no, and the log said so: `Regions8` and `Regions9` both read
`relief 19.2..144 voxel(s), mountains 25% rare` with no flags. So the setting was arriving and the
worlds still felt alike, which is a better question than the one asked.

**They were alike. Exactly, at spawn, on every seed.** Gradient noise is *zero at its lattice
points* — that is what makes it gradient noise rather than value noise — and world origin is a
lattice point of the relief field. So the relief sample at (0, 0) is 0 whatever the seed, and four
of his worlds measured an amplitude at spawn of **34.6 voxels, to the digit, all four**. The one
place a player judges a world from was the one place that could not differ.

**The fix is a seed-derived offset into the relief field's own lattice cell**, a hash as a fraction
in [0, 1) added to the sampled coordinates. Measured after: **30 distinct spawn amplitudes over 32
seeds, spanning 81% of the floor-to-ceiling range** — 19.2 v (a world that starts on a plain, right
on the floor) to 120.6 v (one that starts near the summit). On his own four seeds: 34.6 / 34.6 /
34.6 / 34.6 became 71.4 / 43.4 / 19.3 / 32.8.

**It needed no care about the recorded figures, which is the good kind of safe.** A uniform world
never reaches the relief sample at all — that is the `_reliefVaries` early-out — so every
measurement in this project is untouched *by construction* rather than by a guard somebody has to
remember. The r6 control read 2601 / 325 / 3446 at 411 after it, as expected rather than as a
relief.

**The same defect is in the surface noise and is deliberately left there.** (0, 0) is a lattice
point of every octave of the surface fBm too, so the spawn column has been **exactly sea level in
every world this project has ever generated**. Fixing it means offsetting the surface sample, which
moves every landscape including the fixed profile seed's and would retire every recorded figure —
for a cosmetic detail no player can see. Recorded, not done.

**Watched fail**: with the offsets zeroed the new test reads `only 1 of 32 seeds start somewhere
different — if this is 1, the origin is sitting on the relief field's lattice point again`, which
is the failure naming its own cause.

The distance measurements that came with it, on the shipped shape: something hilly is **0.4–0.9 km**
from spawn and something flat **0.1–0.5 km**, so the variety was always reachable in a minute or
two of walking. It was only ever invisible from the doorstep.

Suite 1,760 → 1,761.

## 2026-09-23 — Relief is a floor, a ceiling and a rarity; the multiplier lasted a day

Matthew built the first world with regions in it and reported back: *"produced massive hills idk,
like I kind of want them somewhere but not everywhere, i may have to experiment in another project
with our noise function? Do we use like Perlin noise something like?"* — and then, on the
recommendation, *"go, build base/peak/rarity as recommended"*.

**The noise was never the problem.** It is Perlin — ours, `GradientNoise`: eight fixed 2D gradient
directions, the quintic fade, corners hashed through `Hash64`, `Fbm2D` summing octaves under a
*separate seed each* so octaves do not correlate their peaks. The problem was the mapping from the
relief field to an amplitude. v6 used `amplitude × (1 + variation × n)` — **a multiplier centred on
1**, so the typical place gets the typical amplitude and turning the relief up makes everywhere
bigger together. That is exactly the sentence he wrote.

**And it could not have been tuned out of it.** The sweep, over 1,024 two-hundred-metre windows
across 32 km: at `--relief=3 --reliefvary=0.5` the flattest window in the world still held 21.8 m
of relief and 89% of the map was hilly; **at variation 1 — the dial at its limit — the flattest was
still 15.0 m and 0% of the world was flat**, because Perlin rarely reaches its extremes so the
factor sits near 1 almost everywhere. A centred multiplier cannot produce a plain. A floor and a
ceiling cannot fail to.

**So: `ReliefBaseVoxels` and `ReliefRarity`, with `SurfaceAmplitudeVoxels` redefined as the
ceiling.** A column's amplitude is `base + (peak − base) × share(n)`, where `share` is a square
ramp above a threshold that rarity slides. **Equal floor and ceiling is uniform and skips the noise
sample entirely** — the record's default, every older world's reading, and what a `--profile` run
gets, which is what keeps the r6 control at 2601 / 325 / 3446 at 411 to the digit.

**The replacement has its own trap and the table is what caught it.** The obvious mask,
`max(0, n)^k`, reads "0% hilly" at k ≥ 2 — and that is not mountains being rare, it is mountains
*never occurring*, because 2D gradient noise spans about ±0.7 and cubing puts the threshold outside
the field's own range. By eye it is a plausible rarity setting. `ReliefLowestSample` and
`ReliefReachableSample` are calibrated against the field's real reach, and
`TheRarestSettingStillLeavesTheSummitsReachable` is the test standing over it.

**The shipped shape is a measured row rather than an interpolated guess**: base 0.4×, peak 3×,
rarity 0.25 — 53% flat, 37% rolling, 10% hilly, tallest places 36 m. The rows either side are in
the sweep, so moving it is a lookup.

**Header v7, and it is the one exception to "additive" this file has ever taken.** v6 lived for a
day; a v6 header is read by keeping its stored amplitude as the ceiling and taking `A(1 − v)` — the
flattest it could ever have produced — as the floor, so **a v6 world of even lumpiness comes back
bit-identical**, which is every world anyone was playing, and only the half-dozen scratch worlds
made while settling the shape change distribution. Written down in `OldestVersion` as grandfathered
rather than as a precedent. The reflection test that counts the record's properties fired for the
second time in one day, both times before the fields had a reader.

**Two defects, and neither could have been caught where it was made.** The v6 migration fixture cut
four bytes at offset 53, which removes the *floor* and leaves the rarity where the old variation
was — so the migration read as "a world that never used the feature" and the test passed for the
wrong reason until the expected value was wrong. And `WithRelief` read the amplitude off the
settings it was given while being called twice per created world, so `--relief=4 --reliefbase=0.2`
built `38.4..768` instead of `9.6..192`: **the multipliers applied twice, and no test in the suite
could have seen it because none of them goes through `Main`.** The headless wire check is what
found it, which is the M5c-2 lesson again — every layer tested, the wire between them not.

**Cost, measured headless at r6, shaped against uniform in one session**: the fill's derive +2.5%
and all-settled 4.03 → 4.05 s, invisible end to end; the box-difference sweep, which is
`SkyColumn.Seed`'s 1,024 surface evaluations a column, goes **`viewer ms` mean 6.53 → 7.82, p50
6.49 → 7.80** — about 1.3 ms against a 16.7 ms frame. Named lever, not built: the amplitude is
near-constant over 2 km and could ride a coarse lattice the way cave noise already does.

The wire, verbatim: a new world prints `relief 19.2..144 voxel(s), mountains 25% rare`;
`--relief=4 --reliefbase=0.2 --reliefrare=0.6` prints `9.6..192 voxel(s), mountains 60% rare`;
reopening it with `--relief=9` warns and keeps what the header holds; `--reliefbase=2 --relief=1`
warns once and builds a uniform world; and `--relief=lots`, `--reliefbase=-1`, `--reliefrare=9` are
each refused out loud.

Suite 1,749 → 1,760.

## 2026-09-23 — A world has regions, and how mountainous it is is a flag

Matthew, after the measurement above: *"build 1, and 2 as recommended"* — a scaling knob for the
world's highs and lows, and the regional variation that makes two worlds feel like different
places rather than the same place reshuffled.

**Half of it needed no design at all.** `SurfaceAmplitudeVoxels` has been one of the header's
fields since M6a, so it is already per-world and already persisted; what was missing was a way to
*ask* for it. `--relief=<x>` multiplies it and is resolved to an amplitude in voxels at creation,
so the world carries a number rather than a multiplier and reopens with no flag at all. It follows
`--seed=`'s rule exactly — new worlds only, refused out loud when mistyped, warned and ignored on a
world that exists — and for `--cavestep`'s reason: an unedited chunk regenerates from the header,
so honouring a relief flag on an existing world would rebuild the landscape *around* the chunks it
has saved and leave the mine hanging in it.

**The other half is the fourteenth worldgen field and header v6.** `ReliefVariation` multiplies the
amplitude per column from a second noise field at `ReliefFrequencyRatio` times the surface's own
wavelength, so a world has plains in one place and highlands in another. One octave, because a
region is not a place to put more hills; the sample is clamped before use, because `Sample2D` is
documented as only *roughly* in [-1, 1] and a negative factor does not read as flat — it mirrors
the surface, valley for hill, with a cliff along the join.

**The ratio was 8 and the measurement said no.** That put a region at 500 m — the same size as the
watershed window — and the roughest place in a world came out 2.7× the calmest, which reads as one
landscape with noisy edges rather than as somewhere to walk to. **The first version of the test was
wrong in the same breath and in the opposite direction**: it fixed its windows at 128 m over a 1 km
span, so every window straddled a peak and a trough of a 500 m field and the sample could not have
seen the effect whatever the ratio was. Both are fixed by the same realisation — a window has to be
small against a region and the span has to cover several of them — and the test derives its window,
step and span from the constant now, so it states the property rather than a number. At 32 a region
is 2 km, four times the watershed window, and the test passes at over 4×.

**The default is 0 and that is a measurement decision, not a taste one.** Every recorded figure in
this repo is a statement about the landscape the defaults produce, so a non-zero record default
would have moved the ground under all of them with the suite green. The neutral value is what the
record ships, what an old world reads back, and what a `--profile` run gets; the shipped 0.5 is
applied in exactly one place — the `header is null` branch, beside the seed draw, under the same
`_profiler is null` guard. **Verified rather than argued: the r6 control reads 2601 / 325 / 3446 at
411 to the digit with regions shipped.**

**v6 is the first bump that grows a section in the middle rather than appending one to the end**,
and all four earlier migration tests went red the moment the field was added. They were right to:
each builds a payload with today's writer and relabels it as an older version, which under every
previous bump was a faithful old header and now is a v4 payload with four bytes of float wedged in
front of its material table. `SettingsBytesFor(version)` is the reader's half and
`WithoutReliefVariation` the tests'. The reflection test that counts the record's properties fired
before the field had a reader, which is the whole of what it is for — the guard M6a wrote and
nobody had ever seen work.

**Cost, measured headless at r6, `--reliefvary=0.5` against `0`.** The fill's derive 1,680 → 1,722
ms (+2.5%) and all-settled 4.03 → 4.05 s, so end to end it is not visible. The price is where M6d-2
said it would be — the box-difference sweep, which is `SkyColumn.Seed`'s 1,024 surface evaluations
per column: **`viewer ms` mean 3.85 → 4.37, p50 3.37 → 4.26**, half a millisecond against a 16.7 ms
frame. Affordable, and stated rather than hidden. **Named lever, not built**: the relief factor is
constant over 2 km, so it could ride a coarse lattice and be interpolated exactly the way cave noise
already is, which would take it to nothing.

The wire, headless and verbatim: a new world prints `relief 48 voxel(s) varying 50% by region`;
`--relief=2 --reliefvary=0.25` prints `96 voxel(s) varying 25%`; reopening that world with
`--relief=3` warns and keeps 96 at 25%, read back out of its own header through SQLite; and
`--relief=lots` and `--reliefvary=7` are each refused out loud rather than falling through to
"unknown flag", which is `--seed=`'s rule and its reason — from inside, one landscape looks much
like another.

Suite 1,738 → 1,749.

## 2026-09-23 — What a change of terrain shape costs, measured: eight tests, one fixture

Matthew, thinking about a scaling knob for the world's highs and lows and about inserting
artifacts: *"how much am I going to break in the way of unit tests?"* Measured rather than
reasoned about — the defaults moved hard (sea level 0 → 24, amplitude 48 → 140, frequency
0.004 → 0.0013, four octaves → six), the suite run, the change reverted.

**Eight of 1,735, and every one of them the same fixture.** Five `LightPipelineTests`, one
`ChunkCacheLightTests`, one `PersistenceTests`, one `FluidPersistenceTests` — all four suites
run on `PipelineHarness`, whose generator pinned `Seed`, `SurfaceOctaves` and `CavesEnabled`
and left amplitude, frequency and sea level to the record's defaults. Their fixtures place a
lamp at a literal voxel; move the ground and the lamp is inside it. The failures read
`fixture: the lamp needs air around it to light anything`, which is the fixture saying so.

**What survived is the more useful half.** Every hydrology, machine, fluid, portal, enclosure
and collapse fixture runs on a synthetic `ISurfaceHeights` — `SampleGrid`, `AnalyticSurface`,
`LightTestWorld` — and the sixteen sites that do build a real `WorldGenerator` state all their
settings as literals. `WorldGeneratorTests` is entirely property-shaped: seam agreement, order
independence, lattice exactness. Nothing in this repo asserts a height at a coordinate.

**So the fix was three lines, and the interesting part is what those three lines cost.** The
harness now states its shape. Re-run with the same aggressive change: **eight failures → zero.**
But pinning every fixture means *nothing anywhere* would notice the shipped world becoming a
plain or losing its caves — the immunity is bought, and it has to be paid for. Hence
`TheShippedDefaultsMakeAWorldYouCanStandOnAndDigInto`, the one test that reads the defaults
rather than stating its terrain: three seeds, bands rather than numbers, asserting the three
things that make a world playable instead of a parameter set — relief of at least 8 voxels over
512 m, a non-uniform chunk at the surface, and 0.2%–30% cave void in the 64 m under the cave
margin. **Watched fail**: amplitude 0.4 gives `0 voxels of relief over 512 m, heights 24..24` on
all three seeds and fires nothing else, which is the pinned harness being correctly indifferent.

**Its first version was degenerate and the tall-and-lumpy arm is what said so.** The cave probe
sampled a 128 m square and read 0.16% on one seed — not a world without caves, but one hillside
whose field sat under the threshold. A share is a claim about a world; it is sampled over a
kilometre now. The lesson is the familiar one in a new costume: the fixture was too small a
sample to mean what its assertion said.

**The real cost of a shape change is not the tests.** `Main` takes everything but the seed from
the defaults, and `--profile` pins the fixed seed, so the r6 control, the keystone's 18,718 at
risk and *"the first forty seconds of the profile seed are dry"* are statements about *this*
landscape. Moving the defaults retires all of them with the suite green — the same hazard the
`--seed=` work was written for, one field along. A world already on disk keeps its old shape,
because the header carries all thirteen fields.

**And for artifacts, the bill is where they are placed, not what they break.** Inside
`GenerateTerrain` costs nothing: an artifact lattice sampled per chunk the way caves are lets a
structure larger than 8 m be computed independently by every chunk it touches, with no neighbour
peek, and `GenerationOrderDoesNotChangeTheResult` and `AdjacentChunksAgreeAcrossTheSeam` stand
over it. `ApplyFeatures` costs one test by design (`FeaturesStageIsAHookAndChangesNothingYet`)
**and cashes the revisit trigger recorded at `ChunkPipeline.AdvanceLight`** — light derives at
`Terrain`, so anything written at `Features` is a voxel light has already been derived against,
and it has to route through the relight path the way `SetVoxel` does, plus a lock over the
3 × 3 × 3 if it writes into neighbours. A new `WorldGenSettings` field costs one test by
construction (`TheSettingsLayoutCoversEveryPropertyOnTheRecord`, 13 → 14), `SettingsBytes`, the
writer and reader, and a header bump to v6 — all of it avoidable by deriving an artifact
sub-seed from `Settings.Seed` the way `_caveSeed` does.

Suite 1,735 → 1,738.

## 2026-09-23 — A new world is a new landscape, and the seed is on the screen

Matthew, after asking whether the world a `--world=` name creates is one of mine: every world
this project has ever made was created with the same constant, `0x4D494E455243` — ASCII for
`MINERC`, a leftover from the old name — so a *fresh* world was a reset rather than a new place.
His ask: `--seed=`, random by default, and the seed shown on screen for a while after launch.

**The hazard was the default, not the flag.** Every recorded figure in this repo is a statement
about one landscape — the r6 control's 2601 / 325 / 3446 at 411, the keystone's 18,718 at risk,
*"the first forty seconds of the profile seed are dry"* — and a random seed applied everywhere
would have retired all of them without a single test going red. **The rule: a measurement keeps
the constant.** The draw happens in exactly one place, the `header is null` branch of
`OpenWorld`, and only when no `--seed=` was given and `_profiler is null`; a run with no world
file never reaches that branch and so keeps the constant too. `--seed=` still wins under
`--profile`, so a measurement on other terrain can be asked for — it just has to be asked for.
Verified rather than argued: `--profile --world=<new>` reads `seed 0x4D494E455243`, and the r6
control reads 2601 / 325 / 3446 at 411 to the digit.

**Nine digits, not sixty-four bits.** A seed is only worth having if it can be read off the
screen and typed back in, so the draw is `[1, 10^9)`; splitmix64 decorrelates a small number as
happily as a large one, and a billion landscapes is not the constraint. The log line carries
both forms — `seed 0x292EC410 (--seed=690930704 builds this landscape again)` — because the hex
is what every earlier line printed and the decimal is what you type.

**Ignored on an existing world, with a word.** An unedited chunk is regenerated rather than
stored, so honouring a seed on an opened world would rebuild the terrain *around* its saved
chunks: the `--cavestep` rule, its reason and its warning, a second time. And a *mistyped* seed
is refused out loud rather than falling through to `unknown flag`, because the quiet version
hands you a random world and the two are indistinguishable from inside one.

**The banner is the half headless cannot check, and it took a screenshot to believe.** Upper
right, the world's name and `--seed=<n>`, plus one line for a world that is new; driven off the
frame delta `Hud.Refresh` already takes rather than a tick count, which is what his own second
message asked for once he saw what a per-tick hook would cost. Measured at seven settle times:
full through ~8.5 s, 15% at 11 s, gone by 12.5 s. **The intermediate reading looked like a
broken fade and was not** — at 9 s the banner is still at 0.89 alpha, because the clock starts
when the HUD is built ~1.5 s in, and one screenshot at 20 s (gone) plus four more between
turned an apparent defect into an offset. Eyeballing two screenshots said "identical"; sampling
the pixels said 565 against 565, which is what made it worth chasing rather than shrugging at.

**Also:** a world name may contain spaces, provided the whole flag is quoted
(`start.cmd "--world=Deep Mine"`) — `%*` forwards the quotes and Windows hands the game one
argument; unquoted it arrives as four and the run says so. Checked through a `cmd` stub and a
create/reopen round trip.

## 2026-09-23 — The undo is played, and *disallow* is not *silently empty*

First press, his words: **"Ctrl z feels good, disallow if something falls yes"**. UNDO-PLAN's
decision 4 — a fall clears the stack — is settled by play rather than by argument, and the
Ctrl+Z bind and the three-step depth go with it.

**One thing his wording changed, and it is the difference between two words.** The build
cleared the stack and printed why *at the moment of the fall*; a press afterwards read
`nothing to undo`. That is *silently empty*, and the fall's own line has scrolled past while
you are running out from under it. *Disallow* implies being told, so `FellSinceLastEdit`
carries the reason until the next journalled write clears it, and the press now reads `nothing
to undo: the roof came down since your last edit, and rubble cannot be put back`. One test
asserts both halves in sequence — the fall's message, then an ordinary `nothing to undo` after
one more edit. Suite unchanged at 1,735; the headless fall oracle prints both lines in order.

## 2026-09-22 (evening, later) — The three-step undo, built

Planned and built the same session, on *"Build it please Claude"*. Suite 1,719 → 1,735, ten
break-recipes and ten caught, r6 and the a-3 oracle to the digit. Read "Built" in
[docs/UNDO-PLAN.md](docs/UNDO-PLAN.md). Five things worth keeping:

- **The plan put the journal one level too high.** Its decision 1 threaded a fourth
  collaborator through seventeen verb signatures; the code offered two hooks instead —
  `ChunkPipeline.SetVoxel` is the single write and already reads the previous material for its
  own early-out, and `MachineSet` owns every row change. No verb signature moved, and a shape
  that forgets to journal cannot be written.
- **A step is a frame, not a click**, because a click's writing is not all in the click: the
  wet fill defers to the boundary, the dismantle lands at the machine drain, the chunk fill is
  queued. `EndStep()` after `DrainMachines()` catches all three.
- **The battery's catch was the undo journalling its own writes** — the press after an undo
  redid the edit, and three steps bounced between two states. Two tests failed on it, both on
  the whole-world oracle; a counter-based assertion would have passed. `Undo` turns recording
  off around its own writes, which is *no redo* falling out for free.
- **Two edges that would have shipped as defects, both found by reading rather than by a
  test.** `MachineSet.Restore` adds a row per stored machine, so a world opened with 141 of
  them would have handed the player an undo whose first press deleted one — the journal is
  attached after the restore. And the collapse sweep writes through `SetVoxel`, so the fall's
  own rubble landed in a step and the clear reported it as the player's.
- **The memory is four times the estimate and still small**: the dedupe wants a dictionary per
  chunk, so an excavator bite is ~800 KB and three of them read `94,112 voxel(s) held` — about
  2.5 MB at the worst case, nothing at rest. `EditHistory.Recording` is the off switch and has
  no flag; named rather than built.

## 2026-09-22 (evening) — A three-step undo, planned

His ask mid-play, after the quantum excavator took most of a world: *"how hard to implement 3
step undo Claude? :-{D Just plan um if its like too difficult i might skip it, ignoring water"*.
[docs/UNDO-PLAN.md](docs/UNDO-PLAN.md) — six facts, ten decisions, all recommended, one session,
not built. Four things worth keeping:

- **It is small for a reason that is five milestones old.** Light, support, the fluid surface,
  the mesh, the sky columns and the collider are all derived from the voxels and repair
  themselves from `ChunkPipeline.SetVoxel`, so an undo that writes through it is a player
  writing voxels by hand. What must be reversed is the voxels, the inventory and the machine
  rows, and nothing else.
- **The journal is free at the point of the write.** `Carve.Take` has read the material before
  it writes air and `Place.Put` has read the voxel before it fills it, and both already take
  three optional collaborators — so `IEditJournal` is a fourth parameter of a shape that is
  already threaded through every shape, with no second copy of the geometry.
- **The two traps are gravity and unloading, not water.** A fall mints rubble, so bite → roof
  comes down → undo would restore the roof *and* leave the rubble: matter from nothing. A
  chunk that leaves reloads its edited state from the store, so its journal entries can
  neither be applied nor deferred. Both are answered by clearing the stack, printed — honest
  at three steps, which is seconds of play. *Ignoring water* is the cheap half: M9d's
  displacing path already exists, and the water simply is not undone.
- **Two rules that would be exploits if taken the other way**: an undo refunds no joules (or
  bite-undo-bite is free energy), and a step whose credit has since been spent is refused
  whole rather than clamped (clamping mints or destroys volume, and this game's oracles are
  exact totals).

Also read off his session as it ran, for the play: `enclosed 82,543 kept / 1,052 closed` on the
walled pool — the enclosure holds a 450 kL pour with `handed 0` from it — and the pumps at
236,594 L against 1.9 ML drawn into the mine, `0 unpowered`, `45,846 no water`: the pumps are
not where the water is, which is recipe 1's finding rather than a defect.

## 2026-09-22 — The surface's previous-readers rule reads what each build read, and rain lands on the player's material

Two things, both from his fresh world's log. **The settled-state read the surface change owed**
(TODO under M10d) came off a small world at rest — 2.3 ML in 36 panels, 965 active, 0 `ERROR`
lines, `live 214 MiB` flat over 3,600 ticks, install 8 ms mean — and read `last rebuild 28
panel(s) (own 2, previous 26)`: two panels moving a tick (the pump's mound) and twenty-six
rebuilt because the geometric fifteen a moved previous surface *could* reach were all dirtied.
The exact rule is what each build actually read: `PanelRecord.ReadPrevious` records every panel
whose previous surface the build looked up — its own and the two in its column always, a sideways
neighbour's and theirs above and below only where a side or a fall search reached into them —
and a moved surface dirties only the readers that recorded it (`ReadAll` for a build that ran
with no previous surface anywhere, which the first pass is). Exact by the same argument as the
rest of the rule: the lookups a build performs depend on inputs that are dirty for their own
reasons if they changed, so a panel that never read R last time would not read it now. The oracle
held unchanged; the lake-band test's neighbours went 3 → 1 rebuilt, because they draw no side
against the panel whose tops went and so never read it; the bench's flood at rest 12 → 6 of 16.

**The rain rule** is its own entries in M8-PLAN (the pass and the built section) and TODO: his
clay pond was never leaking, rain was not landing in it, and now a column whose top is above its
seed gets its rain on that top, owed by the basin under it. Suite 1,713.

**And a leak that was not one — *"Is water falling through my roof? Like there is a gap"*.** The
2% random droplets spawn at the top row of the drawn vertical box and checked only that the row
was not underground; with the adaptive radius the box is one ring while he moves, its top row
8–16 m above his chunk, which can be *under* a roof — so a droplet spawned inside the building
and fell from the ceiling. A drop now spawns only where nothing solid stands above its row in
that column (the sky column's open height, which counts a roof as it counts the ground), and the
ones it skips under a roof are counted on both rained terms (`skipped of which N under a roof`).
Placed rain never had this: its cell lands above the column's topmost solid, or waits.

## 2026-09-21 (afternoon) — The Tier B surface is per panel, rebuilt only where something moved

*"the Tier B surface install, i'm playtesting now thanks Claude"* — the lever recorded at
M8b-4b with the crash log's number (40 MiB a rebuild, 100+ ms, four times a second on a 50 ML
world), built while he played, so everything here is Core, the bench and a Game build compiled
into the scratchpad; the Game binary he is running is untouched and **the played-world figure is
owed** (TODO under M10d — the windowed A/B against `--fluidsurface=full` on a copy of the flooded
world). What it was: `FluidSurfaceMesher.Build` walked every held panel every tick and handed back
one mesh for the whole wet surface, and `FluidSurface.Install` marshalled all of it into one
`ArrayMesh` — whether or not anything had moved, which on a world of resting lakes is nearly
nothing, and the garbage the crash log's managed heap was climbing on.

**The mesh is one `ArrayMesh` an instance per wet panel now, and `FluidSurfaceMesher.Update`
hands back only the panels it rebuilt and the ones that emptied.** A panel is rebuilt when
something its build reads has moved, and nothing else:

- **its own cells** — `FluidGrid` gives every panel a grid-wide stamp, moved by `Write` on a
  change of value and by `Touch`; `Disturb` touches the panel of every held cell it wakes (rock
  placed beside resting water: the visit finds nothing to move and writes nothing, and the face
  against the new rock would otherwise stay), `ChunkArrived` touches the chunk and the neighbours
  with water on its faces;
- **a face neighbour's**, or a neighbour released — the sides at the shared face are drawn from
  whichever cell holds more, and the cell above the top layer decides a top;
- **the column below it**, up to `ColumnReach` (8) panels — the depth attribute is the wet cells
  under a vertex carried across panel floors, so each record keeps the carry leaving its top
  layer and a change at the bottom of a flooded shaft reaches the top's colour exactly;
- **the lake band over its column** — `IFluidTerrain.LakeStamp`, the `ColumnBand`'s build count
  through `LakeBoundedTerrain`: a lake draining off bed water exposes a top no cell write
  announces;
- **a previous surface it reads changed at the last build** — its own, so a panel whose water
  moved is built once more with its previous equal to its current and the `tick_phase` lerp
  settles instead of replaying at every install; or a neighbour's, because a side's bottom edge
  and a fallen surface look up where the water stood in the panels beside and above — and the
  fall search reads a sideways neighbour's *upper* panel, a diagonal dependency read off the code
  and not guessable. A removed panel's previous stays through the pass that removes it (a surface
  that fell out of the panel lerps down from where it was) and goes after, which rebuilds its
  readers once more.

**The settle rule took three tries, and the two wrong ones are in the class remarks.** *A vertex
with its previous different from its current* is never satisfied by a side against a dry cell
under a surface — its previous is a lookup that never returns its current — so a stepped lake
rebuilt forever. *The arrays differ from the build before* (a per-panel hash) settles, but the
settle build itself differs from the build before it in its previous-height attributes alone, so
every change built twice. The right rule is about the *input* — the drawn surface compared entry
for entry at the swap — and never builds twice for one change. **Dirty by the inputs a build
reads, never by what its output did.**

**The oracle is the other arm**: `ForceFull` is the pre-2026-09-21 mesher, and a test holds the
two equal array for array across 220 ticks of a relay pour into one pit while a second pit rests
under everything the run does to it — rock over the sheet, a lake band built and dropped, a cell
drained at the bottom of a shaft through three panels, a panel drained and one evicted — with the
incremental arm skipping over 600 panel builds and every equality exact; the clauses have a test
each, the two wires from the simulation too. **Two fixtures were wrong first**: the pour alone
kept every panel jittering for the whole run, so the arms agreed by doing the same work (the
second pit is the skip), and the disturb wire's sheet was put down with `Add` and was still
moving. Suite 1,690 → 1,702. `Build` is kept for the tests and the bench as the concatenation
of retained panel meshes, in chunk order, so `TheSameGridBuildsTheSameArrays` still holds.

**The bench (`--surface`, Release, 1.07× the reference):**

```
                                  full build           update (rebuilt / held, KiB, ms)
lake at rest, 144 panels          837 KiB   57.5 ms        0 / 144       0     0.09
lake, two levels, a step          563 KiB   27.4 ms        0 / 144       0     0.07
flood of 10,000 L at tick 5       233 KiB    1.6 ms        8 / 8       239     1.33
flood of 10,000 L at tick 100     675 KiB    1.1 ms        4 / 4       688     1.02
roof open, 2x2x2 block, tick 20 4,154 KiB   16.5 ms       27 / 27   4,156    14.21
```

A lake at rest costs nothing; a flood in progress costs what it did, because every panel of it
moves; the update's own overhead is under the noise. **What the game pays is the install of the
update's KiB**, per panel, and each panel's instance carries its own bounds, so the renderer culls
water behind the player that one mesh drew whole. `--fluidsurface=full` is the control. The
`M8b:` line's `surface` term prints `over N panel(s)`, `last rebuild N panel(s) (own, new,
neighbour, column, lake, previous; KiB) and N freed`, and `install mean / max over N rebuild(s)`;
the profile's `fluidsurf` line the same with panels and KiB a rebuild. No recorded headless
oracle can move — headless builds no surface — and the r6 control is re-run once the Game build
can land.

## 2026-09-21 (small hours) — The first play ran out of memory: the enclosure's cache was unbounded

*"um did I run out of memory?"* — the process did: four `ERROR: Parameter "mem" is null` from
`alloc_static`, Godot's allocator refusing inside `FluidSurface.Install`'s `AddSurfaceFromArrays`,
after 1,752 ticks on `default` (84 pumps, 121 outlets, 50 ML of Tier B, the surface mesh at 40 MiB
a rebuild). The log had no memory figure, so the periodic `M2c:` line prints one now — `memory
N MiB static, N MiB managed, N MiB working set, gen2 N` — and the first suspect was the Godot
arrays every mesh install leaves to the finaliser, disposed now at all four sites (`using var`).
**Measured windowed on a copy of the retired flooded world, 60 s standing, `--fluidnear=2
--fluidjob=1`: the control's working set climbed 862 → 1,100 MiB, the dispose arm's 820 →
1,196 — the same slope, ~4–6 MiB/s, and the *managed* heap was the half climbing.** Not the
arrays. The enclosure's line on the crash log read `enclosed 19,060 kept, 5,884 flood(s) / 62
closed` — **5,884 cached regions, one per level a lake's top passed through under rain and per
level the surface sweep asked at, and nothing but an edit ever dropped one; at ~16k dictionary
entries and ~44 B each, over 4 GB.** Two fixes, both measured:

- **A cap** — the oldest regions evicted silently past it (`Evicted`, never `Changed`: nothing
  in the world moved, and telling the ceiling would rebuild bands that would flood again). At
  512k cells the working set went flat at ~1.45 GB **and the flooded world thrashed**: 15,195
  floods in 120 s, ~200 a second, because a lake needs a region every 32 m of its footprint at
  every level it stands at and the cap held thirty.
- **A region is a bitset over its box** — `BitArray` of 129², 2 KB, indexed by (chunk column,
  level) with a `Covers` test, in place of 16k dictionary entries — and the cap is
  `MaxRegions` 4,096 (~12 MB, an estimate). **120 s windowed: working set flat at ~1.06 GB from
  40 s on, managed ~280 MiB, 81 floods, 64 regions.** The wall's own cells are cleared from the
  bits so a wall column is never answered by a region.

Suite 1,689 → 1,690; r6 to the digit; the courtyard oracle unchanged (`handed 0 L`, six
closed). **Two lessons.** A cache keyed by what was *asked* grows with the asking, and the
surface sweep asks four times a second at whatever level the rain has moved the lake to — bound
every cache by what it holds, not by what it was told; and *count the log's `ERROR` lines* was
the right first move again, then the term that was new that day. The probe world `probe-mem`
is deleted; Matthew's `default` has whatever the last autosave wrote (38 session saves on the
line) — the crash was in a mesh install, after the boundary, so the world file is whole.

## 2026-09-20 (night) — The courtyard: the player's material encloses, nature's does not

*"1 and 3 as recommended"* — this is 1, arm B, built after the fill's budget. **`Enclosure`** in
`Overburden.Core/Fluid/`: whether a column is walled off from the outside at a level, asked by
the three readers Tier A has for a wall it cannot see. A 4-neighbour flood over the voxel columns
at one level from the column asked about; the only obstacle is the player's material; open at the
bound (`BoundVoxels` 64, 16 m — an estimate; an enclosure wider than 32 m reads as open) or at an
unloaded voxel; enclosed otherwise. Cached per (x, z, level) with the flood's whole visited set
sharing one answer, indexed by the chunk columns its cells *and its walls* stand in and the
columns it reached as unloaded, and dropped by the pipeline's three hooks — an edit at its level,
a chunk with edits arriving or leaving, an arrival of a column it could not see past. And **a
column with no edited chunk within the bound is answered open with no flood and no cache**: no
edits, no walls, nothing to enclose — the r6 control's arm, every oracle that places nothing.

- **The rule the pass did not have: a wall claims its footing.** The pass's obstacle was *a solid
  voxel above its column's seed*, natural rock walked through so a pit's rim never encloses. Built
  that way, the headless courtyard on the spawn's slope handed 19,991 of 20,000 L: at every level
  below the uphill wall's ground, that wall's columns are natural rock (their seed is above the
  level) and the flood walked through them and out to the bound. So natural rock carrying a placed
  voxel at its seed + 1 is an obstacle at every level below it — one read a rock column, the first
  voxel above the ground, because a brush lands on the lattice and fills every air voxel of its
  cell. A footing edit drops every cached level below it. A pit's rim with nothing on it is still
  walked through; three walls and a hillside still read as open, and the fourth wall may stand on
  the hill. **Both rules leave a courtyard on a slope open below its uphill *ground* if that
  ground is inside the walls** — dig it level or floor it; a dug pit's water was never on the
  plane and was never handed.
- **The readers.** `SurfaceHandoff`: a rested cell on the plane whose column is enclosed at the
  cell's own level is left standing (`EnclosedKept`, counted per pass it was listed — a pool still
  levelling counts its cells each rest). `LakeCeiling`: a column enclosed at the lake's top has no
  band, asked only where the level would otherwise put it in the lake; the enclosure's `Changed`
  event (column, level range) marks a band dirty when one of its sample tops is in the range —
  `AnyTopIn`, so a bite at the bottom of a mine under a lake rebuilds nothing — and the next
  refresh rebuilds it past `SameTops` (`RebuiltForEnclosure`); a wall taken down grows the band
  back, wakes the pool as submerged, and the lake takes it. `WaterSurface`: an enclosed sample at
  the lake's level draws no plane and the ring never dilates into one (`EnclosedSamples`).
- **Wire.** `Main` builds it before the ceiling over the streamer as the world and the columns'
  seed; the three hooks feed it beside the tracker's; `--enclosure=0` is the control (printed);
  `--courtyard=<m>` / `--courtyardwalls=<m>` build a ground-following ring of stone through the
  pipeline's edit path before the relay's ball lands inside it — the provocation, because `--place`
  builds a column and cannot ring anything. The `M8b:` line, the profile's `enclosure` and
  `surface` lines carry the terms.
- **Oracle.** `--profile --speed=0 --courtyard=8 --injectlitres=20000 --measure=25`: `handed 0 L`,
  `6 flood(s), 6 closed` (one region a level of the slope's steps, 3,456 cells cached, 19,982
  hits), the pool at rest by tick ~85 with every litre inside; `--enclosure=0`: `handed 20,000 L`
  over 3,447 hand-offs. r6 to the digit (`0 flood(s)` — quiet). a-3 to the digit — and its
  `enclosure` line reads `4 flood(s), 0 closed, 66,484 cell(s) visited`: the outlet body and the
  breach's chunks make the lake's columns non-quiet, so the ceiling's rebuild floods four open
  regions once and caches them — the open answer's price, ~16k reads a region, stated.
- **Tests.** `EnclosureTests` (fourteen: four walls and three; the hill; the footing; per level;
  the bound both sides; unloaded-then-arrived with no edits flips the answer; an arrival that
  never reached it drops nothing; quiet; the pre-check's reach; a start that is not air; a wall in
  the next chunk column drops the region; an edit at another level does not; the cache; a forget),
  the courtyard twins in `SurfaceHandoffTests` (kept, then handed when a wall comes down; a natural
  pit still handed with the enclosure on) and `LakeCeilingTests` (no band, kept, the lake
  untouched; the wall down, band back, handed whole; the control arm reaches the guarded

## 2026-09-20 (small hours) — A fluid row that named an empty awake cell holed a chunk for good

*"i think i may have upset the chunk loader or the godot sync function in the 2nd screenshot"* —
black blobs on a Tier B sheet over grass, the compound's floor. **Count the `ERROR` lines first:
four, one line** — `Chunk job failed at Chunk(1, -1, -9): … Fluid panel blob … awake cell 4732
holds nothing; an awake cell is a held cell`, once per return to the chunk. The chain: the
blob's reader refused the row, the `LoadFluidJob` faulted, and a faulted chunk job is not
retried — *the chunk steps back, sits out of the work list and renders as a hole* (the
pipeline's own comment) — so the chunk under the sheet drew nothing and the unlit insides of its
neighbours showed through the water as black. Leaving and returning read the same row and
faulted again, four times.

**How the row got there.** Two writers listed a chunk's *paused* cells as awake without asking
whether they held anything — `TakeDirty` (the unview path) and the eviction's — where the
autosave's `TakeAllDirty` has filtered through `AwakeHeldCells` since M8b-4b. A visit never
pauses an empty cell (an empty visit sleeps before the loaded test), so the paused cell was held
when it was paused and drained after, while its chunk was away; the one drain I can name is the
hand-off taking from a cell the solve levelled on the worker's captured view (still loaded there)
after the live terrain had said the chunk left, and I have not proved it — the writers' invariant
is the fix either way. **Both ends**: the writers filter to held cells (`HeldIndices`), and the
reader drops an awake index that holds nothing and counts it rather than refusing the row
(`FluidPanelBlob.Read(…, out awakeDropped)`, the count on the `M6:` lines as `N awake index(es)
dropped for holding nothing`; the awake count's guard is the chunk's bound now, not the held
count, because a pre-fix row can name more awake cells than held). Dropping changes no water:
`Wake` refuses a cell that cannot hold and holds nothing. Two tests (the blob's refusal became
*dropped and counted*, the ascending rule still refused; a restored pre-fix row written back by
both writers listing only the held cell, read back with nothing dropped) and four recipes, four
caught. **His world's row, read through the new reader on a copy: 31 cells held, 18 awake
named, 2 dropped, 16 kept, 471.9 L restored** — the next open heals it, no file surgery.
Suite 1,660 → 1,661; the r6 control to the digit.

**And the world at 23:53, off the same log**: 34.3 ML moving in 2.25 M cells, 962k deferred,
64 pumps over 127 outlets (1.85 ML pumped, 168,817 `no water` — most intakes dry), worker wall
1,620 ms mean (max 6.2 s), 4,282 of 4,295 boundaries waited, the last pass seeded 66,364 cells
(30,861 from the carry) with the longest pass 3.1 s. The seeds are bounded now; what the solve
pays for is the sheets it *does* level on a 34 ML world fed and drained at 191 machines — the
M8b-3b "pass per boundary is O(sheet)" item proper, with this number, in TODO. *"she seems quite
happy to chug along"* — at half a tick a second, she is.

## 2026-09-19 (night, later) — The solve is seeded from what changed: a carried cell is offered once

*"go please Claude"*. The lever from the afternoon's finding, planned against `Sheets.cs` and
`NearField.cs` and built in one pass:

- **What the cost was.** `Pending` lists the far carry so a wholly far sheet is not invisible
  to the solve (slice 1's rule), and every seed is flooded three layers before the share can
  freeze its sheet — so 456k carried cells tiling the played world's resting sheets were 294k
  cells visited a pass to level twenty, the worker's 750 ms, the tick at 1.2 Hz.
- **The rule.** A carried cell is offered to the solve once, on the first solve after it enters
  the carry, and again only when it is woken again. `_queued` is a `Dictionary<VoxelPos, bool>`
  now — the offered bit a cell; `Wake` on a queued, offered cell clears it and lists the cell;
  `SolveSeeds()` is the pending list, the carry's unoffered tail and the re-woken list, both
  snapshotted so the cells the solve itself wakes go to the next one; `MarkCarryOffered()` after;
  admission takes the bit with the cell; a re-classification keeps the offered prefix (the
  survivors of the old prefix are a prefix of the new carry), so a viewer chunk change every
  second on foot does not re-offer the backlog. Sound because an unsettled pair needs a cell
  that moved and a move wakes both cells of every pair — what is not re-counted is the pairs the
  share already left alone, which is the share rule's own trade one pass further, with the
  quota's visits still the floor.
- **Measured on a copy of the retired world, the same run before and after** (`--profile
  --speed=0 --world=probe-solve --fluidjob=1 --fluidnear=2 --measure=30`): solve mean 92.78 →
  5.28 ms, worker wall 106.4 → 28.9 ms, settle cells visited 7.1 M → 399k over 60 passes, and
  more levelled rather than fewer — 229 → 276 sheets, 22,340 → 57,967 cells written, the
  backlog 32,736 → 14,962 at the end. The control's passes were frozen floods around 33k seeds;
  the seeded arm's are levels.
- **Tests and recipes.** Offered once and again on a re-wake — isolated through an enclosed
  carried cell *taken from* (an add into a full cell accepts nothing and wakes nothing, and a
  far cell woken since the last Begin is pending, not carried, so the fixture reads
  `DeferredCells`, new); the mark surviving a viewer move that keeps the cell far (the first
  fixture moved the viewer off the near tap and the quota came off — nothing deferred, nothing
  tested); a far sheet still levelled on its first offer. Five recipes, five caught, one only
  after the fixture stopped adding water to a full cell. Suite 1,657 → 1,660; the r6 control to
  the digit; every recorded oracle runs `--fluidnear=0`, where the carry is empty and the path
  is byte-for-byte the old one.

The `settle` term prints `last pass seeded N (M from the carry)`. The play check is the `M8b:`
line's `worker wall mean` and `boundary(ies) waited` under the same water — waited should stop

## 2026-09-19 (evening, last) — Rain drops Tier B cells: `--rainshare`, a drop owed to the sky

  `Weather.DepthNanometresOver` the basins are rained from is read over the drawn horizontal box
  (nanometres × square metres is microlitres, the accumulator's own arithmetic), `--rainshare=`
  percent of it accrues as whole 15,625 mL cells, and each cell picks a random column in the box
  and the top row of the drawn vertical box — skipped where the seed surface is above it (the
  player underground; rain under a roof) or the cell cannot hold. Put down at the boundary through
  the pour's path, the lake band covered first so a drop over a lake lands on its top and is
  handed. Two percent by default, an estimate: ~1 kL/s falls on a 96 m box at the heaviest scaled
  weather, so a drop a second or so; `0` is off and the arm every recorded figure was taken in.
- **A drop is rain, not water from nothing.** M8-PLAN's rule makes a *debug* source a reported
  term; this is a mechanic, so it comes out of the rain: `WaterSystem.DivertRain` owes each landed
  cell to the sky and `BasinRainfall` pays it in microlitres from the next rain before a litre
  reaches a basin — global rather than per basin, because rain is uniform over the window and a
  cell against megalitres is noise, and a per-basin debt would sit unpaid on a basin the drops
  favoured. The debt crosses a window move and the first window (unlike the sub-litre remainder,
  whose one stated cost is a rounding — a drop nobody paid for would be a cell of water invented).
  Four tests: the basins receive exactly a cell less than the same hour with nothing owed, to the
  microlitre; the hour-in-one-call oracle holds with a debt in it; a debt in a dry spell stays
  owed and the next rain pays it; the debt crosses the first window and a move with the paid total
  intact. Suite 1,652 → 1,656.
- **The lines.** `M8b:` — `injected … rained N L (D drop(s), S skipped)` and `+ rained` in the
  identity; `M7d:` and the profile's `water` — `rained into it as cells (N L still owed)`.
  Headless at `--clockscale=20` over 40 s: 642 drops, 10,031 L rained, 6,771 L handed back, owed
  paid to zero between reports, identities exact. The profile seed's first forty seconds are dry,
  so the wet-fill wire (`171 wet / 93 filled`) and the r6 control read as recorded.

## 2026-09-19 (night) — A fill into water displaces it: `FillWater`, the machine's rule on every shape

*"ok so I want the fill function to either absorb the water or displace it or remove it your
choice i do not mind which, it makes it impossible to build where there is even a slight amount
of water?"* — the first play that built in water, an hour after the quantum tiers landed. M9d's
answer was *refuse* (decision 3: a brush pushed into a flooded room has nowhere to displace to,
so displacing would be deleting with a nicer name); his log that session read `18 wet` and every
one of them a wall he could not put up.

**Displace**, because the rule already exists — M10a-2's `Place.MachineDisplacing` lifts a
cell's water, writes the body and returns the water bottom-up over the box around it, the rest
`displaced` — and generalising it keeps every identity exact. Remove would be the same thing with
all of it displaced; absorb has no unit to absorb into. Built:

- **`FillWater`** in Core beside `MachinePlacement`: handed to any shape, it turns `Put`'s wet
  refusal into a lift before the write, puts a refused write's water straight back into its
  voxel, and at the end of the shape returns what is in hand bottom-up over the shape's box grown
  by one brush cell (Y ascending, then x, then z — the level rises), the remainder to
  `DisplaceLifted`. The shape's own voxels are not skipped: a ramp leaves air in its cell and that
  air may take water back; a voxel just written is solid and `Return` refuses it through the
  terrain. `lifted == returned + displaced` by construction. Every shape — voxel, cube, slab, ramp,
  sphere, chunk — takes it as an optional last argument; without it the click's path is exactly
  M9d's.
- **`PlaceController.RunPendingWetFills`**: a click whose result has `Wet > 0` lands its dry part
  at once and queues the same shape with its wet count; the boundary runs it again behind the
  chunk fills' fresh `Publish`, asks the pack for the wet count only, and records only what
  landed (the dry part reads `Occupied` on the re-run and would inflate the session's count).
  The chunk fill at the boundary takes the water too. `Main.RunPendingFills` replaces
  `RunPendingChunkFills` at the boundary; a wet fill prints one `M9d:` line with its litres and
  the `M6c:` line's `wet` carries `(N filled displacing at the boundary: lifted / returned /
  displaced)`.
- **`PlaceDisplacingTests`** (+8): a cube into a pool lifts 16 cells and returns all of it around
  the cube; the return is bottom-up (the first cell is a full cell below); no water in hand still
  refuses; a ramp's own air takes the water back when rock is all around; a full box under a roof
  displaces the whole fill's worth; a refused write puts the water back where it was; every shape
  displaces the same voxel (the fixture had to move off the cell's corner — the 0.6 m sphere does
  not reach it); nothing wet moves nothing. Suite 1,638 → 1,646.
- **The wire**: `--place` from the first frame builds a column under the crosshair before any
  water arrives (M6d-2), so `--placeafter=<seconds>` holds the button off. A brush into a 200 kL
  pour at −60° reads `171 wet (93 filled displacing at the boundary: lifted 1,082.0 L, returned
  1,082.0 L, displaced 0.0 L)`; a chunk fill into it `28,543 placed … lifted 55,207.7 L, returned
  55,207.7 L`. The fill oracle and the r6 control are unchanged.

One thing the wire's run showed and the play will meet: `displaced 176 L` on the fluid line from
the *instant* brush — the click's dry writes into cells the published copy had not seen wet, M9d's
64-cell staleness bound. Now that a boundary path exists for every shape, the lever is a brush
that defers whole whenever its box is wet at all; in TODO under M9d, unbuilt.

## 2026-09-19 (later) — Q held runs the quantum miner; Alt's held repeat goes with the modifier map read back

*"Um so i've mashed up the modifier keys on this one can you examine and tell me what we have
there?"* The map, off the code: Shift and Ctrl touch movement only (sneak / descend, sprint / ×5),
and Alt means three things — precision on both buttons, crawl in fly, and the inverse of a debug
key (Alt+P fills the cells, Alt+R takes the water back). Two mash-ups fell out of holding two at
once: Ctrl+Alt in fly is 6 × 5 × 0.2 = exactly base speed, and **Alt on the cube arm re-enabled

**Q tapped puts the quantum miner on the mouse; Q held runs it.** Built the same session:

- **`TapOrHold`** (`Overburden.Game/Player/`, Godot-free like the controllers) — a press released
  under the threshold is a tap, past it a hold, and a hold never taps. The tap fires on
  *release*, because a toggle on the key-down edge cannot share the key with a hold without
  flipping the mode on every hold's way in; the toggle is up to 0.25 s late for it, an estimate,
  `--holdafter=` the sweep. E reuses it at M10g (tapped the screen, held the crank).
- **`MiningController.Running`** and `Quantum => Entangled || Running` — tool, reach, shape and
  cooldown read the union, so a hold from the pick swings the entangled tool at its reach and
  its cube and hands the pick back on release; the toggle is only about what a click does.
  `PlaceController.TakesCube` is the fill's own flag, so a held Q from the pick does not make the
  5 m brush edge-triggered on its way past.
- **`Main`** polls Q beside P, R and L (`UpdateQuantumKey`), fed every frame and acted on only
  while the mouse is captured — which covers the panel, whose focused field swallows the event
  but not the poll. `mining = running || (TakesCube ? leftPressed : leftDown)`, `precise =

  profile's own `mining = true` path with Alt as precision. The HUD reads `RUNNING (Q held)`,
  the mode lines gain `hold Q: run`, the pick's `Q: tap mode / hold run`.
- **`--holdq`** holds it for a run, past the profile's refusal by the flag's own hand. From the

## 2026-09-18 (evening) — A swapped-out pack keeps its charge: `CarriedPacks`, header v5, `stowed`

Play recipe step 6, answered by the play and by one sentence: the swap threw a 2,650.6 kJ pack
away — *"keep its charge as an item please"*. That reverses the ladder's decision 15 (*a second
pack in the inventory is a count with no charge*) and the one rule c-3 recorded as *"the only
rule under which a swap is exact"*. Built the same evening; three things worth keeping:

- **The count stays the truth and the charges annotate it.** `CarriedPacks` is a list of
  `(material, charge, channel)` beside the inventory's voxel count of the pack material — never
  a second count. An empty pack has no row (`Stow` keeps nothing for 0 J, so a pack swapped out
  empty loses its channel, stated as the cost), a right-click equips the fullest carried one,
  and the header refuses — at write and at read — a material whose charged rows outnumber its
  voxels: *"a count is the truth and cannot be exceeded"*. Header v5 appends a count and a
  `PackSave` row per entry after the equipped pack's section; a v4 world opens with none, which
  is true of it. The hotbar assignment folded into M10g that morning as "v5" is v6 — the version
  is a counter.
- **The swap was exact under `forfeited` and is exact under `stowed`, and the difference is one
  round trip.** `EquipPack` moves the outgoing pack's charge into `PackStowedMillijoules` (the
  identity's last term, renamed) and a stowed pack equipped again comes back through `initial`,
  the world file's path — two terms that cancel, asserted in the swap test's re-equip, the

- **The whole-litre floor was an identity against thirty-one tests.** Every offer was a budget or
  a box that happened to be whole, and every room sixteen cells or a rigged multiple. A box holding
  20,500 mL against a basin outlet, and a lake pump into a layer with 15,125 mL of room, are the
  fixture now; the recipe is caught by that test alone. Nineteen recipes, nineteen caught, once it
  was written.
- **The rate override is a seam and not a content change.** `--pump=<L/s>` on the game and
  `--pumprate` on the bench set `MachineTick.RateOverrideMillilitresPerSecond`, the shape
  `--seepscale` has over the JSON's permeability; a row's definition is the content's and the tick
  cannot change it. The pass wrote `--pump=<L/s>` as if the flag chose the pump; it chooses the sweep.
- **Headless, the seam closes on itself.** A lake drains through the portals into the shaft, the
  pump takes it from Tier B, the outlet pours it on the surface, the hand-off returns it to the
  basin: `drawn 1,000 == pumped 1,000 == emitted 1,000`, `handed 986`, every identity exact. With
  the outlet's chunk unloaded, `emitted 1,000 L into Tier A`, Tier B empty, `handed 0` — the litres
  never rested anywhere.
