## 2026-09-15 — M10a planned: hooks queue and frames write, `Lost == Carved`, and the lake is `InLake`

Matthew took the ladder whole — *"As recommended, lets do M10a's planning pass"* — so all
twenty-three decisions stand as written and M10a's own pass ran against the code, at the end of
M10-LADDER-PLAN. Six things the code said that neither M10-PLAN nor the ladder had, each of which
moved a decision:

- **An autosave is three store calls, not two.** Header, then `WriteBasins` in its own
  transaction, then the batch. The ladder counted two; the basins are a third, and the crash
  window between them already loses whatever the portal drain moved in the interval — unpriced,
  and a pump would add a second path across it in each direction. So the batch becomes a record
  (`WorldBatch`) carrying an optional session — machines, basins, header — in one transaction,
  and `SaveAll(SessionSnapshot?)` is what the autosave and the quit call. `Dispose` saves too, as
  the backstop, and carries none.
- **The plans put writes inside two hooks.** `onVoxelsReady` fires inside `Complete` before the
  neighbour push (the M2c-2 stall if it throws; mid-tick under `--fluidjob=1`), and M10-PLAN
  decision 4 had the reconcile rewriting 64 voxels there and the dismantle "at once after a
  swing" from `onVoxelChanged`. Neither hook writes now: the arrival hook queues the chunk if the
  set has rows in it or the palette may hold a machine material (`VoxelChunk.MayContain`, public,
  an over-approximation because `Compact` never runs); the edit hook bumps a row's `Lost`; a
  per-frame drain does the reconcile and the dismantle through `SetVoxel` where the brush writes.
- **A fall and a swing write the same thing into a body**, so the ladder's *credited unless any of
  its 64 is rubble* is right for a short fall and wrong for a long one, and a body falls *partly*
  (the at-risk set is per voxel, a fall is a column run). What distinguishes them is who credited:
  `Carve.Take` credits per voxel and the fall credits nothing. So `Carve` tells the set what it
  took through an optional `IMachineBodies`, and at the drain `Lost == Carved` dismantles with the
  remainder credited while `Lost > Carved` destroys without — whole or half, however far the
  rubble went, and the voxels the player mined first are theirs. The reconcile follows the same
  logic without counters, because an unload never writes a partial body from a swing: none
  present → rebuilt (or credited, if the cell regenerated as rock); some present → destroyed;
  an orphan → cleared.
- **The water table is a level, not a footprint** (M9d decision 1), so *draw from Tier A when the
  sample's table stands above the pump* would let a pump in a dry pit beside a lake drink it
  through the rock at 100 L/s where the seep index lets it in at 1.76. `LakeCeiling.InLake` is the
  question, and the live sim terrain has answered it since M8d-5.
- **`BasinAtSample` folds "off the window" into `Outlet`**, and `Receive(Outlet)` sends litres out
  of the world — right for a sample draining off the edge, wrong for one the window does not cover.
  `TryBasinAtSample` separates them so `unanalysed` is a stall and not a sink.
- **`FluidGrid.Panel.Held` already is the per-panel wet count** the ladder wanted `Publish` to
  cache. Public as `HeldIn`, it makes a pump over dry panels eight lookups; every row ticks every
  boundary and the sleep set — whose wake rule the ladder itself called one recipe from a pump
  that never restarts — is a lever with `machines` > 1 ms as its trigger.

Twelve decisions, all recommended; the ladder's 5, 12 and 14 and its reconcile rule amended;
M10-PLAN's 2, 4, 5, 7, 10 and 11 amended. Whole litres cross a tier and millilitres move within
Tier B, so nothing is ever pending at an outlet (a slow pump on a lake keeps an *owed* counter
that is a want, not water, and is not persisted). `Pump`/`Emit` twins on both tiers carry their
own counters into both identities, on `HandOff`'s shape, so `PortalDrain`'s *drawn mL == drawn L
× 1000* stays true. The channel's cursor lives in memory and resets at open — determinism is
within a session, the cost one boundary's litres to a different outlet once after a reopen. A
machine material places as one cell whatever the brush, mode or modifier; `P` seeds 64 + 64 for
the play; the relay bodies ship at hardness 3.0, not the ladder's 5.0, because `steel_pick`'s
threshold is 3.5 and a body nobody can mine is a body nobody can dismantle. The loader takes the
whole `machine` grammar and refuses a `via` this build does not serve, naming the part that will —
a lamp that does not glow was a day inside one milestone; against a format mods write to it is
not the state to ship. Split three ways at the Core/wire seam: **a-1 the store slice first and
alone** (its first test the store that throws inside the batch after the header), **a-2 the
entity** (the loader, `Place.Machine`, the hooks and the drain, `P`, `--abort=`), **a-3 the pump**
(`MachineTick`, the unloaded-outlet rule, `--pump=` / `--pumpoutlet=`, the bench's `--pump`, the
lifecycle battery with machines running). Nothing built.

the walk**, against the recorded 5.9× and ~10× Release penalties (the propagation's cells-visited

## 2026-09-15 — the ladder planned: connection is membership, and there is no solver

Matthew, the evening after M10's pass: *"m10 is going to be a lot longer than this … the first tech
we make will be the last tech in the game, like plan with me some kind of crafting system that we
will use to create the machines from components we have made previously … hand cranked → steam
(needs a boiler and mechanical output) → electrical (wires/solar panels … dc not a lot of travel …
because our solver consumes cpu) → bespoke electrical ac (no distance limit, higher currents, 3d
printed stainless steel parts) → quantum (no distance limit, inputs and outputs need not be
physically connected)."* [docs/M10-LADDER-PLAN.md](docs/M10-LADDER-PLAN.md): twenty-three
decisions, ten parts M10a–M10j; the morning's M10-PLAN is its first rung with eight decisions
amended. Nothing built.

**How the pass was run, because it is the first of its kind here.** Four readers mapped the code
and the notes; four designers wrote independent designs from four angles (engine cost, gameplay,
mod format, physical plausibility); three judges scored all four adversarially (Core and the
non-negotiables, CPU, gameplay-and-Matthew); one synthesis took the winner and grafted the rest;
one critic asked what was missing. Thirteen agents, ~2.9 M tokens, 34 minutes. It earned its keep
in the judging: the engine-first design's hand pump poured into the column above its own top,
which is inside its own 3 × 3 × 3 intake, so it pumped its outlet back and the room never dried
while `pumped == emitted` held perfectly; three designs bounded a run by *voxel* count, which
gives a 2 m dc run by the right-click brush and 32 m by Alt+right for the same copper; the
format-first design's coal stock lasted 34 h by its own arithmetic where it said 2.3; three designs
multiplied a pool by the raw float `OvercastAt`; and three asserted the header and the machine
table were "one transaction" against a store whose `WriteWorldHeader` is a separate call. None of
those would have been found by one designer reading its own plan.

**The one idea.** A wire, a shaft or a pipe is evidence that two machine rows share a pool, never a
thing that carries anything: no current, no pressure, no water in a pipe, no steam in a boiler.
Every tier moves litres and joules with the relay pump's three lines, and the five tiers differ
only in the membership rule — the player at a crank, a shaft component of 16 cells, a copper
component of 24, a cable component unbounded, a channel number 0–15. *Who is connected* is
answered at edit time by a per-chunk conductor index of PortalIndex's shape, marked dirty from the
three hooks and rescanned at the boundary under a cap, relabelling only the component touched;
the tick is O(awake machines) at every tier. *"Our solver consumes CPU"* is false because there is
no solver — the DC tier's short run and the AC tier's unlimited one are one code path with one
number different, and the number is a cell count, not a search.

**Four facts from the code the morning's plan did not have.** `ViewDistanceVertical` is 2 (16 m)
against a 64 m mine, so *"no distance limit"* is only true if membership survives unloading —
per-chunk summaries persist as the chunk's own derived data on the batch write, and the forget
path must rescan a dirty chunk first or "an unloaded voxel cannot change" is false. The header and
the machine table are two store calls, so a recipe queue that moves voxels from the inventory
into a station is a crash that duplicates them until a batch overload carries the header — the
store slice's first test, and no inventory-to-row transfer ships before it. `FluidGrid.IsWetIn` is
a dictionary lookup a voxel (~25 ns, estimate), so a pump's naive intake read is ~45 µs and 500
pumps are ~22 ms Release on the frame that is already the played build's worst; the read is 27
cell lookups with a per-panel wet count cached at `Publish`, and a machine active set with a
`hasMachines` bit on every chunk the box touches is the design rather than a lever. And a 0.25 m
wire with `supportDistance` 2 costs 60 a step under M9's rule, so a run along a roof falls in the
collapse window — conductors declare 8, and a cable that falls with its roof is the tier-3 moment;
`Place.Put` refuses `Wet`, so a hose through the flooded room the hand tier is about takes the
machine body's deferred, displacing path.

**Five things taken in his words during the pass.** Iron under the water table (seepage is the
tax on ore) and the first age stone and wood (wooden tools exist) — WORLDGEN-NOTES' questions 1
and 3; trees found and planted, seeds from fire, growth on a worker after the tick as a pure
function of (planting time, now) — question 2; channel 0–15, outputs cycling, every input firing
every tick, the cursor per channel so two pumps go to two outlets in one boundary; the channel set
by right-clicking with a computer — the programmer is an item, not `E`; and faces on sub-quantum
machines. His hose as a FIFO that fills was answered in the chat as a shift register holding litres
and is returned as decision 2 with a cheaper arm recommended: an *energised* bit in the merge key
so the hose visibly fills from the pump end, and a cut hose spraying the pump's own flow at the
break — the two things the FIFO was for, with no third home for water. The FIFO is honestly cheap
and stays the arm if the fill has to be physically delayed; its costs are written beside it.

**Two things the pass decided that go beyond the brief.** The boiler drinks — 0.5 L/s from the
cells around it, leaving the world as `consumed`, a `Watershed.Outlet`-shaped term on both
identities — so steam is the tier where the antagonist becomes a resource, which the lithium tier
finishes. And parts are materials (`unit: count`, `placeable: false`) rather than a second
inventory: one registry, one ID table, one save form; the cost is ~30 IDs shifting the hotbar and
a placeable filter that must ship with the recipes. Hand crafting is instant and time belongs only
to powered stations you walk away from — two designs had a cranked workbench at five minutes a
pump body, which is busywork wearing *"the fun part"*'s costume.

## 2026-09-15 — M10 planned: the boundary is the tick, a machine is a material plus a row, an outlet is out of the box on day one

The planning pass for M10, from [M10-NOTES](docs/M10-NOTES.md) against the code as M9d left it:
[docs/M10-PLAN.md](docs/M10-PLAN.md), split M10a–M10d, eleven decisions, nine recommended and two
Matthew's (the programmer's key; the battery's numbers). Nothing built. Three things the code said
that the notes could not have:

**The boundary is the machine tick, and DESIGN's 20 Hz has no consumer.** `FluidSimulation.Add`,
`Remove` and `HandOff` refuse mid-tick, and under `start.cmd`'s `--fluidjob=1` the grid is a
worker's for up to a third of every second. A pump is a drain and an outlet is a pour; every pass
that moves water runs in `Main.UpdateFluid`'s boundary block, so a machine that touches water ticks
there — between the chunk fills and the table-move sweep, so an outlet raising a lake over a roof
requeues the roof in the same boundary — and nowhere else. DESIGN's *fixed 20 Hz sim step,
spatially partitioned update list* is amended to *machines tick at the fluid boundary*, with M11's
drill (a voxel every half-second reads as stuttering; litres do not) as the trigger for a second,
faster rate beside it. Rates are litres a second in the JSON and an exact `L/s × 500 ms`
millilitres a boundary in the code, so a late boundary is a slower pump and never a wrong one.

**A machine is a material plus a row, and the material half costs nothing.** M10-NOTES piece 6 said
a machine *cannot be a voxel* — true of the channel number, not of the body. One brush cell of
`overburden:relay_pump` is meshed, lit, collided with, supported, gated by hardness, credited per
voxel by `Carve.Take`, shown with a swatch on the hotbar, placed by the right button and placed at
range by `Q` + right click, with no new code in any of it. The `machine` block goes *inside* the
material JSON — `kind` an engine behaviour picked by name, the numbers a mod's — so there is one
ID, one registry entry and no second ID table; the row (origin, material ID through the world's
table, ports) is the only new state, in a `machines` table at schema 4, read whole at open and
written whole at autosave like the basins. **The rows are the truth and the body follows**: at
every chunk arrival a row rebuilds a missing body and a body with no row is cleared without
credit — the crash between an unload's chunk write and an autosave's row write can produce either,
and the one lag left is the inventory's, which every brush placement has had since M6c. Placement
is atomic (64 or none) and, into water, deferred to the boundary and *displacing* through
M9c-1's `Lift`/`Return` — because M9d's wet refusal exists for a fill that deletes water, and the
play case is a pump placed in a flooded room.

**An outlet on the surface is outside the loaded box the first time anyone pumps a mine out.**
`ViewDistanceVertical` is 2 — 16 m — and the played mine is 64 m deep, so the notes' *"does an
output in an unloaded chunk still exist?"* is M10a's rule, not a later lever: an unloaded outlet
at or above the seed surface inside the watershed window credits its sample's basin through
`Receive` — the hand-off's rule without the wait, `BasinLedger` paying off a third time — and an
unloaded outlet underground accepts nothing and the pump stalls, printed. The pump itself reads
Tier A when its sample's table stands over its top (`Draw`, the portal drain's call) and the wet
cells in the 3 × 3 × 3 m around it otherwise, **and the delivered rate is the automaton's
throughput into that box, not the JSON's number** — M8a's one-voxel hole at 29 L/s is the same
physics — so the bench's `--pump` arm takes the delivered L/s at three intake sizes before the
100 L/s estimate is believed. `min(offered, accepted)` in one boundary, nothing held by a machine,
`pumped == emitted` on both tiers and across them, and the M8 lifecycle battery with machines
running as the test rather than a machine test.

Two things the pass decided beyond the notes. **Power is a pool per channel with no wires** — the
pipe argument a second time, and the fiction already said *wireless* — with the first generator
solar off `SkyColumn`'s openness and `Weather.OvercastAt`, both of which exist, so the storm that
floods the mine dims the panels that pump it: DESIGN's loop closed with two inputs the game
already has, and no fuel material the world does not. And **shoring is not built**: a placed stone
pillar already carries a full budget to its top under `SupportRule.Rest` (`K/30` a voxel, 32 voxels
to the cap), so DESIGN's *raise local support distance* is true of what M9 ships and the play
question is whether it *reads* so. The inventory's move to millilitres, which MATERIALS-NOTES had
riding header v4 with the machines, goes to v5 at M11 alone — a change in a field's meaning is a
refusal under the format policy and a data-loss-shaped bump goes by itself. Header v4 is the
carried battery's (M10c); the machine table is a schema bump, not a header one, which corrects
M10-NOTES' shorthand.

## 2026-09-15 — M9d built: the trigger is a comparison, a timer only shortens, the wet answer is a copy

Matthew took the pass whole — *"As recommended"* — with the jitter widened and decision 3's lake
edge left open (*"not sure about 3 yet"*); built in one session, Core first, 1,392 → 1,411 tests,
21 break-recipes and 21 caught. Read M9-PLAN's "M9d — built" for the shape; what is worth keeping
here is what the build corrected in the pass and what the numbers said.

**The memo is per sample, not per basin.** The pass said "memoised per basin the way
`WaterSurface` solves `LevelAt`", and the region cannot: `IWaterTable` is `TableAt(sampleX,
sampleZ)` and hides the basin. Per sample is what the interface allows and it is where the saving
actually is — chunks stacked in a column share their sixteen — so the 2 × 2 room's twenty analysed
chunks in twelve columns cost 192 asks, not 320 plus 528 a rebuild. **The test's first assertion
of that was too weak** (*fewer asks than analysed × 16*), and the battery's one miss said so: the
unmemoised sweep asks fewer than that anyway, because the reading loop breaks at the first moved
sample. The claim is exact and the test now says exactly it.

**A flat move has to be re-recorded.** A lake already past the curve's last point rises another
voxel: the readings moved, the rebuilt table matches, nothing is queued — and unless the fresh
table replaces the old, every sweep from then on rebuilds it for the same nothing. One line, and
its own fixture (`ALakeRisingPastTheCurvesLastPointRebuildsAndRequeuesNothing` asserts `TableRebuilt`
stays put on the second sweep).

**The keystone reads in the game, and the number is the plan's last row.** `--bitechunks=2` with the
pour held 5 s: the dry plug's four `fell 5`, `at risk 0` at open, then `table 20` and **18,718 at
risk in 7 chunks** — the whole roof of each room chunk, since a bite 24 m down under a lake at −6
puts every row past stone's 10 m point — and four falls of ~6,200 voxels each with `lifted 30 ==
returned 30` (the seepage's litres, lifted from under the fall and put back), `displaced 0`, `at risk
0` after. `--saturation=0` sheds 20 and nothing more with the lake standing; `--tablemove=0` reads
`table 0 (0 sweep(s))` and 20 after the pour; r6 to the digit.

**The sweep costs 7 µs a chunk in Debug, not the pass's tens of microseconds a sweep.** 0.14 ms a
boundary over 20 analysed, 2.56 on the boundary that rebuilt all twenty; the estimate counted the
lookups and not the dictionary behind the memo. Under a millisecond on the played world's ~120,
against a field sync of 23 ms on the same line, so no lever is built; one is named in TODO.

**The exponential's tail is the point and also the oracle's risk.** `−ln(1 − u)` has no upper
end short of the cap (13.8× at 0.999999); the plug's mean stays 56 s, its median is 39, one draw
in twenty is under 3 s and one over 168 s. The seed-world oracle's four stages at `1,2` still land
inside `--measure=20` — checked, since a wider draw could have pushed one out.

**The fill cannot be wire-checked by the flythrough.** `--place --injectlitres` reads `0.00 wet` at
every pitch, and it is M6d-2's finding again: the profile builds a column under the crosshair and
the pool round it is never the aimed cell. The wire is a pipeline test with `GridOwnedByTick` true
and a `FakeFluid` answering wet; the first fill to meet water in the game is the play's.

**Two identities named rather than counted.** Wet-before-stock is a cost claim — the stock check
debits nothing, so no fixture can see the order. And `≥ 1.0` against `>`: the half-voxel fixture
separates a threshold of 0.5 from 1.0 and would not separate `>` from `≥`.

**The SDK was replaced under the session.** Between two battery runs `dotnet` reported "No SDKs
were found": `sdk/10.0.302` had emptied to a lone `Roslyn` folder with two `setup.exe` and an
`msiexec` running — Matthew's update, *"Yeah sorry … its finished"* — and 10.0.401 came back
minutes later. The suite is green on it; the new analyzers surface one pre-existing CA2014 in
`LightPropagator` (a `stackalloc` in a loop) that is not M9d's.

## 2026-09-14 — a quit with the tick's surface in hand threw past the save

Matthew's last two sessions of the evening (20:08 and 20:42) ended on `ObjectDisposedException:
Godot.ShaderMaterial` out of `FluidSurface.Install`, under `Main._ExitTree` → `WaitForDetached` →
`OnFluidTickCollected`, and `535 RID allocations … leaked at exit`. **Neither log has `M8b: at
quit`, `M6: world written on quit` or `M6c: saved the player` after it** — the throw unwound
`_ExitTree` before `_pipeline.Dispose()`, so the quit's save never ran and everything since the
last autosave (up to 30 s of edits, the water rows, the player's position) was lost, with no line
saying so. The leaked RIDs are the 533 drawn chunks the skipped dispose would have freed.

The order: `_fluidSurface?.Dispose()` is the third line of `_ExitTree`, and the cancelled tick is
collected after it. A tick cancelled during its visits throws out of the worker and carries no
surface; **one cancelled during its settle or its walk — or already complete and waiting to be
pumped — completes with `job.Surface` set**, and the callback installs it wherever `_fluidSurface`
is non-null, which it still was, disposed. On the played world the walk over a 125,000-cell
surface is tens of milliseconds a tick, so play lands in that window often enough for twice in
thirty-five minutes.

Two lines. **`_fluidSurface = null` after its dispose**, so the callback's own guard skips the
install; and **the wait is inside a `try`** that prints `M8b: collecting the tick in flight threw
on quit — …; the quit goes on to the save`, because a render-teardown defect must not be able to
cost the world. The second is the general shape of the `Complete`-hook lever in TODO: a callback
that throws inside `Apply` unwinds whoever pumped it, and the quit is the pump that saves.

Verified windowed with `--quit-after 700 -- --nosave --fluidjob=1 --injectlitres=2000000`: the
quit prints `M8b: cancelled the tick in flight before the quit — 124,039 cell(s) were still to
visit`, no error, no leak. **The same run on the stashed pre-fix code did not throw either** — a
2 ML pour's tick is in its visits for most of its wall, so the fixture reached the cancelled state
and not the surface-carrying one, twice. The mechanism is read off the trace rather than
reproduced: the guard is `job.Surface is not null && _fluidSurface is not null`, and the field is
null now. A deterministic fixture wants the quit to land in the walk — a `WorkerGate`-shaped seam
after the visits, which does not exist and is not built for one line.

## 2026-09-14 — the entangled bite is the brush cell, and so is the fill: *"make it all the same 4x4x4"*

One sentence from Matthew after the stall fix — *"just take an 8x8 cube like right click"* —
and a question back before touching it, because both buttons already worked on the same 8 m
chunk while `Q` was on and "like right click" could have meant three things. The answer was a
smaller cube, and I read "8x8" as eight voxels and built a 2 m cube. **It was the cube brush's
cell he meant** — *"match the 4x4x4 grid on the right click function"* — and then the fill as
well: *"make it all the same 4x4x4"*. Three passes for one lattice, and the last is the one
that was right by construction rather than by a number.

`Carve.Cube` beside `Chunk`, sharing `Take`, so the hardness gate is still the one gate in the
game — four shapes now, one edit breaks all four. **`CubeVoxels` is `BrushCell.Voxels` and
`CubeOrigin` is `BrushCell.FromVoxel(...).OriginVoxel`**: the dig's cell is the fill's cell
because they are the same code, not because two constants happen to agree — the
`IsCaveAt`/`GenerateTerrain` argument, and a literal 8 is a recipe the lattice test catches
alone (every other test derives its edge from the constant and scales with the mutation). The
brush's snap is a shift, so voxel −1 is in the cell at −4 and a tidy-up to `/ 4 * 4` puts a
seam through the origin (caught by 7). The cell divides the chunk, so a cube never straddles a
chunk face and 512 tile a chunk exactly — both asserted. **Snapped rather than centred on the
hit, for the reason the brush is**: consecutive bites tile into flat-walled rooms instead of
overlapping into one-voxel steps.

`MiningController.EntangledTakesChunk` became `Bite`, an `EntangledBite` of Sphere / Cube /
Chunk with Cube the default. **The fill moved with it**: `EntangledFillsChunk` is true only on
the chunk arm, so with `Q` on the right click is the selected brush at unlimited reach — the
place controller already did that when the flag was off, the outline already drew the cell, and
the only new piece is `PlaceController.BrushCooldownSeconds` so dig and fill pace the same. The
HUD reads `1 M CELL (Q) · dig cell / cube brush (B)`. `--entanglechunk` restores the chunk pair
of 2026-09-03 (every recorded bite figure is that arm, so a profile reproducing one needs the
flag), `--entanglesphere` the sphere. The rate is **0.05 s, an estimate** between the sphere's
0.025 and the chunk's 0.25, `--cubecooldown=` the sweep: a cell is four `hand_pick` spheres, so
the sphere's forty nearly transfers and the chunk's four would take two minutes to clear a chunk.
**Then his number: *"10/second eventually this will cost a lot of power"* — 0.1 s ships**, and
the reason is the one that matters: the entangled miner's gate is M10's battery, so its rate is a
design input to what a charge buys, not a ceiling the frame carries. Every rate before it was a
cost argument; this is the first chosen for the game. **And then the repeat went**: *"one click
is one click"* — on the cube arm a bare press fires on its edge and never again while held, both
buttons, in `Main` where the buttons are read; the cooldown stays underneath as the floor between
clicks. Alt keeps its held repeat, because chipping single voxels at range is what the L+Q
pairing was reported load-bearing for. A tool that will one day drain a battery per press should
not be a hose you lean on.

Headless on the `--entangle --mine` profile arm, r4h/2v, 6 m/s: **17.8/s delivered against 20
nominal, 47 voxels a swing, swing 0.42 ms mean / 4.3 ms max, 1.7 remeshes a swing** (the
eight-voxel cut at 10/s read 9.4/s, 379 voxels, 1.3 ms / 7.1 ms, 3.3 remeshes). Suite 1,370 →
1,392; recipes at eight: division 6, bounds 13, `hit.Previous` 5, edge 6 → 9, edge 16 → 10; at
four: division 7, `hit.Previous` 6, literal 8 → 2. One assertion was wrong first and the code
was right: `CarveResult.Complete` means nothing was unreachable, not nothing was refused.

## 2026-09-14 — the "standing on air" stall was the M8d-5b hook asking the grid mid-tick

Matthew relaunched, loaded fine, and pasted a log full of `Grid asked with a tick job in flight`
thrown from `Main.<_Ready>` line 997 — the M8d-5b wake in `onFluidReady`, which read
`_fluid.Grid.HasPanel(position)`. That read is refused while a worker owns the grid, and the hook
fires mid-tick for **every dry arrival**: slice 3a parks only the arrivals that may hold water,
and hands a dry chunk on at once so the world keeps drawing under a flood. Under `--fluidjob=1`
a tick is in flight a good share of the time (worker wall mean 150–240 ms of a 500 ms period on
the played world; 1.4 s at the open), so a few dozen arrivals a session threw.

**And the throw is the TODO's top item, not the cache.** It unwinds `ChunkPipeline.Complete`
at the `ArriveFluid` call, *before* `PushWithNeighbours` — the M2c-2 stall to the letter: the
chunk sits at `Generated`, its neighbourhood is never pushed, every report reads idle. The
"floated out of the vertical box and back" session's kept log (`godot2026-09-14T18.45.59.log`,
137 reports) has 85 of the same refusal, unread under the reports. The hypothesis recorded
there — the cache's reseed path — was wrong; the cache was only the thing that made a vertical
trip revive a whole slab of dry chunks at once.

The fix is one read: `_fluid.MayHoldWater(position)`, the question 3a built to be asked
mid-tick (it reads the published panel set and the captured view while a job is in flight, the
grid at a boundary). At a boundary it is `HasPanel` plus the evicting marks, a superset, and a
false positive costs a band walk whose wakes are already deferred. Measured headless on a copy
of the played world under `start.cmd`'s flags, r6h/2v, 12 m/s turning every 10 s, 30 s window:
**62 refusals → 0**, `ERROR` lines 0, both arms 358 drawn at the end (the flythrough returns to
a box it had meshed), `grown` 23.6 s → 15.8 s.

Two things worth keeping:

- **A hook on `onFluidReady` runs mid-tick by design, and the M8d-5b pass did not say so.**
  3a's rule — *`MayHoldWater` is the one question it asks mid-tick* — was written about the
  pipeline, and the wire's hook is the pipeline's caller one layer out. The rule now sits on the
  call site, in the comment, where the next hook will read it.
- **A hook exception eats the neighbour push.** `Complete`'s generate branch runs three hooks
  before `PushWithNeighbours`, and any of them throwing turns one bad read into a silent stall
  that reads as idle in every report — nothing counts it, `faulted` stays 0. Named in TODO as a
  lever, not built: push before the hooks, or count and swallow a hook's throw the way a job
  fault is counted.

## 2026-09-14 — M8d-5 played once: a chunk out of a lake's centre reverses decision 7

Matthew's first play on the new build: `Q` on a chunk in the middle of a lake — *"this happen
if you take a chunk out of the center of a lake … this might be my fault"*. Not his fault, and
not what the pass thought either. The screenshot is a dark box inside the plane with pale patches
on its top; the mesher already draws no side against a cell it cannot hold, so it is not walls.
**A bite in a lake's bed is below the seed surface, so Tier B fills it only to the seed, and the
cells from there to the level are the band — Tier A's water.** Decision 7 skipped A's plane over
the bite and left Tier B's top a metre or two down inside a hole, dark for its eight metres of
column; the pale patches are the top cells' unequal fills that A's flat plane never showed.

The fix is the reverse of decision 7: **the plane draws over the bite, because the water above
the seed there is the lake's, and Tier B draws no top under a lake cell, because the water goes
on upward.** One rule in `FluidSurfaceMesher` — a would-be surface cell whose cell above answers
`InLake` is drawn full with no top, the same clause as a cell with Tier B water above it — with
`UnderLake` on the surface terms. The skip, `--lakeoverdug` and `dug sample(s) skipped` are
removed rather than kept as an arm, because the arm is a hole in a lake. The test runs the
bed-bite in both arms: a 4 × 4 pit four deep fills to the seed (988 L drawn, rest at 34 ticks)
and draws 0 tops with 16 cells under the lake; the control draws the merged top the screenshot
showed. Suite 1,368 → 1,370; r6 control unchanged. What the eye judges next: the bite as the
lake with its walls seen through the water — and the shade step between A's flat tint and B's
depth tint where they meet is still a look question, named and not built against.

## 2026-09-14 — M8d-5a built: a lake is a body Tier B cannot enter (Core half)

Matthew's afternoon play, twice: the rain-filled spawn plain with `R` pours on it, then a fresh
world with a channel dug from a higher lake into a lower one — *"the topmost sheet of water does
not fall in line with most of the water cells underneath."* The log for the second: `drawn 32,936
L`, `handed 5,389 L`, `27,552 L` still Tier B, `56,270 cell-ticks left under a lake`, `injected
0`. **M8d-3's bank rule, whose cost was written down as "a pour into a lake stays Tier B on its
bed", produces two surfaces from the game's own loop**: the first arrivals in the lower basin land
on dry bed and merge, the bed is then under a lake, and every litre after is refused for ever.
Planned as M8d-5 in [docs/M8-PLAN.md](docs/M8-PLAN.md) (eight decisions, all taken — *"Lets
build it now"*), split at the Core / wire seam on *"break into smaller parts"*, and 5a built the
same afternoon. Suite 1,359 → 1,367.

**The rule.** A voxel in natural air above the seed ground and at or under its sample's lake
top — `seed < Y ≤ floor(TableAt(sample))`, M8c's Tier C floored — is not holdable to Tier B, the
way rock is not. Water resting on the lake's top is handed as water on the ground is (`PlaneAt +
1`, one test for both); water found inside a lake is listed `Submerged` by the visit and handed
whole at the boundary. `LakeCeiling` holds the band per chunk column, refreshed at the boundary
from sixteen sample tops, arrays replaced never mutated so a worker's view is never torn;
`LakeBoundedTerrain` wraps any terrain — the field's own shape, so nothing else changed.

**Why not just drop the bank rule.** The treadmill it cut is the bed under a lake being, to Tier
B, dry ground the chamber's sheet can spread onto; the hand-off then returns it and the drain
draws it again. The chamber test runs that shape in both arms: **with the ceiling, 9,869 L into
the chamber, the level 36.1 → 35.5, rest at 2,834 ticks, nothing on the bed, nothing handed;
without, 600 ticks draw 40,268 L and hand 32,079 L back and it never rests.** The control arm
asserting the treadmill is what says the guarded boundary is reached.

**Battery: 17 recipes, 16 caught, one identity** (`InLake` before `IsLoaded` — the wrapper's
`InLake` needs the inner terrain to hold, which unloaded never does). One recipe found a hole
in a test rather than the code: a view sharing the live dictionary passed because the view's
per-column cache had read the probed column already; the test probes an unread column now.

Three things worth keeping: **the plane is one over the floor** (four voxels of depth stand at
35 over a floor of 30, and every first-draft fixture was one low); **a full cell on a flat bed
spreads for hundreds of ticks**, so "asleep on the bed" is a cupped cell, and water gets into a
band only by being there first, because `Add` refuses a lake cell — `R` over a lake lands on its
top; and **`floor(level)` at an exact integer includes an empty top cell**, so a pour can turn
cells on the lake into cells in it — handed either way, a boundary later, named as residue.

**5b — the wire — is briefed in TODO as an ordered list**, with the three oracles (the r6
control, the headless pour, the played `default` handing its 27,672 L of bed water over at its
first boundaries) and the screenshot A/B for the plane over a bite.

**What is built.** `Overburden.Core/Structure/Collapse.cs` is the act — `Collapse.TryFall(region,

**Five things the build found, each by a test failing first:**

- **The barrier makes a plug fall one roof per boundary, and that is the design working.** The
  plug straddles four roof chunks; the first roof's fall is an edit that requeues it and its six,

  2 × 2 plug comes down over four boundaries (two seconds) and a 4 × 4 room piece by piece at
  2 Hz, each piece's fall unsettling the next, which reads as crumbling and costs no cascade rule.
- **The dirt roof cascades, and not the way the plan said.** The plan had "a wedge's core is
  unreached, so each stage re-arms at the minimum" for a 4 × 4 room; the field says a stone or dirt
  wedge under anchored walls is *one* fall — every held voxel above it has a sideways path through

- **A stone chunk over an unloaded chunk falls twice**, as the pass recorded rather than built:
  the rubble rests on the loaded edge as on rock, the timer is cleared; when the chunk below arrives

- **Two runs in one column need arithmetic, not a second walk**: the upper run's drop is where
  the lower one landed plus its length, because the world between them is air by construction (a
  held voxel cannot sit under an at-risk one) and reading it again after the lower's writes is an
  identity that costs a walk.
- **The plan's "16 columns of one rubble, four of two" is 12 and 4** — twenty voxels, sixteen
  columns. The test says which.

**Timers are cleared for every chunk a fall fell from**, not only the firing chunk — a slight
extension of decision 3, because the chunks a run reached into have a new deficit too; a neighbour
that did not fall keeps its timer, and the two-stage stack test pins both halves.

## 2026-09-13 — M9c-1 planned: a run falls as one, and the snapshot is not the gate

*"M9c-1 planning pass please Claude"* — decisions 6–9 and 12's M9c row read against the built
`SupportRegion`, the pipeline's edit hook chain, the fluid boundary and the ownership rules. Eleven
decisions in [docs/M9-PLAN.md](docs/M9-PLAN.md)'s "M9c-1 — the planning pass", all recommended,
waiting on Matthew; two correct an oracle the plan wrote and one moves a line of the split. Nothing
built. Four things worth the entry:

- **A derived fact does the work: the voxel under an at-risk voxel is non-solid or at risk.** Rest
  from a held voxel gives at least `+4`, an anchor gives `K`, so only air, water, an unreached voxel
  or one below `−r` leaves the voxel above at risk. That is what makes "drop it straight down"
  strictly descending — and it is also what shows the plan's two rules disagree: decision 8 fires
  per chunk and decision 6 drops every at-risk voxel, so a run straddling a horizontal chunk face
  would turn to rubble *in place* on the lower chunk's still-standing rock, `Σ(Y)` unchanged, and
  fire as a no-op every boundary until the lower chunk went. The fall is a **column run** now,
  followed downward across faces into settled chunks, waiting on an unsettled one — `Σ(Y)`
  strictly down at every fall is kept rather than weakened.
- **`SettledField` is the last settle, not a promise the chunk is settled now.** The snapshot is
  kept until the next settle replaces it, so a chunk edited since its timer armed — the player
  mining the plug out — has a stale snapshot, and a collapse reading it would put rubble at a
  landing for a voxel that is air. `IsSettled` is the gate (`TryReadSettled`), the world is the
  source of what falls, and `stale skipped` is printed so a non-zero says the gate has a hole.
- **The cascade needs no rule.** Clear the timer at a fall and let the re-settle re-arm it from
  the new deficit: a wedge's core is unreached, deficit `K`, so each stage re-arms at the minimum
  and a 4 × 4 room comes down in stages seconds apart, while the plug's deficit of 8 gives 20
  voxels 28–84 s of warning. The timer is a sweep at the boundary over settled at-risk counts, not
  a hook on the settle; half a second of arming latency against a 2–60 s window.
- **The re-pour goes above the rubble, not into the cavity first, and it is Tier B's term alone.**
  Per column a run of *n* lands in *n* cells and vacates *n*, so the lifted water always fits;
  pouring bottom-up from the first cell over the new rubble puts it where a stone in a pool puts
  it, and in a flooded room it still ends in the cavity. `lifted` / `returned` are two counters,
  equal by arithmetic, the identity untouched; a fire waits for fluid-ready chunks so `displaced 0`
  stays an oracle rather than usually-zero. Priced by last night's bite — 131,072 voxels in 197 ms
  Debug, 1.5 µs a voxel through the whole hook chain — a per-chunk fall is a few milliseconds and
  the mid-air fill is two bites in a frame.

And one line of the split is handed back: the unstick moves into c-1, because a body with rubble in
its box before health exists is not unhurt, it is stuck on every axis with `F` as the only door.
Damage and death stay c-2.

## 2026-09-12 — M9b planned: the derive is a detached job, and the tint waits for the barrier

*"M9b's pass is next not sure if planning pass or work pass?"* — a planning pass, by the
arrangement, and it is in [docs/M9-PLAN.md](docs/M9-PLAN.md) under "M9b — the planning pass":
nine decisions, all recommended, read against `SupportRegion`, `ChunkPipeline`'s `Advance` /
`Submit` / `Neighbourhood` / `Apply`, `IDetachedJob`, `PortalTracker`, the mesher's `FaceKey` and
the converter. Nothing built. Three findings worth the entry:

- **The chunk's slot is the wrong home for the derive.** `Advance`'s *never two jobs for one chunk*
  would serialise the derive with the urgent remesh the same edit queues — either the broken rock
  waits a millisecond and a round trip, or the tint lands as a second remesh anyway. `IDetachedJob`
  already exists for a job that is not the chunk's state machine, and `Apply` routes it by name
  ahead of the chunk lookup; the submission still lives in the pipeline, because the 27 references
  need `VoxelsSharedWithJob` set the way `Neighbourhood()` sets it. A `ChunkSupport` is a new
  object per derive, so the mesher can take it by reference with no copy.
- **The plan's 250 ms coalescing timer is a second mechanism with no number.** Correctness needs a
  per-chunk in-flight mark whatever else is built — a derive on a snapshot older than the last edit
  is a field the oracle rejects — and that mark caps a chunk at one derive per round trip. The timer
  is deferred with its trigger on the `support` line: 40 chips a second is ~30 derives at 1 ms,
  0.4% of eight workers.
- **The tint reads only settled fields, and settled is per chunk over its seven.** M9a's join
  climbs, so the transient is *at risk where it will hold*; a tint reading it flashes and clears.
  Decision 7's barrier — a chunk and its six neither queued nor in flight — applied to the tint,
  with a remesh only when the at-risk set changed (a 32 KiB compare, not a hash) and never urgent,
  so the played world's at-risk shell arriving at the open does not reorder the distance queue.

Two smaller corrections to the plan's own sentences: `--bitechunks` bites three chunks down, not
"under the player", because a metre of soil makes the chunk under the player's a soil-roofed bite
(fixture 4) where the oracle is the stone plug (fixture 2); and the region wires to `onVoxelsReady`,
not the tracker's `onFluidReady`, because support reads Tier A's table and not the panels. The
first measurement is the played world's open in the Debug build with tiering on, against a Debug
`--support` — the profile figure wants a reference from its own build.

## 2026-09-12 — M9a built: the support field, and the byte that moved the constant

*"m9a please"*. The pass first — decisions 1–5 and the bench section read against `ChunkLight`,
`LightPropagator`, `PaddedChunk`, `SeepNeighbourhood` and `Saturation` — then the build in the
same session, because every finding was a representation or an algorithm and none reversed a
decision Matthew took. Both are in [docs/M9-PLAN.md](docs/M9-PLAN.md) under "M9a — the planning
pass" and "M9a — built". Suite 1,296 → 1,319; eleven recipes, ten caught, one an identity.

**The first number: 0.8–1.1 ms a searched derive over 32,768 voxels, 0.2 ms to gather the padded
copy, Release with the JIT's tiering off.** The plan estimated 1–3 and named 4 as the cell rule's
trigger. The join from nothing is 34 derives in 2 rounds for a 2 × 2 room and 128 in 3 for a 4 × 4;
a wall chunk is the closed form and costs the gather alone.

**The plan's byte could not hold its own rule.** `K = 240` in `0..240` leaves fifteen codes for a
deficit, and the plug's own derivation needs deficits exact — its second layer is `−8 + r` and its
third is zero, and a deficit quantised at a chunk face moves that sign. `K = 120` with an offset:
241 values, every cost halved exactly, the geometry unchanged to the voxel.

**And then the floor, three times.** A byte needs a bottom and the plan's rule has none, so where a
path's budget goes below `−K` had to be decided, and the first two answers were wrong in ways only
the tests could show:

- **The floor as a source at every solid voxel** — the natural reading of "the deficit saturates" —
  let a chunk placed in mid-air recover one refund a layer off its own floor and hold its top two
  layers: 30,720 at risk of 32,768. The floor was supporting things.
- **The floor as a source only where an anchor reaches** fixed that, and a column straddling a
  chunk face then converged to the floor rather than to unreached — 118 rounds, each half's floor
  justifying the other's — and the fixpoint oracle *accepted it*, because a floor is a fixpoint of
  that rule. A second fixpoint is the oracle's completeness gone, which is the whole of M5b's
  argument for it.
- **A path dies at `−K`, and a voxel no live path reaches is `Unreached`** — a state, code 0, the
  plan's `−∞` and every deficit past `K` alike. Max over live paths from the anchors: one fixpoint,
  and the derive needs neither a flood nor a clamp. The cost is stated on the constant: a deficit
  past `K` is not counted further, so a wide roof's centre is unreached rather than "recovered
  thirty-four layers up", and it is reached from the anchored top face or not at all. Mechanically
  the first two designs were not label-setting either — a hang from the floor to the floor lands
  in a bucket the scan has passed — so the height potential that makes the derive Dijkstra was
  also what ruled them out.

**The join climbs.** Decision 4 said an underived neighbour is an anchor and the iteration descends;
on a body across a face that loses one refund a round — 33 rounds and 156 derives for the 2 × 2, 61
and 724 for the 4 × 4. From below, an underived analysed neighbour contributes nothing and every
round carries live paths one chunk further: 2 and 34, 3 and 128, at-risk counts identical to the
voxel. The transient inverts — a chunk derived before its neighbour reads at risk where it will
hold — and decision 7's barrier is what keeps M9b's tint and M9c's fall from reading it.

**Seven cross-sections, drawn.** Six agree with decision 1's arithmetic, two of them correcting the
table's words: the 4 × 4's wedge is cut flat at seventeen layers by the hang from the anchored top
face (4.25 m, not 8.5; 47,600 voxels against ~52,000), and the soil roof has sky above it, not
stone (975 against 1,024, on a terrace flat over 39 of 64 samples). The 2 × 2 sheds twenty, with a
row of zeros over the plug. Under head, the bench measures at the underside where the plan measured
at the lake: 532 / 3,028 / 14,060 under 2 / 5 / 10 m. **The seventh is decision 3's cost in a
number**: the bench found a bite whose roof chunk is 21,061 voxels of natural cave, and nothing is
at risk, because the cave's *ceiling* is in the chunk beyond the shell and anchored — the first
bite beside a wide cave sheds nothing, the second may bring the cave's ceiling down. M8c's *"the
portal rule wet a natural cave beside the first shaft"* asked of the roof, and answered.

**Two fixtures were wrong before the code was**, both about anchoring: a run of dirt placed ten
voxels up a chunk anchored at its side started at `+17` because the arch from that side rises at
45°; and a loaded stone chunk placed over a hanging column as its "ceiling" is analysed, not an
anchor, and its own bottom layer was dead before the column began. An unloaded chunk anchors, a
loaded one is analysed — the difference is decision 3 entire.

**Two instrument findings.** The bench's per-derive figure read 3.2 ms on its first two rows and
0.8 on the rest in one run, and 2.5–4 on every row in the next: `Derive` at tier 0, with the JIT's
promotion postponed for as long as the process keeps jitting new methods, which a bench walking
through fixtures does; `--watershed`'s warm-up-by-call-count does not help (that is OSR, a different
delay). `DOTNET_TieredCompilation=0` is the arm that means anything and the bench says which arm it
is. And the shared `LayerIndex` transposed was an identity — writer and reader agree — while the
layer test used `LayerIndex` as its own oracle; the asymmetric recipe (the reader alone) fails five
tests, and the test spells the index out now.

**Content:** `supportUnderHead` in the shipped JSON — stone `[[2, 24], [10, 12]]`, dirt and grass
`[[1, 4], [3, 1]]`, the plan's estimates — the loader refusing `supportDistance` outside `0..48` and
any curve it could not interpolate, `lamp.json` 4 → 8, `MaterialTable.SupportDistanceAt` the
projection, `MaterialTable.IsSolid` the complement of Tier B's holdable. `PaddedChunk.MissingMaterial`
moved down from `SeepNeighbourhood` so the seep scan and the support derive read one constant.

**The seventh picture put to Matthew, same day: *"isn't an issue, feel free to make dangerous any old
save."*** So the shell stays as built for the caves' sake, and the played world — 4,584 stored
chunks, a 264 × 304 m void bitten 64 m deep — gets no grace at open: wherever the field says at risk,

M9b is next and wants its own pass against `SupportRegion`; the TODO names what it inherits.

## 2026-09-11 — M9's planning pass: no bedrock, and no arch

*"M9's planning pass please"*, opened fresh as the last session asked. [docs/M9-PLAN.md](docs/M9-PLAN.md),
split M9a–M9d, twelve decisions all recommended. Two things the code said before any decision:

- **There is no bedrock.** DESIGN's *BFS from anchored material (bedrock, …)* names a material the
  mods do not have and a world floor the generator does not make — stone continues forever under a
  metre of soil. The anchor the engine *does* have is the rule it has used three times: an unloaded
  voxel is solid. So the anchor is the edge of what is analysed, and the analysed set is the portal
  rule's — dug chunks and their six face neighbours, because a bitten chunk is all air and its roof
  is the undug chunk above. Analysing the whole box was rejected on one count: a collapse edits, so
  every natural cave that fell would turn a regenerable chunk into a stored one, by the thousand.
- **DESIGN's literal rule has no arch, and the bench arithmetic says what that costs.** A voxel
  more than `supportDistance` lateral steps from a wall is at risk — and so is every voxel resting on
  it, to the surface. Over a 16 m square room (a 2 × 2 bite) that is a one-metre shaft through the
  overburden. The plan's rule is a budget: sideways spends the material's share, resting on rock
  *refunds* a constant, hanging costs double. **The refund had to be a world constant and hanging had
  to cost double for a proof, not for physics**: with a per-material refund a dirt voxel over a stone
  one pumps itself to full budget and a floating slab never falls; with hanging equal to resting a
  column across a chunk face self-supports forever. Strictly negative cycles give the unique fixpoint
  M5b's oracle needs and the convergence decision 4's chunk-wise iteration needs. Physics came out
  right anyway: stone arches at 45°, soil at 75°.

Three more things from the arithmetic, all labelled derived-not-measured:

- **A path runs to the nearest wall, so a gallery 8 m wide of any length never falls in stone**; the
  smallest stone room that sheds is 2 × 2 bites, and it sheds a 1 m plug of 20 voxels, then holds.
  The first draft said *two bites side by side* and *192 voxels* — the second wall was forgotten.
- **The keystone as a number**: the same 16 m room sheds 20 voxels dry and ~5,700 under five metres
  of lake with the plan's estimated curve — three hundred times — while a tunnel still never falls.
- **Support is skylight upside down**, and the plan says so in one paragraph so M9a reads `ChunkLight`
  and `LightPropagator` first. Where it departs: the derive is from scratch per chunk on a worker with
  the neighbours' faces captured, and the join is re-deriving whoever's input changed — because the
  un-light walk is where cache slice 2 found three defects, and a chunk re-derived whole has no
  inverse to get wrong. And unlike light, **the margin does not make the visible box exact** — a
  support path can run 30 m to a wall or upward at 45° indefinitely — so a roof whose wall is beyond
  the box stands until the box moves. The failure is a *later* fall, which the deferral licenses;
  recorded so nobody adds a ring for it.

Two things handed to Matthew beyond the numbers: **health at M9** (DESIGN puts it at M11, but *the
mine kills you* is M9's line and his proposal names damage) — the plan recommends the minimum, with
death a respawn that keeps the inventory; and **a fill refusing a voxel that holds water**, which
answers the fill-into-a-flooded-chamber question TODO parked for this pass and makes M10's pump the
only way to reclaim a flooded room. Nothing built; DESIGN is amended after the decisions, not before.

**Taken the same evening — *"As planned, see you in a fresh chat for M9a"*.** All twelve, the
estimates in 5 and 8 shipping as written. DESIGN's *Structural integrity* section, its M11 row,
SCALE's M9 paragraph, MATERIALS-NOTES decision 1 and `MaterialDefinition.SupportDistance`'s comment
are amended; M9a opens fresh, against `ChunkLight` and `LightPropagator` first.

tracker's burst and flush, `SeepIndex.IsDug`, `Saturation.HeadMetresAt` (M8c-3), `--seepscale=`,
the `seep` profile line and `seeped` on every line. Suite 1,257 → 1,270; 30 break-recipes, 29 caught after three fixtures were fixed (nobody filled the room under a low lake, nobody placed rock at a cave's face from the dug side, no cave sat on a chunk's side face), the miss an identity — the tracker marks a chunk dug before it tells the index, so the as-inside dug check on the edit path can never fail through it. Read
M8-PLAN's "M8c-2 — the planning pass" and "M8c-2 — built" first. Five things:

- **The portal rule is too loose for seep faces, and the wire check found it.** "Every pair
  touching a dug chunk" filed a natural cave in the undug neighbour of the first shaft bitten,
  and it kept seeping after the shaft's pit had drained. Portals survive that rule because a cave
  is never a pit and a bank needs a cliff; a seep face needs only rock beside a hollow, and caves
  are everywhere underground. The rule is on the inside's chunk now (`IsDug`, bound by the
  tracker, in the definition), and the cave stays dry until someone digs in its chunk.
- **A full chunk is skipped, and that is where "never settles" is paid.** The rate is measured
  against the lake, not the mine's own water, so a flooded room under a lake would walk every face
  every tick for ever; now a pass that delivers nothing for want of room marks the chunk at the
  index's revision and skips it until an edit moves the revision or sixteen passes go by. A lake
  running dry mid-pass is *not* full — the second version conflated them and the rain would have
  waited sixteen passes to be noticed.
- **The block scan is 4.5–8× the per-voxel one, and the bite is a rescan.** `--seep`, Release: a
  solid chunk 0.56 ms against 2.5, a room chunk ~1 against 7, a bitten chunk 1.8 against 4.1.
  Past 64 edits in a chunk between flushes the tracker stops telling the seep index per voxel and
  re-scans the chunk at the boundary — complete, because every face an edit touches has the
  edited voxel as one half. The index is stale in between, so the flush precedes the drain; a
  test that read a coefficient before the flush measured the first 64 edits of a 256-voxel room.
- **The pour provocation measures the pit.** `--breach` bites the basin's pit, and on this seed
  the pit holds 1,000 L at its saddle; a 200,000 L pour spills into the neighbours below and the
  shaft drains the pit in a few ticks — Tier A's no-siphons rule, correct and dry. Two million

- **Two fixtures were something else in a seepage costume.** A rim tunnel "above the table" ended
  at the bank and filled through its own portal; moved into the rock it then stayed dry with the
  lake over it, because the chunk's pooled rate lands lowest first and the room below had room —

## 2026-09-10 — The shoreline is clipped by the terrain, not the lattice: Matthew's rule, built and shot the same night

Matthew, on the 2 m shoreline's screenshot: *"what if I decided that if any block in the boundary
is at the same level and we just let any voxels above cover the water with their own data (like
the water would still be hidden below any raised voxels)."* Then: *"I was more hoping for early
exit on the comparison function really."*

- **Why the shore stepped.** A cell drew its quad only if its *corner* sample was under the level,
  and inside a wet cell the shore was already exact — the plane runs under the whole footprint and
  the depth test hides it wherever the ground stands above the level. The steps were the missing
  quads: a cell whose corner is just above the level draws nothing though half its footprint dips
  under. **So a dry sample beside a wet one now draws the wet one's plane**, and the GPU clips it.
  `WaterSurface.DilateShore`, `--shore=0` the control.
- **The early exit he hoped for is the comparison's removal, and it was refused for a reason worth
  keeping.** The comparison is 65,536 integer compares — not where the cost is (the quads are). A
  plane over the whole catchment with no compare at all gives the same shore, and is wrong in every
  excavation below the lake's level inside the catchment, because the terrain that clips is the
  *dug* terrain and the level is the *seed's*: dig a pit on a hillside above the lake and water
  appears in it. The ring bounds that error to one cell from real water, where Tier B would flow in
  anyway.
- **The first version hung a slab over a saddle.** It dilated into any dry neighbour; the played
  lakes stand at 108% of capacity (the 388% item, still M8c's), so the far slope beyond the divide
  was under the level and the plane showed in mid-air. Dilation is into the *same lake* only —
  same level, not same basin, because a lake merges basins — and the slab went. A sliver can still
  hang where a same-lake cell's footprint straddles a crest, bounded to one cell.
- **Measured on a copy of the played world, windowed screenshot, `--pitch=-40`**: 1,667 → 2,389
  quads, 6,714 ring samples, rebuild 3.7 → 3.4 ms Debug — the first version's inward scan of every
  dry cell was 6.2 ms and the outward walk from the wet cells is what took it back. `C:/tmp/
  shore-before.png` / `shore-after.png`; the shore follows the 0.25 m contour.
- **It reopens the 2 m decision.** The look no longer depends on the lattice, so 2 m buys the
  curve alone at three times 4 m's analysis; the A/B is now `--waterwindow=128` at 16 voxels
  against the shipped 2 m on a pond filling. Recorded in TODO as the play check.

## 2026-09-10 — Slice 3a is built: the grid belongs to the tick, and the pipeline is what makes a wet chunk arrive at a boundary

Matthew's *"ok lets continue"* took the held decision — the reversal of M8b's "water may be added,
removed or disturbed between slices" is knowing rather than a side effect — and 3a was finished
from the stash. **Suite 1,208 → 1,216; 24 break-recipes, 22 caught, and the two misses are named** — `MayHoldWater`'s panel clause is reachable only with no store (the profile arm, where the wire check's *4 arrivals parked* is exactly it), and the release's "still viewed?" clause only for a chunk retained by a job in flight, the window the `LoadFluidJob` "leaving" branch already guards. Two recipes were missed on the first run and pinned on the second: the deferred list applied in reverse order (a restore then a mark for the same chunk is due a tick later than the reverse), and a parked row for a chunk that left being restored anyway (dropped, and the row read again on return).** Headless wire check, the M8b-4a recipe verbatim: 1,166 edits deferred, 4 arrivals parked, 8 reclaimed, `displaced 0`, both identities exact, all 200,000 L handed to Tier A by tick 50 — against M8b-4a's 195,981 L in the same window. The plan's
"Slice 3a — built" section records three departures from the stash's own recipe, each found by
reading the pipeline against it rather than by a test.

- **The deferred list is applied by the tick's own completion, not by the caller at the next
  boundary.** The recipe said "call `ApplyDeferred()` at the top of the boundary block"; between a
  tick ending and the next beginning the grid is nobody's and a mutation lands directly, so a
  `Reclaim` there could run *before* the `Evict` deferred ahead of it. `Complete()` drains the list
  the moment `Ticks` advances, and *not the tick's* and *nothing deferred* are one state. The
  `Evict` due-tick clause (`TickInProgress ? Ticks + 2 : Ticks + 1`) fell out: a mark deferred
  past `Ticks++` is one tick later by arithmetic, and the strict eviction test still passes.
- **Deferring `Restore` alone is unsafe, and the reason is a flag the pipeline owns.**
  `ArriveFluid` cleared `FluidPending` at arrival, so a visit later in the same tick could flow
  water into a chunk whose stored water lands at the boundary — where `Restore` refuses a chunk
  that already holds some, by M8b-4c's own rule. So the pipeline **parks** a wet arrival while the
  grid is the tick's (flag set, row kept if the lane read one, no second read submitted) and
  `ReleaseFluidArrivals` runs it on the first frame after; `CollectEvicted` skips while owned;
  `SaveAll` refuses up front with nothing half-done; Main postpones the autosave a frame at a time
  and finishes a tick in flight before a quit, printing what it cost.
- **A dry chunk does not wait, and the first battery run said where the line goes.** Parking every
  arrival holds every mesh for the length of a tick — under a flood, the world not drawing. Only a
  chunk with water somewhere waits: a panel in RAM, a mark (including one still in the deferred
  queue — every chunk that left inside this tick), an unwritten snapshot, a row. **The dry branch
  fell through to `Reclaim`, which refuses mid-tick, and three tests threw before a recipe was
  applied**; and the fix's second half is that a chunk with a mark standing must wait too, or the
  boundary's collection evicts a *viewed* chunk's panel once water flows in. `MayHoldWater` is the
  one question the pipeline asks mid-tick, honest here; **in 3b it races the worker's panel
  creation and wants a boundary-published set.**
- **Alt+R is queued to the boundary the way the pour is**, so `Remove` refusing mid-tick is a
  contract rather than a crash; the `M8b:` line prints deferrals and parked arrivals.
- **Two things the first run of the fuzzes taught**: a pour is a boundary call, so a round that left
  a tick in flight finishes it first (the game's relay does exactly that); and the eviction fuzz
  now models the pipeline's parking rather than calling `Reclaim` mid-tick, which is the same
  discipline the pipeline learned. `TakeAllDirty`'s third clause — the unvisited half of a tick in
  progress — is unreachable now and the test asserts the refusal instead; `AwakeHeldCells` keeps
  the clause because the report line still reads it mid-tick, and 3b gates that.

## 2026-09-10 — "Is the water supposed to be stuck or frozen?" — no: the field cached an answer that meant two things

Matthew, on the first play of slice 2. It was a regression and the log named it in one line:

```
InvalidOperationException: Portal { Inside = Voxel(-1280, -1, -320) ... } refused 15000 mL it had
room for: the index holds a portal the terrain cannot hold, so an edit never reached it.
   at PortalDrain.Draw() → Main.UpdateFluid
```

**Thrown at every boundary, before `PourPending`, before `Sync` and before `Step`.** So the settle
ran **295 times** while the tick ran **twice**, 130,000 L stayed queued to pour, and the water
stopped. Nothing about the physics was wrong: the boundary was aborting before it reached the tick.

- **The cause is one line of `IFluidTerrain`'s own documentation, cached.** *"An unloaded voxel is
  solid... but solid is the right answer for flow and the wrong one for water that is already
  there"* — `CanHold` returning false means **either rock or not loaded**, which is why `IsLoaded`
  exists at all. `FluidField.Build` asked `CanHold` 32,768 times for a chunk whose voxels had not
  arrived, got "solid" for all of them, and **cached a condition as if it were a fact**. Nothing
  corrected it, because only an *edit* invalidates and no edit was coming. The portal index —
  built from the real world — knew there was a hole where the field saw rock, and the drain's
  assertion is precisely the one that catches a terrain disagreeing with the index.
- **The fix is to decline rather than to bake.** A chunk the source cannot answer for is left
  `Unknown` and falls through until it can be baked truthfully; `Declined` counts it and is on the
  `fluidfield` line, because the counter that would have made this visible in the first play was the
  one I did not print. And **`IsLoaded` now always delegates to the source**: a field outliving its
  chunk must not vouch for it, or M8b-4a's pause rule is told that water in a departed chunk is safe
  to move.
- **Two tests, and the first is the regression verbatim**: a field asked to bake an unloaded chunk
  bakes nothing, answers `Unknown`, and bakes the truth at the boundary after the chunk arrives.
  The second is the pause rule's: a departed chunk is not reported loaded because a field survives
  it.
- **Verified on a copy of the played world**: no exception, ticks 9 → 19 and climbing against the
  broken build's 2, visits 419,633 → 781,731 in ten ticks, `displaced 0` and the identity exact.
  Suite 1,206 → 1,208.
- **The general shape, worth more than the fix: do not cache an answer whose meaning depends on
  state the cache does not capture.** This codebase has three APIs where "no" means two things —
  `VoxelRay.Blocked` against `Missed`, `TryGetMaterial` returning air *and* false, and
  `CanHold`/`IsLoaded` — and each is documented as such. A cache over the first half of one of them
  freezes the second half.

## 2026-09-10 — Slice 2 is built: the tick reads a baked field, and the miss counter is what says slice 3 may start

`FluidField` implements `IFluidTerrain` and is built from one, so the simulation cannot tell which
it was given: the tick, every fixture and every bench arm are untouched, and *a tick against the
field lands the same water as a tick against the world* is a test rather than an argument. One bit
per voxel behind `ClassAt`, 4 KiB a chunk, over the wet chunks and their neighbours; `--fluidfield=0`
is the control arm. **Suite 1,199 → 1,206.**

- **Nought misses inside a tick, which is slice 3's precondition, measured rather than assumed.**
  The field counts every question about a chunk it has no field for and falls through to the
  streamer, which is what makes this slice behaviour-preserving by construction. A 40 s flood
  (`--fillbasin=400000 --breach=7 --injectlitres=100000`) reports **80 chunks, 0.31 MiB, 51,336
  misses of which 0 inside a tick**.
- **All 51,336 are the pour, and they are structural rather than an ordering bug.** 51,200 of them
  is exactly 6,400 poured cells × the eight `CanHold` questions an `Add` asks. **A pour asks whether
  a voxel can hold before any panel exists there**, so a reachable set derived from the panels
  cannot know about it in advance — and a pour happens on the sim thread, where falling through is
  what the code always did. **So the counter had to be split**: `Misses` is a cost, `TickMisses` is
  the correctness gate.
- **One ring of face neighbours was wrong and the counter refuted it.** The first rule was *wet
  chunks plus their face neighbours*; widening it from 32 chunks to 80 left the miss count
  **identical to the digit**, which is what said the misses were not the shell at all. The rule is
  two rings now — 1 + 6 + 18 — because **an awake cell need not hold water**, so it can sit in the
  first ring and visiting it reads *its* neighbours in the second. Manhattan rather than Chebyshev,
  because every read is along a face: 25 chunks a seed rather than 125.
- **A field is an amortisation, and the test that found it is the one that failed.** *"The field
  asks its source fewer times than the world does"* is **false**: baking 27 chunks is 884,736
  questions against the direct arm's 85,384 over 120 ticks. **A chunk's field costs 32,768 questions
  and saves one per read**, so it loses whenever more is baked than the water uses — which is the
  argument for the reachable set being the wet chunks rather than the view, and the second reason
  (after `--terrain`'s 1.47x) that this slice is slice 3's enabler and not a speed-up. The assertion
  is an equality now: the source is asked once per voxel of every chunk built, and never again.

## 2026-09-10 — The surface mesh was not a threading problem: the walk asked the grid per cell where an array read would do, 28.38 ms → 12.09

The plan was *the surface mesh off the main thread, then slice 3's single worker*. Splitting the
rebuild's timer first — M5c-1's lesson, which costed propagation and found the derive was the larger
half — says the walk is **25.40 ms of 28.38** and the install (`ToArray`, the Godot marshalling,
`AddSurfaceFromArrays`, all of which must stay where the renderer is) is **2.98**. So the walk was
worth moving; and then it turned out to be worth *fixing* instead.

**`FluidGrid.SurfaceCells()`**: every held cell with nothing above it, and its millilitres, in one
array read per cell. **A chunk stores `[z][x][y]` — Y contiguous** — so the cell above is the next
index, and a column is walked downward carrying the value above it; only a panel's top layer asks
the grid at all, once per column rather than once per cell. `FluidSurface` was doing
`HeldCells()` filtered by `AmountAt(cell + Y)`, which is a panel lookup per held cell.

**Measured on the same 3 ML flood, windowed, Debug, ~259,000 held cells:**

```
                walk      install    total
before        25.40 ms    2.98 ms   28.38 ms
after          8.85 ms    3.24 ms   12.09 ms
```

At the 0.25 s rebuild interval that is **114 ms a second of main thread down to 48**, against the
water tick's whole budget of 120 ms a second.

- **Threading is now optional rather than the plan, and the sequencing argument has flipped.** The
  remaining 8.85 ms is a scan of the wet volume — 36 panels × 32,768 slots, ~7.5 ns a slot in Debug
  — and moving it to a worker would need a snapshot of the panels, because the sim thread mutates
  them. **After slice 3 it needs no snapshot at all**: the tick already runs on a worker with
  exclusive access to the grid, so the walk rides it for free. **So slice 3 goes next, and the walk
  moves with it if 12 ms still reads as a hitch.** Sixth named fallback dissolved by measurement.
- **The oracle is two definitions pinned by equality**, the `IsCaveAt`/`GenerateTerrain` shape:
  `SurfaceCells()` against `HeldCells()` filtered by the grid. **The fixture has to stack two bodies
  in one column with air between and straddle a panel boundary**, because *"the highest cell in each
  column"* is a different rule that passes every fixture with one body per column — a flooded
  gallery under a pond is the case that separates them, and it is the ordinary shape of this game.
- **The windowed run is the only instrument here**, because `FluidSurface` is not created without a
  renderer and headless prints `no surface drawn`. A `--profile` run generates its own world, so the
  played world's 19,454 quads had to be reproduced by pouring a comparable flood (3 ML, 259,000
  cells) rather than by opening a copy — a copy opened at spawn holds no Tier B water at all, since
  the wet chunks are elsewhere and Tier B only holds what is loaded.

## 2026-09-09 — The settle's wait is per chunk: a portal drawing into one cell no longer postpones every sheet in the world

`SheetSettle` counted inflow with two world totals — `AddedMillilitres` and `DisturbedCells` — so
one portal drawing 150 L into one cell reset the wait for every sheet everywhere. That is the
treadmill named on 2026-09-07, priced on 2026-09-09 and then met head-on in slice 1's play: **0
passes in 340 ticks with 70,000 cells awake**. `Add` and a waking `Disturb` now stamp their chunk
with the tick; the sheet flood takes the max stamp over the chunks it touches; a sheet is levelled
only when *its own* chunks have been quiet for K ticks. The global gate is gone — every boundary
runs a pass and the per-sheet test decides.

**Measured, same invocation, before and after** (`--fillbasin=400000 --breach=7
--injectlitres=100000`, r6h/2v, 8 m/s, 40 s window, Debug):

```
                      global counter        per chunk
settle passes              0                    79
sheets levelled            0                   818
sheets still fed           —                   630
handed to Tier A      50,963 L             54,912 L
active at the end        6,436                5,721
```

439 ms of solve across the 40 s window, longest pass 15.27 ms. **The control was run from the
stashed working tree rather than argued from the mechanism**, and it printed `settle 0 pass(es)`
exactly as the play log did.

- **The wait's meaning is unchanged, and it nearly was not.** The first condition was `age >= K`;
  the world counter meant `age > K`, because inflow during a tick zeroed *that* boundary's count, so
  K = 2 fired on the third boundary after a pour. `--settleafter=` has recorded play figures against
  it — 80 s at 2 against 12 s at 0 — and a rule that moved the number by one would have invalidated
  them silently. Caught by a test, and the battery's "the wait is one tick short" now guards it.
- **What it does not fix, stated rather than discovered later**: the sheet that *contains* the
  inflow. A lake fed at one point is still not levelled, however large and however far its far end
  is from the feed. That is the share rule's job and it is the honest limit of chunk resolution.
- **Three trigger tests asserted nothing before this, and the same trap wrote three more.**
  `Add(cell, 200_000)` takes one cell's capacity and hands the rest back, so those pours were one
  cell — and `LevelSheets` skips a single-cell sheet by construction. `PourRow` fills a run of floor
  cells and says why in its remarks.
- **Twelve recipes, and the one that could not be caught was answered by deleting it.** The wait
  began as a field the flood accumulated and `Union` merged with a max — and *"a merged sheet
  forgets the fed half"* survived a test written for it, because **the survivor of a merge is
  whichever has more cells, so no fixture can reliably put the fed half on the losing side.** It is
  a walk of the sheet's own cells now, at judgement and after the share's early-out, so there is no
  merge to get wrong; the game's figures are identical to the digit across the change, with only
  the noisy/under-share split moving by one. **A test that cannot be made to fail is a design
  saying the state is in the wrong place.** Two of the remaining misses are identities — the stamp
  forgotten with its chunk is memory hygiene, and a sheet nobody fed looking fed differs only in
  the first K ticks of a simulation's life. **One was a bad recipe rather than a gap**: it reordered
  two assignments that both land before the return. Rewritten as *a new stamp leaves the cache
  stale*, it is caught, which is what says the cache update in `NoteInflow` is load-bearing.
- **The one-entry cache is not an optimisation to trim.** The flood asks per cell and a sheet's
  cells arrive in spatial order; without it the played lake's 162,572-cell sheet is that many
  dictionary probes to *decide* whether to level. Same shape as `FluidGrid`'s panel cache.

                            1.47x                   1.59x
