## 2026-09-09 — "The cross handling overhead": slice 1's deferred cells leave the swap, and the far floor finds the risk it was for

Matthew, on the pass above and before any code: *"the cross handling overhead, makes it less than
optimal?"* It is, and the tax has the wrong shape. Two refinements, decisions 8 and 9 in the plan.

- **The bookkeeping scaled with the backlog being ignored rather than with the work being done.**
  Deferring into `_pending` means the next `Begin()` swaps the deferred cells back in and partitions
  all of them again to admit 512: a 1.3 MiB streaming walk on the flood-on-open's 110,000 cells,
  ~0.5 ms Release and ~2 ms Debug (*estimates*), every tick, to schedule 1.5 ms of Debug visits —
  **more overhead than far water**, and a ~20% tax on a tick with a 3,000-cell near set. **The carry
  now stays out of the swap** in its own ordered list: O(new wakes + admitted) a tick, ~50× less on
  that fixture, and the O(backlog) walk moves to once per viewer chunk change — the only event that
  can reclassify anything — at ~2 ms every 1.1 s walking, under 1%.
- **The price is the "Begin() and nothing else" claim, and the four readers are named rather than
  discovered**: `ActiveCellCount`, `Complete`'s `ActiveAfter`, `Settle`'s loop and `Pending`, which
  `LevelSheets` seeds from and which must be both lists in a fixed order — a `HashSet` seed would
  put the sheet flood back on hash ordering, which this class rejected for the batch on the same
  grounds. **`AwakeHeldCells` stays right untouched** because the carry is still in `_queued`, which
  was the load-bearing half of the earlier shape and survives.
- **The seam is an artefact, not only a cost, and it is what the floor was always for.** Round-robin
  admission puts your own pool's leading edge — cells that just crossed the ring, 16–24 m out, and a
  10,000 L pour spreads ~18 m in five seconds — in one queue behind a lake draining a hundred metres
  off, where it would stall for the length of that flood. **Far admission is nearest-first**,
  bucketed on the same per-move walk, with **one part in eight of the quota reserved for a rotating
  tail.** *"One granule in eight"* was the right fraction against the wrong risk: the quota already
  protects far from near, and what needs a floor is the far tail against the far front.

## 2026-09-09 — The water thread, slice 1: the planning pass says a sort delivers nothing, and the far floor is the wrong quantity

Read slice 1's paragraph against `FluidSimulation.Begin/Resume/Complete`, `Main.UpdateFluid`,
`SheetSettle`, `PortalDrain` and `AwakeHeldCells`. **The slice names the right feature and the
wrong mechanism, twice** — the adaptive radius's grow rule a second time, and both corrections are
the same shape: a rule translated from a sentence naming a quantity the failure is not made of.
Nothing built; seven decisions handed back with recommendations, in the plan's new "Slice 1 — the
planning pass".

- **A sort cannot make near water tick at 2 Hz, because a tick does not end until its batch does.**
  `Complete()` fires when the cursor reaches the end of the batch, and the frame budget lapses
  *inside* a tick, never between one and the next. So bucketing near-first visits near cells in the
  first frame of the flood-on-open's 188-frame tick and then not again for three seconds. The order
  is necessary and not sufficient: **what delivers 2 Hz is far cells being deferred past the
  boundary.**
- **"One granule in eight of each frame's budget" is a frame quantity settling a batch question**,
  and paying it means interleaving far visits between near ones under clock control — which costs
  the property M8b's tick budget slice bought and asserts over 400 ticks, *a tick run whole lands
  the same water as a tick run in slices*. Make admission a function of the sets and never of the
  clock and that test survives verbatim with both arms given the same near centre. **So the far
  floor is cells admitted per tick.**
- **The shape is a change to `Begin()` and nothing else**, and the reason is `_queued`. Partition
  the batch in place, admit `near + max(512, near)`, move the tail into the fresh `_pending`
  *before* the tick runs — so this tick's wakes append behind it and the round-robin is free — and
  leave it in `_queued`. `_queued` then still means "awake and not yet visited this tick", which is
  what `AwakeHeldCells` walks, so the store, the eviction, `ActiveCellCount`, `ActiveAfter` and
  `Settle`'s loop condition are all correct untouched. **A far backlog held in a fourth list of its
  own would be a lake that quietly stops being saved.**
- **Throttling rather than scheduling: with no near water awake the tick is today's tick, exactly.**
  That bounds the change to the case the play is about and is a property a test can assert. Its
  price is a cliff at the first near cell — one drip beside you drops a 110,000-cell far flood to
  the floor — named rather than smoothed, because every floor has that edge and each alternative
  buys it back with a second constant. `max(floor, near)` rather than a constant makes **a tick at
  most twice its near cost**, so the rate the player watches degrades only with the water the player
  is standing in.
- **The boundary work goes back to 2 Hz during a far flood, and that is a rate change in the game.**
  The settle, the hand-off and the drain all run at `begin`, so today a 188-frame tick throttles
  them to ~0.3 Hz; a portal voxel priced at "30 L/s at 2 Hz" is 30 L/s again. A restoration rather
  than an inflation — but it makes the known treadmill turn faster, and the figure that would
  reverse it is the settle pass, up to 275 ms in Debug on the played lake's 162,572-cell sheet. The
  lever if it bites is seeding the settle from the near set alone.
- **Two smaller ones.** Reclassifying the carry is exact if it runs only when the viewer's chunk
  moved, which takes the 110,000-cell case from a per-tick partition to a per-move one. And Core
  keeps the old order by construction — `rings = 0`, no viewer — so every existing fixture, the
  whole bench and `Settle()` are the control arm without being edited.

  the flat floor, because every transfer queues more cells. **Fourth outing for a plan being

## 2026-09-07 — M8b-4c planned: the panel lingers one tick, the chunk is not loaded to the water until its row is read, and the cache keeps nothing

**Matthew: "M8b-4c please Claude also" — then "Oh just plan if we dont have one."** It had a
paragraph in the M8b-4 pass and no pass of its own, so this is the pass: the paragraph read
against the grid, the pause, the pipeline's three arrival paths and save queue, the cache and the
store. Planned, not built; see M8-PLAN's "M8b-4c — the planning pass". Four things worth keeping:

- **"Written and released at forget" strands a flood front on every walk.** The row lists the
  chunk's *paused* cells; its *queued* cells — a front inside a chunk that just left — are found
  only by walking the active set, which 4b refused per chunk of a shell. Released at once, those
  cells are visited, read an empty panel and sleep unlisted; the arrival's face wake cannot reach
  an interior. So the panel stays one tick: the 4a pause visits and lists every queued cell for
  free, the snapshot at the boundary that completes the first tick begun after the mark is exact,
  and what a neighbour wakes into the chunk meanwhile is a face cell by construction.
- **The chunk arrives before its water in all three paths, and the gate is "not loaded, to the
  water".** A neighbour's flow into the chunk's air before the row is read meets `Restore`'s
  throw, which stays as the tripwire. A `FluidPending` flag on the record, read by the fluid
  terrain through the streamer beside `TryGetMaterial` so the hot path pays nothing new; the
  restore as a chunk-slot job on the serial lane so cancellation, retention and revival are M2c-2's
  and M6b's machinery; `ChunkArrived` on a new `onFluidReady` after the restore. Reading the row
  inside `LoadChunkJob` is rejected as one path of three — a never-edited chunk whose cave flooded
  has a row and no blob.
- **A load must not race a save, and the chunks' answer (the lane and a priority band) is not
  needed**: the snapshot the pipeline holds until its batch reports is the newest state, so the
  sources are memory, the evicting set, the unwritten snapshots, then the store's index. The wrong
  order restores the past with the identity exact; the twin sees it.
- **Two silent deletions named as recipes**: `_storedAwake` not forgetting an evicted chunk makes
  the next autosave write its row empty — *the lake deleted by the save*; `_emptied` gaining it
  does the same by another route. And `held` now leaves RAM, so `evicted` joins the identity.

The cache keeps no panel — `--blob` already said the plan's sparse form is the largest of the
three, and a hit's fluid load is 0.1 ms Release for a lake panel. Six decisions handed back with
recommendations; a `--evict` bench arm and the turnaround on a played-world copy price it.

  whole, and the played lake is 1,254 of them — eight seconds at a quit against a tenth of one.
  Both forms ship, the reader takes both, the writer switches at 1,024 cells, an estimate off the
  table in the plan. Sixth outing for *measure before believing the named quantity*, and the
  first where the plan had the right two arms and compared them on the wrong axis.
- **A row that lists awake cells must be rewritten once they rest.** The fuzz found it on its
  first run: 33 paused where 19 were awake. A cell listed awake at one quit, restored, woken at
  its arrival and found at rest writes nothing, so its panel is clean while its row still says
  awake — harmless per open, one visit each, and the played lake would pay a million visits every
  session for ever. The simulation remembers which rows list awake cells and the save rewrites
  those too, so the rows list exactly what is awake now. The fuzz asserts the paused count after
  every reopen equals the awake count before the quit, and the battery has the recipe.
- **A drained panel writes itself empty, which the plan did not say.** The grid releases an
  empty panel, and a row written while the lake was there would put it back at the next open —
  water from nothing, invisible to the identity because `loaded` rises with `held`. A panel that
  has been snapshotted is remembered on release and written as an empty row. The fuzz drains one
  stored chunk dry and quits at the end of every run, because one seed went eighty rounds without
  doing it by chance and the guard on the dice failed.
- **26 recipes, 25 caught, one identity.** The identity is the `Distinct` in the awake-index
  sort — both callers hand over a set already — and it stays as belt and braces with the label.
  Four fixtures were wrong first: a cell at x = 35 in a test about the west chunk; a "lake at
  rest" on a corridor that ran into the next chunk; four cells' worth poured into one cell; and
  the dice guard above. **Not priced: the sim-thread copy at a save on the played world**, ~30–60
  µs a full panel by the bench's read figures, 50–75 ms for the lake at a quit as an estimate;
  the play is where it gets a number, and the lever is a dense `memcpy` with the extraction on
  the lane.

**Handed back on the same message: the fall rule.** Matthew asked what it would cost to let water
fall 2, 4, 8, 16 cells a tick when the cells below are vacant. Answered in the reply, not built:
the visit already reads the cell below; reading up to sixteen is bounded at 16 reads a falling
cell and falling cells are a column, not the waterline, so the CPU is a rounding error on the
budget. What it changes is not cost but the termination proof's vertical term (still monotone —
a longer fall lowers Σ(amount × Y) by more), the wake rule (the cells passed through are empty and
need no wake; the landing's neighbours do), and the hand-off, which reads rest and is untouched.
The per-cell *acceleration* reading — first tick one, next two — needs a velocity byte a cell,
which doubles the panel, and the cheap version is "fall as far as is vacant, up to N", which is
terminal velocity from the first tick. Recorded in TODO under M8d's waterfall question.

  shrink cannot trigger a grow (needs a dwell). That is a fuzzed oracle, not a tuning.

## 2026-09-06 — How often the queue's "200 ms re-sort" fires: 4.6–5.0 a second, and there is no timer

**Matthew: "lets profile how often 'scheduler re-sorts every 200 ms by distance to the viewer'
fires."** The question exposed a piece of folklore: CLAUDE.md, the M2a paragraph and the queue's
own summary all said "re-sorted on a 200 ms timer", and there is no timer. `JobQueue.SweepIfDueLocked`
runs inside a worker's `TryTake`, so a sweep happens when a worker asks for work *and* the interval
has elapsed since the last one — the interval is a floor, not a schedule, and a queue nobody takes
from is never swept. So how often it fires is a fact about when workers wake, and only a count
could say. Counters under the queue's lock (`SweepStatistics`, `JobQueue.Statistics`,
`JobScheduler.Sweeps`), a `sweeps` line on the profile (the window's counts, the run's peaks) and a
periodic `M2a:` line (the delta since the last report). Suite 1,053 → 1,058; five break-recipes,
five caught. Headless, Debug, r6h/2v, 8 workers:

```
arm                              sweeps/s  mean gap  longest  empty     entries/sweep  sweep ms mean / max  TryTake  took a job
standing, 30 s window              4.63     216 ms   289 ms   133/139        18          0.012 / 2.706       3,810       845
standing, 120 s                    4.97     201 ms   224 ms   590/597         5          0.005 / 2.869      11,132       845
12 m/s, turning every 10 s, 30 s   4.47     223 ms   304 ms   112/134        32          0.016 / 3.120      11,410     4,821
12 m/s, turning every 10 s, 120 s  4.60     218 ms   292 ms   475/552        13          0.011 / 3.024      33,033    12,799
40 m/s, 30 s                       5.00     200 ms   272 ms     0/150        63          0.021 / 3.459      47,704    23,256
```

Five things worth keeping:

- **It fires 4.5–5.0 times a second whether the world is moving or not, and the longest gap in
  five arms is 304 ms — so "every 200 ms" is true in practice, for a reason that is not the
  interval.** `JobScheduler.IdleWaitMillis` is 100: an idle worker's semaphore wait times out and
  loops through `TryTake`, so eight idle workers poll the queue about 80 times a second (400 takes
  per 5 s at rest, exactly 8 × 10) and the first poll after the interval elapses sweeps. That is why
  the gap at rest is 201–216 ms rather than 200, and why the longest is always under 300: the
  interval plus at most one idle wait. Set the idle wait to a second and the same code would sweep
  at 200 ms while flying and at up to 1.2 s while standing still.
- **At rest 590 of 597 sweeps found nothing queued.** Sweeping an empty list is the lock and two
  timestamps, 2–5 µs. DESIGN's "sorting a few thousand entries five times a second costs nothing"
  was right about the rate and never said the five are usually over nothing.
- **The cost is entirely where the list is, and that is the fill's first sweeps.** 1,639–1,956
  entries, 2.7–3.5 ms, once — the lock held while every other worker waits on it. Inside any of the
  five windows the sweep held the lock for 0.002–0.010% of a worker's time. Nothing to build.
- **At 40 m/s the list at sweep time is 63 entries, not thousands**, because `MaxSubmissionsPerFrame`
  (64) bounds what enters per frame and eight workers drain faster than that: 47,704 takes in 30 s,
  23,256 of which found a job, so the workers spend half their takes finding nothing at the very
  speed the world stops drawing at. The 40 m/s cliff is the sim thread (main 83.89%, 0 drawn), not
  the queue — M5d-1's finding restated from the workers' side.
- **`SweepNow` has had no caller since M2a**: 0 forced in every arm. The instrument counts them
  because a re-sort asked for by name would be a change of design, and it would show here first.

**And a test flake five milestones old was diagnosed with a control, and fixed.**
`JobSchedulerTests.AThrowingJobFaultsWithoutTakingTheWorkerDownWithIt` failed in the first suite
run of the change, then 3 in 5 alone; with the change stashed and the tests rebuilt, 2 in 5 — so
today's machine exposes a race the test has always had, not one the counters added. The
mechanism, read off the code: before its first sweep the queue pops newest-first (the documented
contract, `BeforeAnySweepTheQueueIsInArrivalOrder`), so the *survivor* runs before the thrower; the
test disposes on the survivor's event, and the thrower still queued comes back `Dropped` from
`DropAll` with the worker alive and well. The test's comment assumed a FIFO. It now waits for both
results before disposing: 10 of 10 after. The five earlier flakes recorded a different symptom, the
ten-second wait expiring, which this race cannot produce — that one is the test's own starved-thread
branch, and stays as recorded.

## 2026-09-06 — M8b-4 planned: the walk's fix is a pause, the store is a mirror first, and the lake is 78 MiB

**Matthew: "M8b-4 planning pass please."** The plan's paragraph — *a `fluid` table, one blob per
chunk holding the resting cells, written when a chunk with settled water unloads, read when it
loads, never woken by the load* — read against `FluidGrid`, the pipeline's unload and save path,
`IWorldStore` and the play's two findings. Three of its assumptions are not so, and the third
splits the part; the section is in M8-PLAN under "M8b-4 — the planning pass", the decisions are
handed back, and no code was written. Four things worth keeping:

- **A walk does not delete water; it deletes *awake* water, and the fix is a pause.** The grid
  keeps a panel per chunk and nothing releases it on unload — the streamer's forget never reaches
  the grid — so a sleeping cell in a departed chunk sits in RAM and is there when the chunk
  returns. The play's 75% was the cells mid-flow: visited, their chunk gone, the adapter answering
  "solid" for unloaded (right for flow, wrong for water already there), displaced into unloaded
  neighbours and drained. Unloaded is not rock; for water that is there it is *unknown*, and the
  response to unknown is to stop. So: a visited cell whose chunk is unloaded sleeps in place and is
  remembered; at arrival, through the one `onVoxelsReady` hook all three paths share, it wakes
  along with every held cell on the chunk's faces and the loaded neighbours' cells touching them,
  since a boundary edit while it was away is the one thing a pause cannot have seen. No water
  moves, so *the same millilitres in the same cells* holds by construction, with no disk. This
  departs from decision 5 and 3b's unload method: a settle cannot run over a chunk the terrain
  calls solid, and a pause is exact where a settle moves water along paths into chunks that are
  also leaving.
- **The store is a mirror of RAM before it is a replacement for it.** With panels never released,
  "read when the chunk loads" has nothing to do: read every panel at open, and each is paused by
  the same rule until its chunk arrives — one mechanism for revival and for load, and the blob
  carries the awake cells' indices so a stored flood resumes as a paused one does. The fluid blob
  rides the chunk batch as a third list on `Write`, M6a's argument again: voxels in one transaction
  and water in another is, after a crash between them, water inside rock.
- **The played lake is ~1,254 chunks of floor at 64 KiB a panel — 78 MiB, over the 64 MiB trigger
  `FluidGrid` recorded at M8a-2, on the first lake the store meets.** So releasing a panel with its
  chunk and reading it back through the serial lane is not a someday lever; it is the third slice,
  priced first on a bench arm that walks the box across the flooded mine.
- **Three slices, by what a defect costs**: 4a the pause and the arrival (Core, no disk, the
  play's `displaced` at zero across a walk is the oracle, a lifecycle fuzz with a control arm);
  4b the store (last and alone — permanent data loss — with the blob battery in M6a's shape, the
  contract suite's third list, and a headless quit-and-reopen with `held` equal across it); 4c
  the panel leaving RAM. Recipes for 4a are filed in the plan before its code exists.

  doubled half under 64 awake cells; the chamber floor's spreading front is a wide disturbance
  and is levelled in both arms, which is the rule working; the spill arm is unchanged to the tick.

  `DugTerrain` bakes a column's cave field on its first `CanHold`, and the first flood over the
  lake paid for every column it read inside the timed pass: 1,385 ms, then 480 with the floor

  same bake over a mine the flow had baked unevenly. The played floor is ~23 ms a pass Release;
  the play's 275 ms is Debug.
- **The battery's first run installed the old solve.** It restored the subject with a git
  checkout and the subject was uncommitted: recipe 1 was caught, the restore put the pre-slice
  file back, and nine recipes matched nowhere. Restore from a copy. Of the recipes proper,

  front flag is woken a tick later by its neighbour's spread, and rest-and-verify cannot see

  tilt rest allows. Two are findings rather than holes: freezing before the border is complete is
  unreachable under the wake rule, and reading the wrong cell's amount as the border is within
  four millilitres of the identity.
- **Eight is a guess inside a measured range**, four to sixteen all negligible on the lake and
  all halving the mine. What a person judges is a poured mound or a merge line sitting
  unlevelled: the merge is the step detector's, the mound is the share's, and `--settleshare=0` is
  how it looked before.

## 2026-09-05 — M8b-3b built: the settle is a solve of sheets, and "never" is now 258 ticks

**Matthew: "M8b-3b please Claude."** The settle designed in the M8b-3 planning pass is built:
`FluidSimulation.LevelSheets()` levels every sheet the active set touches — the wet, holdable,
supported cells at one Y, sideways-connected — to within a millilitre, or packs a sheet whose
share is under a litre into as few of its cells as hold it at 999 mL, through `FluidGrid.Transfer`
only, bottom-up, waking the front and the water above every drawn-down cell and nothing else.
`SheetSettle` fires it at a tick boundary after *K* ticks with no inflow (`--settleafter=`, 2 by
default, 0 settles under inflow), then at every boundary until nothing is awake. Suite 1,006 →
1,032. 23 break-recipes applied, 22 caught; the miss is an identity. `--fluidsolve both` is the bench arm
and `--spill` has the settle as a third. Seven things worth keeping, with the table in M8-PLAN's
"M8b-3b — built":

- **The chamber's 1,915-tick settle is 38 ticks, the 16 m mine's 11,130 is 136, and the 96 m
  mine's *never* is 258** — all reaching a rest `VerifyQuiescent` calls real, all exact. The
  visits fell 53×, 207× and 56× where the wait arm could be run at all. The plan said "one solve
  and a handful of ticks" and the handful is hundreds, because the solve levels a sheet and the
  ticks after are the front creeping and water falling a cell a tick — what a settle that moves
  water only along the automaton's own paths cannot shorten, by the no-siphons rule.
- **A pass per boundary is O(sheet) per tick while a front creeps.** On the 96 m mine at bore 9
  each new front cell makes one pair unsettled and the 28,000-cell sheet is re-levelled for it —
  44.7 M cell writes over 4,241 passes, 17 of the arm's 18 s — so that arm is only 1.8× cheaper
  than waiting, against hundreds of times elsewhere. Lever named in TODO, not built.
- **The pass is atomic and 1–3 µs a cell in Release.** The played world's ~1.3 million-cell mine
  floor is seconds a pass, once, in one frame, when its flood stops; the slice is the lever and
  is recorded with that trigger. Not met: the play drained the lakes, and the flood on open is
  now 91 kL in 29 ticks. On copies of that world the default fired no pass in the flood (the
  drain is inflow every tick) and zero fired 29 at 12 ms each in Debug for no change in the
  active set — the early flood is falls, not sheets.
- **The skip rule is what makes the solve safe to repeat.** A sheet with no transferable pair
  inside it — the automaton's own rest within four millilitres, or a film every cell of which is
  under the threshold — is written nowhere and woken nowhere. A second pass over a levelled
  sheet is a no-op, and a still puddle stays still. Packing applies to a sheet that *has* a move.
- **The wake set is exactly what `VerifyQuiescent` checks, and four recipes say so.** Not waking
  the front, not waking the water above a drawn-down cell, waking the front only when a cell
  rose, and waking above only when a cell emptied were each caught — by fixtures that put water
  down through `FluidGrid.Fill`, asleep and unlevel, so that whatever is awake after a solve is
  what the solve woke. Bottom-up order has its own fixture (a levelled floor unsupporting the
  sheet above it) and both order recipes were caught by it.
- **Two fixtures were wrong first.** The packing test was five cells each under a litre, which
  is at rest already, and the skip rule left it — right; the fixture now has a cell that can
  spread. And `DisturbedCells` counted only cells newly woken, so an edit under moving water was
  not inflow; it counts wet cells touched. The r6 control is unchanged to the digit.
- **The solve and the hand-off had a seam, the first fix was wrong, and the control arm is what
  said so.** The relay's spill handed 10,558 L in the window with the settle off and 4,178 L with
  it on. The hand-off reads the record of no-move visits, and a levelled sheet is asleep without
  one — level, still, on the ground, and never the basin's: the held-for-ever puddle again. Waking
  every written cell for its visit fixed the sealed-box test, left the number at 4,117 L, and
  cost ten times the visits on the 96 m mine — the visit came a tick late, every tick. So the
  solve now lists what it levelled and left with no move as resting, which is what a visit would
  find, and runs before the hand-off. **With that, `--spill`'s new third arm rests in 18 and 29
  ticks against 170 and 314, every litre in the basins, and the relay's whole 50,000 L is the
  basin's inside the profile window, Tier B empty** — a spill soaks away in twelve seconds
  instead of minutes, which is the settle and the hand-off doing together what neither did alone.

The look question — a tunnel floor levelling itself in one tick behind a creeping front, and
*K* = 0's flat stream — is Matthew's to judge in play; `--settleafter=` is the sweep.

## 2026-09-05 — "How do I measure how much is seeping into the hillside?" — the log already does, and it had two numbers nobody asked for

**Matthew asked how to measure a spill soaking in.** The answer is the `M8b:` line the game prints

it`; `start.cmd` runs the console build, so both are in the console window behind the game and in
`user://logs/godot.log`. Press `R`, read `handed` before and after, and the difference is what soaked
in; `received` says the pit's basin got it. Reading the log of his last play (16:51, the session
with the two shots) to give the answer with his own numbers turned up two things the report prints
and nothing had read:

- **Walking away deletes the flood's awake water, and it was 41% of the drawn litres.** `displaced`
  is the term for water in a cell that can no longer hold it, and an unloaded voxel is solid: an
  awake cell in a chunk that leaves the box is visited next tick, finds itself and every neighbour
  unholdable, and is drained — counted, identity exact, gone. In that session 7,163,284 L were drawn
  into the mine and 2,924,347 L were displaced, every jump landing on a window move, with zero
  placements in the run and no other way to make a voxel unholdable. A sleeping cell survives —
  nothing visits it — and comes back with its chunk; in a flood nearly everything is awake. The
  plan's M8b-4 says a *quit* deletes water and writes "a chunk with settled water" on unload; the
  play says a walk deletes it, before any settle exists to write. **M8b-4's first fact, and the
  settle's unload case with a number** — 3b's unload method is on M8b-4's path rather than beside
  it. Tier A lost its own share on the same moves: 1,855,295 L "would not fit back" over six window
  moves, which is `SeedOverflowLitres`' documented cost of a window smaller than the terrain and
  had never read above zero before the mine existed.
- **The tick reached 1,267 frames with 648,204 cells active** — twenty-one seconds a tick at 60 fps
  in Debug — so a spill poured on a hillside in that world moves a cell every twenty seconds and
  the hand-off runs once every twenty seconds. The played world is the wrong instrument for the
  hand-off's decision until the settle exists. The bench's `--spill` is the clean measurement (all
  10,000 L in the basin after 170 ticks, Tier B empty), and a fresh world under `--nosave` is the
  play version.

One instrument label: the water line's `% of capacity` reads 525% because `WindowCapacityLitres`
sums leaf basins only and a merged lake stands above their ridges. Wrong as a label the moment
lakes merge, right as litres, left as a TODO note.

**The number exists and nothing on screen shows it.** A `handed` / `received` readout on the HUD is
the missing instrument for the hand-off's own decision, and it is offered rather than built.

cells a tick visited and found nothing to do for; `SurfaceHandoff` walks it at the boundary and
hands every cell standing on the analytic ground — `SurfaceHeightAt + 1`, the plane 2a pinned — to
the basin under its sample through `WaterSystem.Receive`; `handed` and `received` are terms on both
tiers' lines with a `handoff` line between them; `--spill` on the bench is the measurement. Seven
things worth keeping:

- **Water on the analytic ground is already Tier A's, by Tier A's own model, so the hand-off is
  `BasinRainfall`'s delivery with a different source.** Rain on a catchment is litres in the pit the
  moment it lands; Tier A never holds water *on* a hillside. A Tier B cell resting on the plane is
  rain that has landed. Three things follow and each is a test: a cell on an outlet sample leaves
  the world, counted on `received` and `spilled` both, because kept in Tier B it would sleep on the
  ground until an edit touched it; a tank whose floor is the natural ground leaks into the basin
  exactly as rain inside its walls would, while a tank on a placed floor holds, because the seam
  reads the *seed* surface — pinned so that a change is deliberate, revisit trigger the first play
  that reads the leak as wrong; and only the cell on the plane is tested, since the cell above it
  falls into the space the hand-off leaves and hands off in turn.

  20,000-tick cap with 6,634 still awake and 189.9 M visits, and rests after 314 ticks (2.6 min)

  held, drawn and stored for ever are 9,999 and 49,999 L in two basins with 1,000 mL pending — and
  every identity is exact in every arm. The pass is 0.8 µs a hand-off with the analytic seed
  function. **So M8a's named fallback, a coarser rest tolerance, is dead for the surface**, and it

  The visit that could neither fall nor spread is the visit that would have moved the water; the
  list is a record of visits, cleared when the next tick begins, and a cell topped up after resting

  bowl's floor spreads for several ticks before anything is handed, and a test says so — because
