## 2026-09-05 — M8b-2c: water crosses the seam — a lake drains into a hole in the game, both tiers say so to the litre, and a dead-end shaft takes a litre a tick

**The A → B seam is wired end to end and the water is in the game.** Suite 974 → 989. `PortalDrain`
draws whole litres out of Tier A into Tier B at every tick boundary; `PortalTracker` feeds the index
from the pipeline's three arrival paths, its edit hook and the streamer's forget, and owns decision
1; `StreamerSeedHeights` reads the seed surface off the loaded columns; `--fillbasin=<litres>` and
`--breach=<voxels>` are the headless provocation. **First run at r4h/2v, standing, 20 s: 200,000 L
poured into the basin under the spawn, a 3 × 3 shaft eight deep bitten at its pit, 7 portals filed
and 7 covered, 1,117 L drawn over 144 draws, held == injected + drawn − removed − displaced exact
on Tier B, held == injected − spilled − drawn exact on Tier A, and Tier A's drawn equal to Tier
B's** — the shaft's 72 cells ending full to the litre. The r6 control with nothing breached is
unchanged to the digit, 2601 / 325 / 3446 at 411, with the new terms printing as zeros. Seven
things worth keeping:

- **The covered test is on the outside voxel, re-read per portal, and the flow stops at the face
  and not before.** The Core twin — `WaterSystem` over an analytic bowl, `FluidSimulation` over a
  dug terrain, the index between them — drives a tunnel into the bowl's wall at Y 35 under a lake
  standing at 35.375 and asserts the lake stops within one draw of the face's own volume, with the
  chamber behind the tunnel half empty; a tunnel at 38 under the same lake draws nothing until the
  lake is raised past it. Both identities and the seam's equality are asserted after every tick.
- **The first breach was under the player and drew nothing, and that was the geometry, not the
  seam.** The spawn's sample belongs to a basin whose pit is elsewhere; 200,000 L raised the lake
  to −10 against a floor at −12 and the player's sample sits well above that, so the profile read
  "1 wet, 0 covered" — the detector fired and said the lake was not over the hole. **The breach now
  goes at the basin's pit**, which is where a pour covers first and where a real breach drains a
  lake from, and when the player's sample drains off the window it takes the nearest basin's pit
  and says so. A provocation that can land somewhere its own instrument reports as dry is not a
  provocation.
- **A dead-end one-voxel shaft takes water at about a litre a tick, not fifteen.** The first tick
  draws a full cell; after that the mouth cell passes down only what the cell under it had room for
  when the mouth was visited, and with the column filling from the bottom that is the ~625 mL its
  own last push freed. The window-move twin asserted a draw on every tick and failed on tick four
  with the mouth holding 14 L; it now asserts over a run of twenty. **This is the automaton's
  throughput, and it is M8d's waterfall question with a second number**: the 3 × 3 breach in the
  game filled its 72-cell shaft at 56 L/s over the window, where 7 portals at 30 L/s each would be
  210. M8a's 29 L/s for a one-voxel hole was into a mine with tunnels below, where the cell under
  the bore empties sideways. Recorded, not acted on: a shaft into a chamber behaves as M8a
  measured, and a dead-end bore is the pathological shape.
- **Decision 1 needed one more rule than the plan wrote, and the tracker owns it.** A pit whose
  mouth is the top row of a dug chunk opens onto the bottom row of the chunk above; if that chunk
  arrives second and unedited, "scan dug chunks only" never files the pair. An unedited chunk
  arriving beside a dug one re-scans the dug one, which takes every pair touching it against the
  terrain as it is now and files nothing wholly inside the unedited chunk. And the first edit in a
  chunk scans it, because a natural bank on its cliff joins the set the moment the chunk counts as
  dug. The tracker's fuzz holds it to *the definition over every pair touching a dug, loaded chunk*,
  with natural caves scattered in so that "touches a dug chunk" and "was dug" differ, and the
  natural-bank scenario says the decision's exact shape: not a portal until its chunk is dug.
- **The third arrival path was already distinguishable, so `onVoxelsReady` cost one callback and
  three call sites.** `OnChunkViewed` has told a cache hit from a fresh chunk since slice 1
  (`Unloaded` with voxels); the invoke sits there beside the two `Complete` branches, and the
  forget is forwarded from the light's own departure hook. Tested through the real pipeline in
  both directions: generated, cached and revived fires `[false, true]` on the edited chunk with
  no generate and no load; dropped and loaded from the store fires the same with a load. **The
  first version of both tests wrote air into a voxel that was already air**, which the pipeline
  correctly does not count as an edit, so the chunk came back pristine — the fixture asserts the
  chunk is dirty now.
- **The profile's `held` on the water line counted every in-window basin twice, since M7d-1.**
  Window plus ledger, where the ledger is the truth and the window a view of part of it. Found
  while adding the seam's terms; it banks first and reads the ledger now. The litres-per-minute
  figure was inflated with it. Every M7 conclusion that used the periodic `M7d:` line, which
  prints standing and banked separately, stands.
- **Cost, headless, Debug**: the seam's draw is inside a `fluid ms` of mean 0.14 / max 0.62 per
  frame with 24–79 cells active, and the edit-time index is the 1.2 ms a bite 2b measured. Nothing
  else moved.

**Fifteen break-recipes, fifteen caught after three fixture repairs and one recipe re-aimed.** The
drain: the covered test off by one, the room ignored, drawn not counted, dry basins not skipped.
The water system: draw not counted, the window origin ignored, the pour's spill not counted. The
tracker: no re-scan of a dug neighbour, no scan on first edit, every arrival scanned (decision 1
inverted), forget keeping a chunk dug. The pipeline: revival, load and forget each not fired. The
seed surface never reading a column. Four things the battery said. **The covered test's off-by-one
hid behind a one-draw tolerance**: the bank test allowed the lake to end within one draw of the
face, which is exactly where a `<` in place of `<=` lands, and its draws are not whole cells so
it never sat on the plane; a lake constructed exactly at the face, asserted to draw nothing and to
draw at one litre more, is the sharp case. **The origin mutation landed on the bowl's own
catchment**, because a flat plateau drains into the bowl and the lookup two samples over read the
same label; the mapping test now checks every world sample of a moved window against the window's
own labels and asserts some pair two apart differ. **No test had ever overfilled a basin**, so the
spill counter had nothing to count. **And the spill recipe's two-line pattern first matched the
rain's identical spill accounting**, earlier in the file, so it mutated `Advance` and the pour's
test could not see it — a recipe is only as good as its pattern's uniqueness, and the harness now
asserts a count of one.

**Not built, and stated**: nothing drawn through a portal persists — a quit loses the pit's water
and the lake's loss stays banked (M8b-4); no Tier B → Tier A handoff, so a breach that fills a
chamber under a lake holds it there for ever (M8b-3); the deep-chunk hook skip named at 2b; and
the play — *bite a chunk under the terrace pond with `Q` and watch the pond drop* — is Matthew's.

## 2026-09-05 — M8b-2b: the portal index — a hole in the analytic ground is a pair, filed where the water is, and a bite costs 1.2 ms

**`PortalIndex` is built in `Overburden.Core/Fluid/`, `SkyColumn` keeps its seed surface, and
nothing draws yet.** Suite 963 → 974. Both halves of the same-day session were "Lets continue";
this is the second. Six things worth keeping:

- **A portal is a pair, not a voxel, and it is filed under the outside's sample.** `Portal(Inside,
  Outside)`: the holdable voxel at or below its column's seed surface, and the face neighbour above
  <i>its own</i> column's surface that it opens onto — upward for a pit floor, sideways for a bank.
  The plan said "indexed by the 4 m sample they sit under" and finding 5 already had the covered
  test on the neighbour; the index resolves that: a tunnel driven under a ridge into a lake has its
  inside under the dry hillside's sample and its outside under the lake's, and the tick walks wet
  samples first, so filing by the inside would skip the one portal a bank breach is. Two faces of
  one dug voxel are two portals, because they can open onto two basins.
- **A scan takes every pair touching the chunk from either side.** A pit whose mouth is the top row
  of one chunk opens onto the bottom row of the chunk above; an unloaded voxel is solid, so the
  pair is a portal only while both halves are loaded, and whichever arrives second has to find it.
  `Forget` removes pairs with either half in the chunk for the same reason. Tested in both arrival
  orders, and the break-recipe that scans insides only fell to it.
- **An edit re-evaluates ten pairs, geometry before terrain.** A change at `p` can open or close a
  portal with `p` inside (five outsides) or with `p` outside (the voxel below and the four beside
  it). The five seed surfaces are read once per call, and a voxel above its surface is never inside
  while one at or below it is never outside, so a deep bite is 32,768 geometric exits. **The edit
  path is deliberately a second copy of the geometry**, cost-shaped rather than a call to the
  definition — and that redundancy is what let the fuzz catch a mutation *in the definition*: the
  two disagreed. One function would have made that mutation invisible to the oracle.
- **The seed surface on `SkyColumn` is an eight-fold decision, measured.** `--portal` in Release,
  control 1.05×: a bite costs **1.249 ms** with the seed as array reads and **10.293 ms** with the
  analytic function (deep chunk 0.904 against 9.981; a scan 0.075 against 0.456). The plan's ~3 ms
  estimate holds with the arrays and fails without them by 3×, and in the Debug build people play
  the analytic arm would be ~30 ms a bite. `SeedSurfaceY` throws when unseeded rather than reading
  zero, is never persisted and is left alone by `CopyFrom`, so a restored column keeps its own.
  **Lever, not built: a chunk wholly below its footprint's surface band can skip the hook.**
- **The natural-cave fixture had no caves, and its zero was silence.** The test that says *a
  natural cave is never a pit portal* scanned 64 unedited chunks and found 0 pits — and 0 banks,
  and, when the margin recipe passed, a probe found the cave field's surface maximum over the whole
  region was 0.361 against the 0.42 threshold, with not one cave twelve voxels down either. Solid
  rock, scanned. The threshold is lowered in the fixture until 2,005 columns have a cave directly
  under the margin, asserted, and the margin recipe now fails at `Voxel(-24, 6, -64)`. **Ask what
  a fixture's parameters make unreachable, sixth outing**; 0 banks stays, because this terrain's
  slope never reaches the nine-voxel step a cave mouth needs, and it is printed rather than
  asserted.
- **The oracle is the definition over every voxel of every scanned chunk and its shell**, kept
  where a pair touches the chunk — 90 checks over three terraced-and-cliffed terrains, 76 with pits,
  76 with banks, 29 non-empty after a forget, every filed entry under its outside's sample.
  Cheap enough to be the definition, as the plan said, and it is.

**Fourteen break-recipes, fourteen caught after the one fixture repair**: an edit ignoring its
outside role, no banks in the definition, forget removing nothing, a closed portal never removed,
touching-means-inside-only, filed under the inside's sample, scan of the surface voxel only, the
bank face off by one, pit geometry at-or-below, the row under the chunk floor skipped, the voxel
below ignored, the sky column seeding the plane, the cave margin removed, and the ring columns
skipped. The restore was by writing content this time, and no stale binary followed it.

**Not built, on purpose, all M8b-2c's**: the `ISurfaceHeights` over the streamer's columns that
reads `SeedSurfaceY` and falls back to the generator; the `onVoxelsReady` callback for the three
arrival paths and the forget hook; the dug-chunks-only filter at the scan's call site;
`DrawThroughPortals`; `--breach=`; and the profile lines. The index does not know what an edit is
— a scanned chunk with a natural cave mouth on a cliff will file it — and "a hole is what was dug"
is the caller's filter, stated in the type's remarks so 2c cannot forget it.

## 2026-09-05 — M8b-2a: water leaves Tier A off the top of its lake, the field samples the plane the water stands on, and a lake has had two heights since M7a-2

**`BasinWater.Remove` is built, the height convention is fixed, and building the one found a defect
in `LevelAt`.** Suite 953 → 963. Both decisions handed back by the morning's planning pass were
taken as recommended — Matthew: *"Lets continue"* — so a hole is what was dug (M8b-2b's business;
nothing built for it here) and `HeightField.Sample` stores `SurfaceHeightAt + 1`. Five things worth
keeping:

- **`Remove` is `LevelAt`'s walk reversed, and the two now share the walk.** `LakeTop(basin)`
  climbs while the node is brim-full and the water stands above the ridge into its parent, leaving
  the path in a scratch array allocated once; `LevelAt` solves the top node's curve at what the
  top's subtree holds, and `Remove` takes from the top's slab down the path to the leaf, never a
  sibling, then `Refresh` once, and returns what it took. One definition of "the lake this basin is
  part of" — the `IsCaveAt` / `GenerateTerrain` argument, for a tree.
- **The plan's identity was stated backwards, and the correct statement is the no-siphons rule.**
  `Remove(x)` then `Add(what it took)` restores every slab and every free count, always: 10 random
  terrains × 100 rounds, with the fixture asserting some removal reached a shared slab. `Add(x)`
  then `Remove(x)` restores them only while the add stayed inside one lake; the moment it crosses a
  ridge into a neighbour with room the neighbour keeps its share and the removal comes back short —
  pour 3 then 2 slabs into pit 0 of the twin-pit fixture and two of them are in pit 1, where a hole
  in pit 0 cannot reach them. Correct physics, not a defect; both arms are tests.
- **`LevelAt` has reported one lake at two heights since M7a-2, on the commonest terrain there
  is.** Its walk stopped at a parent whose slab was empty, on the argument that an empty parent
  slab means the water has not risen past the ridge. But Kruskal closes a component at the *next*
  crossing it takes part in, so a composite closed at the same height as its children has zero own
  capacity and a slab that can never hold anything — three pits on one flat shelf produce it, and
  on integer heights sampled every 4 m equal crossings are the norm. The water above such a shelf
  lives in the grandparent's slab; the two pits under the composite reported the shelf and the
  third the true level. `LakeTop` climbs through a zero-capacity parent when both its children are
  full and stops there when the sibling is not. Found because `Remove` would have drained the wrong
  slab for the same reason; caught by a three-pit fixture *and* by the random-terrain fuzz (the
  state after a removal, captured and re-poured, must reproduce every level), so it was reachable
  on random integer terrain rather than a corner. Nobody saw it in play because a wide shot of a
  lake was never obtained — M7d-2's note, now with a consequence.
- **The field samples the plane, and the sky column is the second definition of it.**
  `SkyColumn.Seed` has stored `SurfaceHeightAt + 1` as where the sky starts since M5b;
  `HeightField` now stores the same plane as where the water stands, pinned to it by a test over
  sixteen columns of an analytic surface — and M8b-2b's portal test will ask the sky column while
  Tier A's level asks the field, so the two disagreeing by a slab would have been the seam's first
  defect. A basin's first litre now stands above the ground: empty, `LevelAt` equals the sample
  (flush, and drawn nowhere by `WaterSurface`'s strictly-above test); one litre puts it above.
  Identity, capacities and stored litres are unchanged, **and every played pond's surface is one
  voxel higher than it was**, which is where the water always was. Every level figure in M7's
  entries below reads one voxel low from here on; the litres and capacities in them do not move.
- **The window twin gained its removal, and "absent rather than zero" got a second test.**
  `WalkingAwayAndBackLosesNoWater` takes half the wettest basin through its floor before the walk
  and comes back to exactly what was left; a basin drained to nothing leaves the ledger on the next
  bank rather than being stored as a zero row.

**Thirteen break-recipes, thirteen caught**, on the hydrology filter (68 tests): leaf-first,
take-from-sibling, skip `Refresh`, never climb, the old walk, climb through every empty slab,
report-asked-not-taken, drain-the-path-whole, refresh-from-the-top, both-children-full inverted,
the field's +1 dropped, +2, and the sky column's own +1 dropped. Three things the battery said.
**The old walk is caught by exactly two tests** — the three-pit fixture and the fuzz — so the
finding above is measured against its own recipe rather than asserted. **Take-from-sibling is
invisible to capture-and-re-pour**, because a sibling drained below its rim is a state a fill can
reach; the ridge rule sees it — a removal never lowers a neighbour below the lesser of its level and
the ridge it shares with the path — and the twin-pit scenario sees it by the litre. **The sky
column's +1 is caught by the pin test alone** on this filter, which is what a two-definitions test
is for.

**Not built, on purpose**: `WaterSystem.Remove` and its `drawn` counter, which are M8b-2c's, because
a counter without its consumer is a number waiting to be believed; the tests call
`system.Water.Remove` directly. Nothing on the Game side changed but a comment on `WaterSurface`,
and the headless r6 control (`--nosave --quit-after 2400`) is unchanged to the digit — 2601 / 325 /
3446 at 411 quads, the 512 m window at 346 basins and 11,136,000 L of capacity, which is the
arithmetic saying a capacity is a difference of heights.

## 2026-09-05 — M8b-2 planned, not started: the breach, read against the code, and Tier A has been one slab low since M7

**A planning pass for M8b-2 before any code — Matthew: *"they like mean everything"* — recorded in
M8-PLAN under "M8b-2 — the planning pass".** The plan's paragraph was read against `BasinWater`,
`MergeTree`, `VolumeCurve`, `HeightField`, `Watershed`, `WaterSystem`, `SkyColumn`, `WaterSurface`,
the pipeline's edit hook and the streamer's three arrival paths. Five findings, two decisions handed
back, a three-way split. The things worth keeping:

- **Tier A's height convention is the solid voxel's index, not the plane the water stands on.**
  `HeightField.Sample` stores `SurfaceHeightAt`, the topmost *solid* voxel; the curve counts litres
  from there; `WaterSurface` draws at `level × 0.25 m`, which for a level inside `(h, h+1]` is
  inside the top ground voxel. A pond's first 4,000 L per sample have filled a phantom slab in the
  rock and drawn nothing since M7d-2, and nobody could see it. Tier B puts water in real voxels, so
  the seam is where the two conventions meet. **Recommended fix: sample `SurfaceHeightAt + 1`**,
  the plane `SkyColumn.Seed` already uses; identity, capacities and stored litres unchanged, levels
  up one voxel, one test. Matthew's call, because it moves what a played pond looks like.
- **`Remove` is `LevelAt`'s walk reversed, not `Pour`'s.** Water leaving through a floor comes off
  the top of the lake the basin is part of: up to the lake's top node, take from that slab, then
  down the path to the leaf, never a sibling — once the shared slab is empty the other side is its
  own lake, which is Tier B's *no siphons* rule arriving in Tier A. Four break-recipes named.
- **The analytic surface the portal test needs is computed already and thrown away.**
  `SkyColumn.Seed` evaluates it for all 1,024 columns and keeps only the edited height. Decided:
  `SkyColumn` keeps its seed heights (2 KB a column), so the test at edit time is reads — and a
  chunk bite is 32,768 edit-time calls, M8b-1's `Disturb` rule verbatim. M8c wants the same number.
- **A natural cave can never be a pit-floor portal**, because worldgen keeps every cave
  `CaveSurfaceMarginVoxels` below its own column's surface; only a cliff-face bank under a lake
  could be one. That is most of the argument for finding portals through edits only (decision 1).
- **Cache revival is a third arrival path** that goes through neither `Complete(Generate)` nor
  `Complete(Load)`, so the load-time scan wants one pipeline callback, `onVoxelsReady`, with the
  test that every arrival fires it exactly once.
- **The chamber bench is already this seam's model** — a lake for a source, the top layer as the
  portals — so its figures (43,374 cells for one bitten chunk, 302,182 for 2 × 2 × 2, sliced since
  yesterday) stand as the prediction rather than a number to take.
- **Until M8b-4 a quit loses a pit's water**: the ledger persists the lake's loss and RAM holds the
  pit's gain. Stated in the plan and TODO rather than discovered in play.

**Split**: M8b-2a `Remove` and the convention; M8b-2b the portal index, with the incremental-equals-
from-scratch oracle; M8b-2c the draw, `onVoxelsReady`, `drawn` on both tiers' profile lines, and
`--breach=<voxels>` as the headless seam in the shape `--injectlitres` has. Nothing built.

## 2026-09-04 — The tick budget slice: a tick is a cursor over its batch, the trajectory is unchanged, and a roof falling in is 38 frames instead of one

**`FluidSimulation.Step` is resumable across frames.** Suite 936 → 953. The tick was the one
unit of work here that arrived whole — M8b-1's chamber fixture priced a chunk bitten out from
under a lake at 43,374 cells in one tick and a 2 × 2 × 2 block at 302,182, **73.5 ms in Release
and ~0.7 s in the Debug build `start.cmd` runs**, and an ordinary 6,000-cell flood at 17.7 ms in
Debug — and no tick *rate* can bound a tick that is atomic. So the tick is now a cursor over its
batch. `Resume(maxVisits)` visits up to N cells of the tick in progress and returns its result only
when the cursor reaches the end; `Step(deadline)` resumes in granules of 64 visits until the tick
completes or the injected clock passes the deadline, **checked after each granule and never before**
(the light and apply slices' rule, so a budget of zero still visits one granule a frame); the old
`Step()` is `Resume(int.MaxValue)` and finishes a tick in progress rather than starting a new one.
`Main` begins a tick at 2 Hz and resumes an unfinished one every frame under **`--fluidbudget=<ms>`,
2 ms by default** — the mesh-apply budget's number, labelled an estimate — with the relay pouring
only at a tick boundary. The profile's `fluid ms` is now per *frame*, the number the budget bounds,
and `fluidtick` says how many ticks took more than one frame and the longest. The bench gained the
same arm: `--fluidbudget <ms>` runs each flow tick as back-to-back slices and prints slices per tick
and the worst slice. The timing runs below finished in the small hours of the 5th.

**The claim the whole thing rests on is that slicing changes nothing but when a tick ends, and it
holds to the digit in both instruments.** In the suite, a simulation stepped whole and one stepped
in slices of 1, 7, 64 and 1,000 agree cell for cell after every one of 400 ticks on the fuzz's real
terrain, and so do their tick results, visit counts and active sets. On the bench every figure the
row prints — litres delivered, peak active, visits per tick, held cells — is identical between the
whole-tick control and the sliced arm on all three fixtures. That is what makes the budget a cost
decision rather than a physics one: the same cells are visited in the same order against the same
live grid, and only the frame boundary moves.

**Measured, Release, machine control 1.03–1.05× (divide before comparing), `--fluidsettle 0` so the
settle column reads NEVER by choice — the settle is not what was under test:**

```
fixture                  peak      whole tick ms     sliced at 2 ms: tick ms   slices/tick   worst
                         active    mean / max        mean / max                longest        slice
2x2x2 chambers, roof     302,182   50.33 / 79.97     49.19 / 76.22             38             2.921 ms
1x1x1 chamber, roof       43,374   (M8b-1: -/11.6)   10.89 / 34.52             17             2.351 ms
mine, bore 9              13,347    2.53 /  4.06      2.55 /  3.95              2             2.109 ms
mine, bore 1               1,091    0.49 /  1.86      0.48 /  1.82              1             1.822 ms
mine, bore 9 at 0.5 ms    13,347                      2.92 / 11.02             18             0.997 ms
```

- **The roof falling in is 38 frames at 2 ms instead of one 80 ms frame, and the ordinary flood is
  sliced too.** The 2 × 2 × 2 block's biggest tick spread over 38 slices; the single bitten chunk
  over 17; and **the widest ordinary breach — bore 9, 13,347 active — needed two slices for 436 of
  its 500 ticks in Release**, so the slice is not an instrument for one pathological case. In Debug,
  where a visit is 2.9 µs, the same ticks are roughly ten times as many frames — the headless
  figures below.
- **Slicing costs nothing measurable per tick.** Whole against sliced: 50.3 / 80.0 against 49.2 /
  76.2 ms on the roof-open block, 2.53 / 4.06 against 2.55 / 3.95 on bore 9. The 0.5 ms arm's mean
  of 2.92 against 2.55 is one run inside the machine's own swing and is recorded rather than
  believed; its 11 ms max is one tick and reads like a GC pause landing inside a slice.
- **The overshoot past a deadline is bounded by one granule's *work*, and a granule's work is not
  a constant.** Sixty-four visits is ~16 µs in Release, and the worst slice on the mine was 0.1 ms
  over budget — but the roof-open block's worst slice was **2.92 ms on a 2 ms budget**. The first
  granule of a tick pays `Begin()`, and `_queued.Clear()` on a `HashSet` holding 302,182 entries is
  proportional to its capacity, not to the work of the slice: about a millisecond, once per tick,
  at the largest active set this project has seen. Named as the lever and not built: the bound the
  budget gives is *budget plus one granule*, and at 300,000 cells one granule is a millisecond.
- **Debug is the build that needed this, and the bench cannot measure it** — see the headless
  section below for the frames a Debug tick takes.

**The suite's first run found a real defect, and it was in the whole-tick path.** `Step()` passed
`int.MaxValue` into a slice bound computed as `Math.Min(count, cursor + max)`, which overflows
negative the moment the cursor is past zero — so a whole-tick call that was *finishing* a sliced
tick returned null, and `.Value` threw. Every existing test calls `Step()` from a boundary, where
the cursor is zero and the sum is exact; only the new tests call it mid-tick. Fixed by taking the
remaining count first (`Math.Min(count − cursor, max)`), and kept in the battery as recipe K, which
fails five tests.

**Fourteen break-recipes, eleven caught on the first run, and the three that were not were three
different kinds of hole — all fixtures, none assertions.**

- **Recipe B hung instead of failing, and the hang was in the subject, not the test.** Resetting
  the cursor on every slice means a sliced tick never ends. The test loops were bounded after the
  M3a lesson — but `ADeadlineNeverReachedCompletesTheTickInOneCall` drove `Step(deadline)` with a
  clock frozen at zero, and *Core's* loop runs until the tick completes or the clock passes, so
  against a slice that stops advancing it is an infinite loop no bound in the test can reach. **A
  frozen fake clock is a hang waiting for a mutation.** It now counts, with a deadline further away
  than a tick can need; the same claim, and recipe B fails five tests. The battery script gained a
  per-recipe timeout that records HUNG as an outcome — the M3a lesson's third outing, and the
  first where the timeout had to be on the harness rather than the test.
- **Recipe F — `Settle` looping on the next tick's queue alone — was unreachable by the fixture.**
  A falling sheet's first sliced cells always wake something, so the queue was never empty while
  the batch still had cells, and the mutated loop ran the tick to completion anyway. The shape
  that separates the arms is a body at rest whose disturbed cell has no move: visit it and the
  queue stays empty with the tick half done. `SettleFinishesATickInProgressEvenWhenItsFirstSliceWokeNothing`.
- **Recipe N — the tick's moved counters never reset — was invisible because both arms share the
  mutation**, the M6a writer/reader trap in a new costume: sliced and whole are the same code, so
  they accumulate identically and agree. And nothing in the game reads `MillilitresMoved`, which is
  the counter-without-a-consumer category. Pinned directly by `ATicksFiguresAreItsOwnAndNotARunningTotal`.

**Two fixtures were wrong about the physics, and both errors are in FluidRules already.** The upper
of two layers at rest sits a residue or two under full — FluidRules' "12 mL left standing one level
above" — so `== Cap` on it fails on correct code. And a full cell dropped at the top of a column
falls *two* cells in its first tick, because the cell below it is woken into the same batch and
visited after it; only from the second tick on does it fall one cell a tick. Neither is a defect;
both are what the automaton does, and a test that asserts otherwise is asserting a different
automaton.

**Headless, Debug — the build that needed this — r4h/2v standing, 50,000 L poured when the window
opens, the M8b-1 recipe, three budgets:**

```
arm                        fluid ms per frame                ticks in    took >1    longest
                           mean / p50 / p95 / max            window      frame      frames
whole (--fluidbudget=1000) 16.61 / 14.44 / 22.68 / 22.97       30          0          1
2 ms (the default)          2.00 /  2.09 /  2.32 /  3.05       29         29         17
0 ms (one granule a frame)  0.21 /  0.19 /  0.47 /  1.36       19         19        135
```

- **A Debug tick is a frame and a half whole and a tenth of a frame sliced, at the same tick
  rate.** 14–23 ms a frame with the budget off, against M8b-1's 17.7 / 25; mean 2.00 / max 3.05
  with it on, and 29 ticks in the window against 30 — the 2 Hz rate holds, because the longest
  tick was 17 frames and a frame headless is ~7.5 ms. **At 60 fps windowed that longest tick is
  280 ms, inside the half-second**, so an ordinary 8,600-cell flood does not slow the water in
  Debug either. The roof-open case would: ~0.8 s of Debug work at 2 ms a frame is ~400 frames,
  six or seven seconds of water arriving, which is the design and is the play question below.
- **The zero-budget arm is the wire check.** One granule a frame makes an 8,606-cell tick 135
  frames, so the tick rate fell to ~1 Hz — 19 ticks in the window — and **all 50,000 L still
  arrived with the identity exact and 133,741 visits paid.** A `Main` that only began ticks on
  the timer and never resumed one would have finished its first tick over 135 frames and then
  stood still, because the timer cannot fire while a tick is in progress; nineteen completed ticks
  say it resumes. That is the recipe the suite cannot run, and it is why zero is a real setting
  rather than an off switch.
- **Streaming is untouched to the digit in every arm**: 1521 / 165 / 1926 at 404 quads with the
  water spreading, 2601 / 325 / 3446 at 411 for the r6 `--nosave` control, `near lit` 0.54–0.56 s
  and `first draw` 3.50–3.55 s across the three budgets. `update ms` does not contain the tick and
  did not move.

**What is deliberately not done.** The tick rate is still 2 Hz and the budget does not adapt to
the active set; a tick that outlasts its half-second simply ends late, and the next begins the
frame after, which is DESIGN's *slower than realtime is accuracy* taken literally. **Revisit
trigger: a play in which a roof-open flood reads as the game stalling rather than as water
arriving** — the budget is the lever, and `--fluidbudget=` is how it is swept without a rebuild.
M8b-2, the breach, is next; this was the slice TODO said had to come first, because the breach is
what produces the roof-open case in play.

## 2026-09-04 — The retained-chunk cache, slice 2: the grid comes back with the chunk, and the walk that proved it found three older things

**A turnaround costs no derive for a chunk that left with its grid, and the 20 m/s arm draws.**
Suite 926 → 936. `ChunkStreamer.Retain` keeps the derived light and clears the values;
`ValidateRevivedLight` checks the grid against the column it is given; `QueueLightBuild` drops a
cached neighbour's grid where it would rebuild a loaded one; `ChunkPipeline.ReviveLight` reseeds a
returning grid in the light step. Built from [docs/CHUNK-CACHE-PLAN.md](docs/CHUNK-CACHE-PLAN.md)
§5, which now has a "Slice 2 — built" section beside slice 1's.

**Measured**, r6h/2v, Debug, turning every 5 s, cache 64 MiB against 0, the slice 1 recipe:

| | 6 m/s, seed world | 20 m/s, seed world | 6 m/s, played world |
|---|---|---|---|
| generated | 4599 → 3213 | 9510 → 4590 | 2219 → 1543 |
| loaded | 0 → 0 | 0 → 0 | 2380 → 1670 |
| from the cache (with their grid) | 0 → 1377 (918) | 0 → 4812 (3261) | 0 → 1386 (919) |
| derives | 5157 → 3572 | 8454 → 5611 | 5094 → 3568 |
| reseeded instead | 0 → 918 | 0 → 3261 | 0 → 919 |
| `viewer ms` mean / p50 | 6.69 / 6.11 → 1.06 / 0.50 | 6.11 / 6.07 → 1.21 / 0.36 | 6.80 / 6.22 → 1.00 / 0.37 |
| `update ms` mean | 3.40 → 2.36 | 5.30 → 4.20 | 2.96 → 2.06 |
| main thread | 46.4% → 31.4% | 74.9% → 56.4% | 40.1% → 27.6% |
| first draw / light settled | 6.61 / 6.59 → 6.58 / 6.55 s | never → 12.20 / 12.17 s | 7.34 / 6.42 → 6.44 / 6.37 s |
| held at the end | 612 (482 lit) + 68, 2.0 MiB | 1989 (1525 lit) + 221, 6.5 MiB | 612 (494 lit) + 68, 2.6 MiB |

- **A third of the derives went where the loads and generates went.** 5,157 → 3,572 at 6 m/s,
  8,454 → 5,611 at 20 m/s, 5,094 → 3,568 in the played world. Every hit that came back with its
  grid was reseeded instead of derived; the 459 that did not, at 6 m/s, left during the first fill
  before they had derived — the fill has nothing to keep as well as nothing to hit. The main thread
  follows: 46% → 31%, 75% → 56%, 40% → 28% of one core.
- **The 20 m/s arm draws, and slice 1 said the cache could not touch that.** It said M5d-1's cliff
  is a derive cliff, which is true; what slice 2 changes is that after the first turn the box
  retraces chunks that are lit already, the derive queue empties enough for the drawn box to
  settle, and `first draw` lands at 12.2 s where the control arm never lands. **The turnaround
  shape only**: arriving somewhere new at 20 m/s is the cliff it was, and TODO's levers on it are
  unchanged.
- **The plan's column push became a check at revival, and slice 1 is why.** A dirty column is not
  cached, so a column can be *replaced* while a chunk is out — dropped and re-seeded on return as a
  different object — and no push at the change can name the chunks derived against an object that
  is gone. `SkyColumn.Revision` moves with every height and never repeats across columns (a
  process-wide counter, so two objects can never carry one number); a grid records the revision it
  was derived against; the revival compares once. Three cases, three tests: an edit under the same
  column, a restore landing in a cached column (the chunk is *generated* so it does not wait behind
  the parked read, and derives against the seed before the restore lands), and the replacement. **The
  sharp direction is a voxel placed above a cached chunk** — digging down from above stops at the
  unloaded chunk and cannot change its flags, so the fresh-derivation oracle is what says the
  re-derive was necessary rather than conservative.
- **Test 7 found three things, and its cap-0 control arm said none was the cache's.** Each is a
  Core repair with its own test:
  - *The whole loaded set was never a fixpoint.* A grid that left stopped propagation at its faces
    and kept what it had given the cells next door; M5c-1 accepted that because at margin 2 such
    light cannot reach the visible box, and the walk found where that stops covering it — the
    chunk comes back with different sources, the kept values have no source anywhere, and the
    returning grid imports them. `LightPropagator.RetractFrom` is `SpreadInto`'s inverse: 384 cells
    held to the fixpoint rule with the departed grid contributing nothing, only the unjustified ones
    darkened. Not the boundary thrash M5c-1 refused, because a rock cell answers in one read and a
    sky source in two, and nothing is derived.
  - *The un-light walk had a hole at value 1, since M5b.* It skipped every face through which a
    zeroed cell could have given nothing — and with it the reseeding of a neighbour at 2 that still
    justified the cell at 1. Two lamps whose reach meets at one cell; M5b's fuzz placed lamps and
    seldom removed one, and never there.
  - *A face conducted on one cell's word, and skylight leaked into rock through it.* A chunk
    derived against an absent neighbour read air; the neighbour arrived holding rock; until its gain
    re-derive ran, the stale bit was open from one side. The revival's spread ran a frame before
    that re-derive every time, which is what made a latent race a certainty — and the control arm
    has the same window whenever the derive budget splits the two builds. A face now conducts only
    when both cells say so, in all three passes: a no-op in the steady state, the fresh answer in
    the transient, one read of a byte already fetched. The probe that found it was a rock cell with
    no conducting face holding 14.
- **The oracle is two checks and a control.** Every tracked chunk's derived data equals a fresh
  derivation from the voxels and column as they are now, with faces toward an unloaded neighbour
  masked (the gain-only rule's own blind spot, harmless because a missing grid stops propagation
  whatever the bit says); the whole tracked set is at the fixpoint; and the same walk at cap 0.
  **The first version asserted the fixpoint over the visible box only, on the argument that the
  margin's stale light was by design** — and that would have been narrowing the assertion round a
  defect. Both arms passing over the whole set is the statement the plan wrote.
- **Memory: ~3.4 KB per cached seed chunk with its grid, ~4.4 KB in the played world.** The plan's
  3.5 KB, now measured; 64 MiB is on the order of 19,000 chunks and stays Matthew's number.

**The battery: twenty-one recipes, fifteen caught, six green — and each green one has a name.**
Caught: the face push skipped (2 — the face test and the walk), the revision check skipped (4 —
all three column tests and the walk), the revision not bumped when a height closes down (1), not
bumped by a restore (1), the values kept on cache entry (2), no reseed at revival (6), no re-spread
at revival (1, the walk alone), a revival left at `Lit` (1), `LightNeighbours` zeroed on entry (1 —
the plan named it the oracle's identity, and it is; the cost assertion is what catches it), a
dropped grid's bytes not given back (2), the revision not recorded at the derive (7), departures
not retracted (2), a face crossed on one cell's word (1, the walk alone), and the un-light walk's
reseed hole (2). Green: **the revision not bumped when a height opens further** — unreachable for
a cached chunk, because the downward scan stops at it and cannot open its cells, so that bump is
belt and braces beside its sibling, which is not; **`LightInFlight` ignoring pending revivals, and
pending departures** — identities by ordering, since both are served at the top of the light step
and the pump that could mark a chunk `Lit` runs after it, kept because a budgeted reseed would make
them load-bearing; **the retraction trusting the cell's own word for a face** — an identity at
settle, where the two words agree, and the oracle reads the cell's word too; **the column check
dropping the grid but not `LightNeighbours`** — a null grid derives regardless; and **the retraction
running before the propagator forgets its one-entry cache** — the pre-existing guard at the top of
`StepLight`, green because the cache would have to be pointing at the departed chunk, which is a
flake by nature and M5c-1's category. The walk caught nine of the fifteen and two on its own; the
unmutated control run was green.

Left recorded rather than built: the reseed runs unbudgeted in `StepLight` (a few hundred queue
entries a chunk, and a chunk left pending would be one `AdvanceLight` cannot tell from a lit one);
and the retraction's `Changes` are recorded, so a drawn chunk adjacent to a departing grid would
relight — which at margin 2 with one viewer and one-chunk steps cannot happen, and with a teleport
costs one mesh.

## 2026-09-03 — Rename stage 3: the content namespace is an alias at the identity, and the stage found two guards it needed

**The base mod is `overburden:` from today, and every world saved before today still opens.**
Suite 912 → 926. `Identifier.BaseNamespace` is `"overburden"`, `mods/overburden/` is the base mod,
`config/name` is `Overburden` so the window and the `user://` folder say so, and non-negotiable 3
reads `overburden:air` is ID 0. The played world — 7,745 stored chunks, five materials, 5.3 h on its
clock — opens headless under the new name with `0 error(s)`, `5 material id(s) restored`, 1,033
loaded, `near lit` 0.89 s, and its header after that quit spells every entry `overburden:` with
every number where it was. Six things worth keeping:

- **The alias sits at `Identifier`'s constructor, one level below where TODO put it.** The plan
  said "an alias applied when a world's ID table is read". A read-time alias has to be repeated at
  every reader — the header, a mod's JSON, a dependency list, a command line, M12's scripts — and a
  reader that forgets it turns every stored block into a placeholder without a test failing. So
  `Identifier.RetiredNamespaces` folds `minercraft` to `overburden` inside the constructor, and
  `TryParse` reaches it for free: **`minercraft:stone` and `overburden:stone` are the same value,
  equal and hashing equal, wherever the string enters.** Nothing in memory can hold the old
  spelling. Entries are only ever added; `TheAliasTableIsNeverEmptied` says so in a test.
- **The test failed first, on the real file.** The played world's v3 header was captured from its
  SQLite file *before* the change into `Fixtures/played-world-v3-header.bin`, because a round trip
  through the current writer cannot spell the old name and would test nothing. Changing the
  constant alone refuses it — *"material ID 0 is 'minercraft:air', but overburden:air is numeric ID
  0 in every world, always. This world file was not written by this engine"* — which is precisely
  the failure the alias exists to prevent, and eighteen other header tests went with it because
  their fixtures spelled `Air` the old way.
- **The stage's first headless run damaged a world, and it was the copy.** `dotnet test` on the
  solution rebuilds Core into `Overburden.Core/bin`; Godot runs the DLL in `.godot/mono/temp/bin`,
  which it does not refresh. The stale binary — base namespace still `minercraft` — found
  `mods/overburden/`, loaded it as a *third-party* mod, failed to define `minercraft:air`, printed
  the error, **played on**, gave the five materials fresh numbers 5–9, and wrote all ten to the
  header on quit. The next run refused: *"'overburden:air' resolved to numeric ID 5, expected 0"*.
  The original under `app_userdata/MinerCraft/` was untouched — **the by-hand copy doubled as the
  backup**, which is the argument for a copy over a move. The damaged header is
  `Fixtures/downgraded-world-v3-header.bin`; it is the real artefact of the real accident.
- **Two guards from it.** A table naming one material twice is refused at read, at write and at
  `SeedIdTable`, and the read's message names both slots and the cause — *"last opened by a build
  older than the alias it needs"* — because that is the only way a saved table can repeat itself:
  a saved table cannot hold one spelling twice, but it can hold two spellings that now mean one
  thing. Refused rather than repaired, since nothing can know which number that session's chunks
  used. Holes are not duplicates; several removed mods leave several. **And a content error is
  fatal now.** M1 wrote *"its absence is a load error"* and `Main` printed it and carried on —
  for six milestones, with nothing to provoke it. It refuses the run the way an unopenable world
  does, inside the `try` so the store is disposed and never written on the way out.
- **`ModManifest.Id` is deliberately not aliased; a dependency is.** A mod's folder is its
  namespace, and a folder called `minercraft` would read its files from nowhere, so the base mod's
  folder moved and a third-party mod cannot be called by the retired name. A dependency names a
  namespace, so `"dependencies": ["minercraft"]` in a mod from before the rename is satisfied by
  the base game as it is now — one test, `AModWrittenAgainstTheRetiredNamespaceStillLoads`, which
  also has that mod patch `minercraft:stone` by its old name and lands it as a duplicate of
  `overburden:stone` rather than as a definition nothing reads.
- **The `user://` move was by hand and stays that way.** `worlds/` copied to
  `app_userdata/Overburden/worlds/`; the seven worlds open; the `MinerCraft/` folder is the
  backup and Matthew's to delete once he has played the new one. No first-run copy code, because
  it would be a permanent path for one machine's one afternoon.

**Battery: ten recipes, ten caught, control green.** Storing the namespace raw (11), emptying the
alias table (13), pointing it at itself (13), not aliasing dependencies (**1** — the single loader
test is the whole of that guard), `IsBaseGame` against the old name (2, one of them M1's load-order
test), each duplicate check removed (1 each, by its own test), holes counted as duplicates (1), and
the constant reverted to `minercraft` with the alias in place (**45**, because the alias is then the
identity and every fixture spelling the new name lands nowhere). Nothing uncaught.

Left as history: the lowercase `minercraft` now lives in the alias, its tests, the two fixtures and
the milestone plans and worklog entries that were true when written. `M10-NOTES`' three machine
names moved to `overburden:` because none has shipped.

## 2026-09-03 — The derive queue drains nearest-first: "the ground is gone" fixed

**Postscript, the same evening: the same screenshot has a second cause, and it is not a defect.**
Matthew, after the fix: *"I still cannot get it to render voxels with or without the switch."*
Measured on a copy of his world at the saved position: r6h/2v loads 2,601 chunks, every mesh
builds empty, `near lit` 0.55 s; r6h/6v draws 48 chunks at 10.9 s. He was in fly mode, more than
16 m above the pit's floor and 48 m from its walls, so nothing inside the box had geometry — the
lake surfaces that still drew come from the watershed, not from chunks. *"I was just up too high?
Didn't think of toggling fly."* The vertical radius stays 2; a 64 m pit is the shape where ±16 m
shows nothing, and `start.cmd --vradius=4` is the experiment if that shape recurs.


The first of the three pick-up candidates, on Matthew's "yes to your recommended order". The
morning's diagnosis stood: `_lightBuilds` was a FIFO, the stored chunks round the player arrive
last through the serial lane, and nothing meshes until its neighbourhood is lit, so a mined-out room
lit from the far ring inward. The fix is the job queue's own rule applied to the one queue that did
not have it — a list sorted farthest-first, re-sorted only when something was added or a viewer
moved (`ChunkStreamer.ViewerVersion`, bumped on every add/move/remove), popped from the end.
`--derivefifo` restores the FIFO so the two are measured side by side. **Suite 910 → 912; the r6
standing-start baseline is 2601 / 325 / 3446 at 411 in both arms.**

**The instrument had to be built before the fix could be measured.** `first draw` cannot see the
player's own neighbourhood deriving last — inside a void nothing near the player has geometry —
and `light settled` is the whole box, which an order cannot move. The `fill` line now prints
`near lit`: the moment every tracked chunk within two of the viewer has derived light
(`ChunkPipeline.AllDerivedWithin`). Played world by the `probe-load` recipe, standing start:

| `near lit` | FIFO | nearest-first |
|---|---|---|
| played world, windowed | 5.14 s | 0.62 s |
| played world, headless | 3.27 s | 0.56 s |
| seed world, headless | 2.24 s | 1.04 s |

`light settled` is 6.2–6.3 s in every arm, as it must be. The windowed FIFO figure is the one
Matthew saw: five seconds of nothing near him, in a build where a Debug derive is a frame.

**The oracle is a boolean, and a zero light budget is what exposes it.** The light step checks its
deadline after each build and never before, so a budget of zero derives exactly one chunk per
update — and once every chunk has voxels, the only thing choosing the next derive is the queue.
*The chunk derived this update is no farther from the viewer than any chunk still waiting* is then
a property of the state, asserted after every update until the queue drains, and again after a
viewer move across the box. Four break-recipes — FIFO again, no re-sort on a move, the sort
inverted, enqueue not marking the list stale — and all four caught, with the move recipe caught only
by the move test, which is what it is for.

Cost: one sort of at most ~2,600 positions per frame during a fill, a viewer count of one inside
the comparer, and the FIFO arm's front pop is O(n) because it is the control and not the product.

**And the "lighting switch"** — Matthew, mid-turn: *"remember we need the lighting switch"*, which
is `--lightbudget=16`, the flag that cost an evening when it sat on the engine's side of the bare
`--`. `start.cmd` now passes `-- --lightbudget=16` itself, so the play build has it without anyone
remembering; anything given to `start.cmd` lands after that `--` and a later `--lightbudget=` wins.
The pipeline default stays 4 ms because every recorded figure was taken at it. Whether 16 becomes
the Debug default is an open TODO item, to be decided after a play with the nearest-first queue.

## 2026-09-03 — The retained-chunk cache, slice 1: a turnaround costs no load and no generate

Built from [docs/CHUNK-CACHE-PLAN.md](docs/CHUNK-CACHE-PLAN.md) as planned that morning. Matthew's
"Step 3" from the pick-up list. `ChunkStreamer.Forget` moves a chunk with voxels into a byte-capped
cache instead of dropping it; `View` consults the cache before creating a record; a released column
with nothing to write goes the same way; `ChunkPipeline.OnChunkViewed` takes a new `Unloaded →
Generated` edge for a chunk that arrives with voxels. `--chunkcache=<MiB>` (64, 0 off) and
`--turnaround=<seconds>` on the flythrough. **Suite 895 → 910; the standing-start r6 baseline is
2601 / 325 / 3446 at 411 in both arms**, because nothing leaves the box.

**Measured**, r6h/2v, Debug, 6 and 20 m/s, turning every 5 s, cache 64 MiB against 0 — three
arms, and the played world by the `probe-load` recipe:

| | 6 m/s, seed | 20 m/s, seed | 6 m/s, played world |
|---|---|---|---|
| generated | 4599 → 3213 | 9539 → 4590 | 2266 → 1580 |
| loaded | 0 → 0 | 0 → 0 | 2332 → 1633 |
| from the cache | 0 → 1386 | 0 → 4960 | 0 → 1385 |
| derives | 5233 → 5269 | 8958 → 8952 | 5395 → 5400 |
| `viewer ms` mean / p50 | 6.58 / 6.07 → 0.91 / 0.33 | 6.08 / 6.08 → 1.05 / 0.29 | 6.76 / 6.12 → 0.95 / 0.34 |
| jobs done | 5926 → 4605 | 9539 → 4590 | 6290 → 4953 |
| held at the end | 612 + 68, 1.3 MiB | 1989 + 221, 4.2 MiB | 612 + 68, 1.8 MiB |

- **The prediction held to the chunk: the generates and loads a turnaround costs went to the cache
  and the derives did not move.** 4599 − 3213 = 1386 = the hits. So the derive is now the whole of
  what a turnaround still costs on the sim thread, which is the argument for slice 2 — and at
  20 m/s both arms still draw nothing, because M5d-1's cliff is a derive cliff.
- **The box-difference sweep is mostly column seeding, and that is a finding M6d-2 could not
  make.** M6d-2 measured `viewer ms` at two to four times the pipeline update, named light grids
  and sky columns as the suspect, and did not chase it. A cache hit skips `SkyColumn.Seed` (1,024
  surface evaluations a column) and the record allocation, and the sweep's mean drops seven-fold
  with the p95 untouched — the first fill has nothing to hit. Recorded in TODO as a question.
- **§6 of the plan was wrong: a dirty column is not cached.** A column released dirty is handed to
  the save with no copy-on-write — a chunk has `VoxelsSharedWithJob`, a column has nothing — so a
  revival could edit it under the serialiser. Only a column with nothing to write is kept. In play
  that is nearly all of them (the autosave marks the live set clean); the one that is not is the
  column just dug, which comes back through its restore as before. **And a restore landing after
  its column was released has to be copied into the cached object**, or the revival hands back the
  analytic seed and never asks again — a dark shaft arriving only on a slow disk.
- **§3's dirty-on-evict rule is belt and braces, and its premise was wrong.** `StepBack` does not
  restore `DirtySinceSave` on a dropped save; `ApplySave` puts the bytes back on the pending list
  and leaves the flag alone, so nothing today can dirty a cached chunk. Kept, tested with the flag
  set by hand, because what it guards is a deleted tunnel.
- **The pipeline's queue flags are cleared on cache entry, and the reason is a category worth
  naming: quiescence cannot see a stranded chunk.** Every queue skips an untracked position on
  dequeue, so a stale entry is harmless; a stale *flag* makes `Push` or `QueueLightBuild` refuse
  the revived chunk, which then sits with no grid and no job while `IsQuiescent` reports the world
  settled around it. The first fuzz asserted nothing about the end state and passed with the flags
  left set. It now asserts every tracked chunk derived and the centre reached `Lit`.
- **The stage drops from `Lit` to `Features` on cache entry, and the first test for it was green
  on the broken code.** A chunk revived still at `Lit` passes `CanMesh` before its grid exists,
  meshes dark, is relit and remeshed — and every assertion (same values, fixpoint, meshed) held,
  because the settle waited for the repair. The test now counts deliveries and relight remeshes
  across the turnaround: exactly one more mesh, zero relights.

**Seventeen break-recipes, fourteen caught first time, two after the tests were strengthened as
above, one identity.** The identity is pushing only the revived chunk rather than its 26
neighbours: reaching `Lit` pushes them anyway, so the neighbour push at the hit is belt and braces
and its comment says so. One more stays green for a reason the fuzz did not reach: a stale
`AwaitingLight` heals whenever any neighbour reaches `Lit`, which in a walking box is always — the
stranding case is one chunk revived among neighbours already lit, which no test builds. Recorded,
not chased. **Two fixtures failed first and both were the assertion**: at margin 0 the ring never
passes the feature barrier, so "every chunk reaches `Lit`" and "the centre meshes" were both
unreachable by the fixture's own parameters — M5c-1's sky-shaft shape, twice in one test. **And
the battery's `mv`-restore stale-binary trap, recorded at M4a, bit again**: the unmutated control
run reported the previous recipe's failures, because the restored source carried the backup's
older timestamp and MSBuild kept the mutated assembly. The final suite run was taken after
touching the sources.

**Memory: ~2.0 KB per cached seed chunk, ~2.8 KB in the played world, no light.** The plan's
3.5 KB included 1.5 KB of grid. 64 MiB is on the order of 25,000 chunks and is Matthew's number to
move. Not measured: first draw *after* a turn — the profile reports the run's first draw, and a
standing-start fill is identical in both arms. The `sources` line is the instrument.

## 2026-09-03 — The retained-chunk cache is planned, and the comment it overturns is six milestones old

Matthew asked whether there is a cache between the game and the database (there is none: `Forget`
drops voxels, light and column, and the return is a serial load, a derive and a mesh) and whether
the loader should be more proactive. The honest answer given: the loader is not what he is waiting
on — the derive is — but a turnaround is as dear as arriving somewhere new, and that is the case a
cache fixes. On his "go" it is planned as a slice: [docs/CHUNK-CACHE-PLAN.md](docs/CHUNK-CACHE-PLAN.md).
Three things from the planning pass:

- **`Forget`'s argument against keeping light warm is stale.** It says a returning chunk
  *regenerates from the seed*, so its derived light is guaranteed to be re-derived anyway. Since
  M6 a returning chunk has the identical voxels whichever source it comes from — that is what
  persistence means — so derived light is invalid only if a neighbour or the column changed while
  it was out, and both of those already have a hook site. A comment that was right at M5c-1 and
  nobody re-read at M6.
- **The cache is a fourth source and goes second**, between memory and disk, and it never holds
  the only copy: the save still runs at unview, so eviction is a free drop, with one dirty-on-evict
  rule for a save `StepBack` restored. M6's ordering rule is the correctness argument.
- **Propagated light values are never kept**, because a lamp removed while a chunk was cached
  would leave a value nothing ever darkens; derived data is kept and invalidated by two pushes at
  existing call sites. The load-bearing test is the M5b incremental-equals-from-scratch oracle with
  the streamer cycling chunks and a lamp removed in the meantime — and the fixture has to assert
  the far chunk was really cached, or it is the sky-shaft trap again.

Stated plainly in the plan: it does nothing for the first fill Matthew actually saw. That fix is
still the distance-ordered derive queue.

## 2026-09-03 — "The ground is gone": nothing is hidden, nothing has drawn, and the played world lights its own centre last

Matthew's screenshot from the played world: rain, the hotbar, blue-grey "cloud" shapes near the
top of the frame, and a uniform fog colour everywhere the ground should be — *"the renderer does
not show the ground anymore or it is hidden by fog or water like?"* Reproduced on a copy of the
world (`probe-load`, the M6d recipe) with `screenshot.gd`, and **it is neither fog nor water: no
chunk has meshed, because nothing meshes until its neighbourhood is lit, and in this world the
player's neighbourhood is the last thing lit.** Three causes stacked, and each is measured.

**What the shapes are.** The `--nowater` arm of the same shot has none of them. They are M7d-2's
Tier A lake surfaces, seen from underneath: the player is at −12.4 m in the excavation and the
analytic surface at that column is −2.25 m, so the basins' solved levels hang in the air over the
pit — *"lakes overhanging yes"* from below. The report also says the window holds **640.6% of its
leaf capacity with 0 L spilled**, which is recorded here as a question rather than a defect: the
pit is invisible to the watershed by design, so capacity is the unedited terrain's, but six times
it wants a look before M8b-2 starts moving litres out of these basins.

**Why the ground is not there.** Same copy, headless, Debug, r6h/2v:

```
arm                                     light settled   first draw   drawn at the end
default (4 ms light budget), headless        14.09 s       14.15 s      198 @ 100 quads
--lightbudget=16, headless                   12.81 s       12.86 s      198 @ 100 quads
default, windowed via screenshot.gd, 45 s    not yet       not yet      0   (1,333 / 2,601 derived, 1,268 queued)
--lightbudget=16, windowed, 30 s             —             drew         floor fills the frame
--radius=4 --vradius=2, windowed, 30 s       not yet       not yet      0
fresh world (--nosave), headless             (0.49 s*)     12.73 s      307
```

\* the settle detector fired on an empty queue before the fill began; the first-draw figure is
the one to read. Every arm was taken with Matthew's game running in the background (a 671 MB
Godot process), so the absolute figures are inflated and the bench says by how much: `--light`
reports **0.561 ms/chunk against the recorded 0.241 — the machine is at 2.3× today**, inside
M7a's 2.5× band and the second time that finding has moved a play-facing figure.

1. **A derive costs more than the whole light budget today.** 10,060 ms over 2,601 derives is
   **3.9 ms per chunk** in Debug (the played world) and 3.45 ms in the fresh one — M5d-1's 1.41 ms
   at the machine's 2.3–2.7×. `StepLight` checks the deadline *after* each derive so that every
   frame makes progress, which is right — and its consequence is that at ≥ 4 ms a derive the
   pipeline does **exactly one derive per frame**: 60 a second windowed, ~130 headless. 2,601
   chunks is 43 s windowed on the best ordering, which is why the windowed r4 arm at 30 s and the
   r6 arm at 45 s both drew nothing while headless settled at 14 s. **The 4 ms knee M5c-1 swept was
   measured at 1.0× on a fresh world; at 2.3× the budget is below one unit of work and the knee
   is a cliff.**
2. **r6 doubled the queue the same day** — 2,601 chunks against 1,521. The b38cdb9 measurement
   was honest about first draw doubling (3.80 → 6.66 s) and it was taken on a fresh world at ~1.0×;
   both multipliers moved after it.
3. **In a played world the derive order is the wrong way round, and this is the structural one.**
   `_lightBuilds` is a FIFO `Queue`, so chunks derive in the order their voxels arrived. Generated
   chunks arrive from eight workers in ~90 ms; **stored chunks arrive one at a time on the serial
   lane** — 1,015 of them here — and in a mined-out region *every chunk around the player is a
   stored one* (169/169 at the player's two layers). So the far ring is derived first, at one a
   frame, and the centre — the only part that can mesh, and the only part the person is looking
   at — is derived last. A fresh world hides this completely: nothing is stored, arrival order is
   distance order by accident, and the centre lights first. **The screenshot is M5d-1's "drawn
   goes to zero" cliff reached standing still, by a world rather than by a speed.**

**What was not the cause, checked rather than assumed.** Not the fog: density 0.004 is 17% at
48 m and the voxel shader fogs toward black where there is no skylight, so a fogged floor would
be a gradient, not one flat colour. Not Tier B: `0 L moving`, and `FluidSurface` draws nothing on
an empty grid. Not the vertical radius: the floor under the player is the top of generated rock
at −16 m, 3.6 m under the feet, well inside 16 m — and `--vradius=10` (7,225 chunks) made it
worse, for reason 1. Not persistence: 1,015 loaded, 0 failed, and with light given room the floor
is stone and the excavation is there.

**The instrument had the same defect as the symptom.** `screenshot.gd` waits 8 s, chosen when
first draw was 3.4 s — every shot of this world was a picture of a scene that had not drawn yet,
and it looked exactly like the renderer failing. **It now takes `--settle=<ms>`** and prints the
wait it used; the shots above are 24–45 s. Fourth outing for *eyeballing a screenshot is a
measurement too*, and the first where the picture was correct and early.

**Follow-up the same hour.** Matthew ran `start.cmd -- --lightbudget=16` and still saw no ground
after flying up. `start.cmd` does forward `%*`, and a copy of the world taken from that session's
autosave draws the floor with the flag — 12.99 s headless, and a 30 s windowed shot looking down
is all stone — so the flag works at his position. What could not be checked is his run: the game
printed nothing about which budget it was given, so a flag that did not arrive looked identical to
one that did until first draw. **The `M2c: streaming` startup line now prints the light budget.**
Two other readings from his screenshots: the voxel highlight was showing on the crosshair with
nothing drawn, which is a `Hit` on a loaded, unlit, unmeshed voxel a metre away — the mechanism
made visible; and the header position in the autosave had not moved from the earlier session's,
which is either a session that was killed with its console window (no `_ExitTree`, no header) or
something to look at in what `CurrentHeader()` samples while flying. Not chased.

**And the flag never arrived — found from the shell history, not the code.** The only
`start.cmd` on the machine is the repo's and it forwards `%*`. His last launch was
`.\start.cmd --lightbudget=16`, without the bare `--`; tested from PowerShell 7 with the exe
directly, `-- --lightbudget=16` reports `light budget 16 ms` and `--lightbudget=16` alone reports
`4 ms` with no error, because **Godot ignores an option it does not know on its own side of the
`--` without a word.** The game now warns at startup for any `--name=value` argument found on
the engine's side, since Godot's own options never take that shape. PowerShell passes the `--`
through, checked rather than assumed.

**Corrected the same afternoon (see the stage-2 entry): the 2.3× was Matthew's own game running
beside the measurements.** With it closed the bench reads 0.239 ms/chunk and this world lights in
7.00 s headless with a 1.37 ms Debug derive — two to three a frame at 4 ms, not one. The ordering
finding stands; the arithmetic below it is halved.

**Recommendation, Matthew's to take.** The fix that addresses the played-world case regardless
of machine speed is the cheapest: **order `_lightBuilds` by distance to the viewer** the way the
job list is, so the centre lights first and the ring lights while the person is already looking
at ground. A priority queue keyed on the same band the scheduler uses, re-sorted on the same
200 ms timer. `PaddedChunk.CopyFrom` (59% of the derive, ~1.7×) is still the named lever and
still not built. A Debug default above 4 ms is a play-feel decision rather than an engineering
one and is deliberately not made here; `--lightbudget=16` is the proven workaround for tonight.

## 2026-09-03 — M8b-1: Tier B is in the game loop, and the first thing the seam edits found was that the recorded table does not reproduce

Suite **892 → 895**. `FluidSimulation` reads gravity from one `_fallSign` and room through one
`RoomAt`; `ChunkPipeline` gains `onVoxelChanged`; `Main` ticks the automaton at 2 Hz over
`VoxelFluidTerrain`, with **`R`** putting 10,000 L down at the crosshair, **Alt+R** taking 2 m of
it back, `--injectlitres=<n>` doing the first headlessly, a `fluid` block in the profile and an
`M8b:` line in the periodic report, and `FluidSurface` drawing a quad on every top cell. **The
water is on the screen** — a 50,000 L pour spread eighteen metres downhill in five seconds, and
the `--nowater` arm of the same camera is all grass.

### The seam edits move no digit, and the control arm is what says so

Two break recipes first: room halved fails **6** tests, gravity flipped fails **6** — so the clamp
binds and the sign is read. Then `--fluid` in Release, and **it did not match the M8a-2 table**:
bore 9 peak 20,737 against 17,357, 92.1 L/tick against 136.2. With the edits stashed, **the
committed code gives the identical digits** — 39,809,482 and 111,222,865 visits, to the visit —
so the edits and the fixture refactor moved nothing, and **it is the recorded table that does not
reproduce.** A 1,000-tick flow window reproduces its L/tick, panels and MiB exactly and not its
peaks, so the table was taken with a shorter window and a pre-commit state of the automaton.
**The committed code is the baseline from here**, same fixture, 2,000-tick window, 5,000-tick
settle cap, machine control 1.04x:

```
bore       L/tick   L/s   hours to   peak     visits/s   ms/tick   ms/tick   held     panels  MiB   awake at
voxels                    drain 9M   active   @2Hz       mean      max       cells                  the cap
1  (0.25 m)  14.3    29     87.4      4,096     4,370     0.483     1.795     5,872     51    3.2   11,017
3  (0.75 m)  24.6    49     50.9      6,046     7,323     0.747     1.770     7,804     53    3.3   13,936
5  (1.25 m)  39.6    79     31.6     12,531    15,930     1.461     3.229    12,131     64    4.0   16,699
9  (2.25 m)  92.1   184     13.6     20,737    31,173     2.941     5.291    21,648     73    4.6   26,723
```

Every conclusion survives and three figures move: every hole drains, at **29 L/s** for a single
voxel; the widest breach is **6.0%** of the light budget, not 5.1, with the 50,000-cell trigger
still not reached; and a `hand_pick` bore empties the lake in **51 hours**, not 38. **The one
claim that does not survive as stated is *"9× the width gives 9.0× the rate"*** — it is 6.3× over
2,000 ticks and 10.5× over 1,000, because **the rate decays as the tunnels back up, so a mean rate
is a property of its window.** Quote the window with any L/tick from here on; the report prints it.

### The chamber fixture: an 8 m floor settles, and a roof falling in is the biggest tick there is

`--fluidshape=chamber --fluidchambers=<n>`, a block of bitten chunks with a shaft into its roof,
roof 2 m under the surface; a bore of 32 or more opens the whole roof, which is a chunk bitten out
from under standing water. Same lake, same window:

```
block          bore    void      delivered   L/s   peak      visits/s  ms/tick    held      settle
                       cells     L                 active    @2Hz      mean/max   cells     ticks
1×1×1 (8 m)    3       32,840    264,105     264     4,914     9,089   0.88/6.5    17,408    1,915  rest is real
1×1×1 (8 m)    32      41,480    668,606   ~inf    43,374     3,010   0.37/11.6   42,791        0  full in two ticks
2×2×2 (16 m)   3      262,216    264,541     265    16,157    26,060   1.94/6.6    20,480    4,936  rest is real
2×2×2 (16 m)   64     295,944  4,693,299   ~inf   302,182    36,443   4.55/73.5  300,375    2,558  rest is real
```

- **A chamber floor settles where a corridor does not.** An 8 m floor came to real rest in 1,915
  ticks (16 min of world time) and a 16 m one in 4,936; the mine's 96 m corridors were still
  spreading at the 5,000 cap. The O(n²) finding is about *length*, and a bitten chunk is wide.
- **Through a bore, a chamber takes water 5.4× faster than the mine** (264 L/s against 49 through
  the same 0.75 m hole), because there are no 0.75 m tunnels behind it to back up into.
- **A roof falling in is a one-tick spike proportional to the void's cross-section, and it is the
  biggest active set this project has seen: 302,182 cells in one tick, 73.5 ms in Release.** Six
  times the ~50,000-cell revisit trigger — reached, but in one tick rather than sustained, and the
  set then collapses as the block fills. In the Debug build people play that tick is ~0.7 s. **So
  the tick budget is not a rate question but a slice question**: `Step` has to be resumable across
  frames, which is the M8a "named, not built" item with its number attached.

### The game: the identity holds, the digits hold, and the tick costs a frame in Debug

- **Streaming unchanged to the digit with water pouring**: 1521 / 165 / 1926 at 404 quads standing
  at r4h/2v with 50,000 L spreading, and 2601 / 325 / 3446 at 411 for the r6 default with the tick
  running on nothing. `held == injected − removed − displaced` exact in every report.
- **The tick is 17.7 ms mean / 25.0 max in Debug for ~6,000 active cells** — 2.9 µs a visit against
  Release's 0.2–0.3, the light derive's Debug cliff again (M5d-1). At 2 Hz that is a frame and a
  half twice a second in the build `start.cmd` runs. Part of the same slice question as above.
- **The relay's ball is sized to its litres, and two runs said why.** A fixed 1 m ball delivered
  15,871 of 50,000 L in the window in mid-air and 11,837 on the ground: the automaton falls one
  cell a tick — 0.5 m/s at 2 Hz — and spreads diffusively, so a source region drains only at its
  boundary's rate and the run measures the hose. A ball big enough for the pour lands in one tick
  and the run measures the spread. **The fall speed is also M8d's waterfall question with a number
  on it**: four metres takes eight seconds.
- **`Disturb` wakes only cells holding water**, never the opened voxel — a chunk bite is 32,768
  voxels and waking each for an empty visit is 229,000 visits in one tick — and returns at once on
  a grid holding nothing, which is every edit before the first flood. Two tests, plus the pipeline
  hook's own: told *after* the write, and not told at all when the material was already there.
- **Two instrument traps.** The bare default headless run opens the *played* world, whose spawn is
  inside the bitten-out void: 198 drawn at 100 quads a chunk, which reads as a regression and is a
  fixture — **the streaming control is `--nosave`.** And `--quit-after 900` is ~6 s at headless
  frame rates, before the r6 fill settles at ~7 s; 2400 is what reaches the report.

**Play note (2026-09-04): the relay met by accident, and the water read well.** Matthew pressed
`R` without remembering it was bound — it went in the day before, on his own M8 wording that the
relay would be *"invaluable"* for testing — and 10,000 L a press went down the terraced hillside as
stair-stepped sheets, one 0.25 m layer a step. His verdict on the look: *"looks cool going down the
stairs."* That is Tier B falling one cell a tick at 2 Hz on the integer heightmap's risers, and it
is the first eye on M8d's waterfall question, ahead of the milestone that owns it. Not saved, so a
quit clears it; Alt+R takes it back within 2 m; `--nowater` turns the tier off. **And a second
remark, which is M8d's first requirement**: *"it would be nice if eventually it's a bit more 3D,
like it's a very flat affair right now, but I assumed this would happen in later steps."* It does —
what he is looking at is the debug surface, one flat quad per cell, drawn so the automaton could be
