## 2026-09-02 — M7d-1: rain reaches the basins, and a lake survives a quit

**M7d is split in two on the seam M5c and M7c were split on**: this half is the wiring and the
measurement, which a headless run can verify; M7d-2 is the water surface and the play, which needs
a renderer and a person. Suite **804 → 814**. The default headless run is unchanged to the digit —
**1521 viewed / 165 drawn / 1926 jobs at 404 quads**.

`MinerCraft.Core/Hydrology/WaterSystem.cs` is the join the whole milestone was designed around: it
owns the analysed window, the water in it and the ledger that outlives it, and it is deliberately
Godot-free so the threading policy lives where the platform is.

### The headline: a lake survives a quit, to the litre

Session one rains into a named world and quits at **9,404,288 L**; session two opens it and reports
**9,404,288 L standing, 346 basin(s) banked**. That is the round trip M7b-2's ledger was built for,
now end to end through the store.

The in-memory version of the same property is the suite's oracle,
`WalkingAwayAndBackLosesNoWater`: a `BasinWater` only ever holds what is inside the analysed
window, so **every window move is a chance to lose a lake**, and the assertion and the feature are
the same statement.

### Two measurements, and the first confirms M7a exactly

```
                     Release bench    in-game (Debug)
512 m window            13.63 ms         53.1 ms warm / ~102 ms cold
1024 m window           64.97 ms
machine control          2.46x slower than the M2d-2 reference
```

**M7a's recorded "1 km window costs 66 ms measured / 27 ms reference-equivalent" is confirmed**:
64.97 ÷ 2.46 = 26.4 ms. The shipped window is 512 m — **13.63 ms Release, 5.5 ms
reference-equivalent** — analysed on a worker roughly once every 128 m of travel.

**The new fact is the Debug penalty: ~3.9× warm.** The game project builds Debug, so the figure a
profile prints is not the figure the bench prints, and the same trap has now caught worldgen (3×),
the light derive (5.9×) and this. **Never quote an analysis figure without its build.**

**The water costs nothing measurable on the sim thread**, against `--nowater` at 40 m/s:

```
                    water        no water
update ms mean      6.107          6.064
viewer ms mean     10.845         11.125
main               83.55%         84.19%
```

The water arm is *lower* on two of the three, which is noise around zero. A tick is one
multiplication per basin — not per cell, not per voxel — which is Tier A's whole claim.

### `rainfallScale` is picked, and it is picked from numbers

**Forty.** Two measurements decided it: the bench says the median basin in a 512 m window fills in
**32 minutes of this world's heaviest possible weather** unscaled, and the game says a whole window
reaches **10.2% of leaf capacity in 40 minutes of ordinary weather** — which puts a full basin at
about six and a half hours. At ×40 that is roughly ten minutes, and measured in real time from a
36 mm/h downpour the window took **25.3% of capacity in 35 seconds of wall clock**, 6.5 M litres a
minute.

It scales the depth applied to the world and nothing else, so `Weather` goes on stating real
intensities and the sky, the wet term and the rain particles all still read a real storm.
**M7d-2's play confirms or moves it**, and `--rainscale=` is the sweep.

### A first-draw regression that was the machine, and the control is what said so

`first draw` came out at 7.2 s against the 3.4 s recorded earlier the same day, which reads exactly
like the analysis stealing thread-pool time from the fill. **The `--nowater` control ran *slower*
still, at 8.65 s.** The machine had moved — the bench's own control line put this session at 2.46×
the M2d-2 reference — and the water had nothing to do with it.

**This is the first time the machine-variance finding has been applied to a streaming figure rather
than a bench one**, and the lesson generalises: `first draw` is as machine-sensitive as
`ms/chunk`, and a fill time quoted without a same-session control is not a measurement.

### Four things the design turned on

- **The analysis is a plain `Task`, not a job on the scheduler, and that is the decision rather
  than laziness.** M7-PLAN is explicit that a watershed is not a chunk-shaped computation and that
  the instinct to make it one is the thing to resist. `JobPriority` ranks work by distance from the
  viewer in chunks, which says nothing about a window already centred on the viewer and analysed
  once every few hundred metres; and there is no chunk to cancel it with. One at a time is enforced
  by there being one slot.
- **Absorb before seed, always.** The old window and the new one overlap almost entirely, so a
  basin usually appears in both; seeding first would pour the ledger's stale figure into the new
  water and then overwrite the ledger with it, losing everything that fell while the analysis ran.
  A break-recipe for it was **not caught** until the fixture was rescaled — see below.
- **The accumulator starts at what has been *delivered*, not at now.** Across a window move those
  are the same instant; on the first window they differ by however long the analysis took, and the
  rain from that interval lands rather than being lost. The mirror of that is the one that would be
  unrecoverable: a reopened world must start at its own clock, or the first window to land pours
  the whole of the world's history into basins the ledger has already filled.
- **The window origin has a whole step of hysteresis.** It snaps to quarter-spans and only moves
  when the quarter changes, so a player standing on a boundary cannot re-analyse every time they
  shift their weight.

### The break-recipe battery found the thing reading could not

**Ten recipes, eight caught on the first pass and all ten after one fixture change.** The two
misses were *both* the same trap and both were real defects: the fixture rained at a scale that
filled every basin to the brim, so "the move dropped a step's rain" and "the move delivered it
twice" produced the same brim-full number as correct code. **A test whose scenario makes both arms
agree is worth nothing**, and this is the fourth outing for that specific failure in this project.

Rescaling the fixture then exposed a genuine cost that the saturated one had been hiding: **a
window move discards `BasinRainfall`'s pending sub-litre remainder**, because each move builds a
fresh accumulator. `BasinRainfall`'s own remarks warn that dropping the remainder *every step*
stops a drizzle ever accumulating; this drops it per *move*, which the hysteresis makes rare, so a
drizzle still fills a basin between moves. **Bounded at under a litre per basin per move, asserted
as a bound rather than waved at, and stated in the source with its revisit trigger** — anything
that re-analyses often, where the fix is to carry the remainder keyed by pit exactly as the ledger
carries litres.

The test that found it is now written the other way round: a move may only *lose*, never invent,
and by no more than the remainder can explain. That catches both original defects and prices the
real one.

### Still open, and M7d-2's

- **The Tier A surface.** Nothing is drawn yet: the levels are solved and `LevelAt` returns them,
  and no pixel says so. That is the same position M5b was in with a light grid that did not glow.
- **The play**, all five questions, including whether ×40 is the right scale and whether the 4 m
  shoreline is tolerable.

## 2026-09-02 — M7c-2: rain you can see, and a splash system that was cut rather than shipped dead

The rain falls, it is killed by the ground, and it stops at a roof. **Splashes are not delivered**
— see the last section, which is the most useful part of this entry. Suite unchanged at **804**;
the default headless run is unchanged to the digit — **1521 viewed / 165 drawn / 1926 jobs at 404
quads** — because the rain is not created without a renderer.

### It costs one draw call, and that is measured rather than claimed

Windowed, r4h/2v at 8 m/s, storm forced, against the same run with `--norain`:

```
                    rain on        rain off
draw calls             85              84
primitives         112,332          64,332
update ms mean      2.696           2.872
main                38.38%          40.93%   of one core
frame ms mean        7.025           7.018
```

**One draw call and 48,000 primitives**, which is exactly 24,000 drops × 2 triangles — the buffer,
drawn once. The sim-thread arms are *lower* with rain on than off, which is noise around zero:
everything a drop does happens in the process shader, so there is nothing on the main thread to
measure. DESIGN's "camera-locked box of GPU-instanced billboards, one draw call" is now a number.

### The occlusion field, and the estimate that was ten times out

The kill is a texture of ground heights around the player, built from `SkyColumn` — *edited*
height, which is what makes rain follow a shaft you dug rather than a heightmap you did not.

**M7c-2's plan estimated ~0.25 ms to rebuild on a chunk crossing. At the recommended 128 m window
it measured 2.5 ms mean / 3.6 ms worst**, on the sim thread, next to `viewer ms`'s 4.7 ms on the
same crossing — so it roughly doubled the cost of crossing a chunk. **The window is now 64 m and
it measures 0.98 ms mean / 1.60 ms worst**, still four times the estimate but no longer the largest
thing on a crossing.

**The resolution — the decision the plan actually argued — is untouched at 0.5 m.** 128 m was only
chosen so the rain box could be retuned without touching the field, which is a convenience; 64 m
still clears the 48 m box by 8 m a side. Two things fell out of shrinking it: the refill is 2.5×
cheaper (not 4×, because the upload does not scale with area the way the reads do), and **the
"unknown" share at r4 went from 34% to 0%**, because a 64 m window fits inside the loaded region
where a 128 m one does not. That artefact was recorded as expected-at-small-radii and has simply
gone away.

Each texel takes the **minimum** of the 2×2 voxel columns it covers rather than point-sampling one
of them. Point sampling would work for a `hand_pick` bore — three voxels always contains an even
index — but that is a parity argument that breaks silently the first time the resolution moves,
and the minimum is a guarantee that does not.

### The field is a terrain, and that had to be checked rather than assumed

Chasing the splashes turned up a real doubt about the main feature: if the `Rf` texture were being
normalised or clamped anywhere in the path, the kill would be a **flat plane** a metre or two down
— and *rain stopping at a flat plane looks exactly like rain stopping at the ground* from anywhere
the ground happens to be a metre below you. Every screenshot taken so far would have passed.

So the field now prints its own range: **`ground -3.5..5.0 m`** over the window. A spread is
terrain; a spread of zero would have been the bug. **This is the third outing for "eyeballing a
screenshot is a measurement too"** and the first where the doubt came from an unrelated failure.

Two smaller instrument notes:

- **The rebuild counter is split by cause — `24 moved / 0 dug`** — because a crossing rebuild is
  bookkeeping and a dig rebuild is the feature. The dig path is the one link between "a voxel came
  out" and "rain falls in there" that no Core test can reach, so a run that dug through to daylight
  and reports zero has a wire off. `ChunkPipeline.SkyHeightChanges` was built for it, and it counts
  height *moves* rather than voxel writes — so a tunnel dug underground, which is most of mining,
  rebuilds nothing.
- **The counter's own first reading was wrong.** `_skyChangesAtRebuild` started at −1, so the first
  refill compared unequal to zero and was attributed to digging: every run reported "1 dug" before
  anything had been dug, which is exactly the false positive the counter exists to rule out.
- **The field is guarded behind the rain existing.** Without that a moving *headless* profile would
  carry a millisecond per crossing that no run since M2d has carried, which is the comparability
  contract this project keeps.

### Splashes: not delivered, and what was established

The plan asks for splashes at the kill point. Two implementations were built and neither drew
anything that survived scrutiny. **Cut rather than shipped, because a particle system that draws
nothing is indistinguishable from one that is working and subtle** — and leaving it in would have
read as "splashes exist, they need tuning".

What is now known, each from counting pixels in a forced-colour screenshot rather than from
looking:

- **The splash draw pass and process shader work.** Self-emitting with the sub-emitter link cut:
  **85 pixels**. So neither half was the problem.
- **The sub-emitter link suppresses self-emission and delivers nothing in its place: 0 pixels**,
  with the emitter demonstrably hitting the ground thousands of times a second.
- **Re-parenting the sub-emitter as a child of the emitter** — which is how Godot's own examples
  wire it — got particles out of it, but **all at a single point**, so `FLAG_EMIT_POSITION` was
  still not arriving. (`EMIT_FLAG_POSITION`, the name the docs suggest, does not exist; it is
  `FLAG_EMIT_POSITION`, and that one *is* a compile error rather than a silence.)
- **A `texture()` call inside a particle `start()` silently produces particles that never
  appear.** Identical shader, ground looked up in `start()`: 0 pixels. Reading a constant instead:
  drew immediately. Nothing is logged and nothing fails to compile. **This is the most valuable
  thing in this entry** and it is why any future attempt must do the lookup in `process()`.
- Moving the lookup to `process()` did not on its own bring them back, so there is at least one
  more thing wrong. That is where it was left.

The alternative design — a second emitter placing droplets on the same field rather than at the
kill point — is written up in the removed shader's header and is the right shape: the difference
from "at the kill point" is invisible, and **the one place it would have mattered is preserved**,
because the same field means splashes land at the bottom of a dug shaft rather than on the roof
around it.

**Held rather than brute-forced**, per the working agreement: the two features the milestone is
actually about both work and are measured, and this one had consumed more iterations than it was
worth.

### Screenshot seams added

`--pitch=<degrees>` joins M7c-1's `--yaw`: a shot of rain going into a shaft has to look down it,
and `screenshot.gd` could not point the camera anywhere until now. `--norain` is the A/B arm that
priced the particles, and it is the only way to get the storm without them.

### Still open

- **Splashes**, with the four findings above as the starting point.
- **A positive shaft photograph.** Underground shots correctly show *no* rain, which is the
  occlusion working in its negative form; a picture of rain visibly pouring into a hole was not
  obtained, because the entangled miner digs broad chambers rather than narrow shafts and the
  reopened player falls to the bottom of whatever it dug. **This is M7d's play question**, not a
  test, and a person standing next to their own mine entrance answers it in a second.

## 2026-09-02 — M7c-1: the world gets a clock, and the rain gets a look before it gets particles

**M7c is split in two, on the seam M5c was split on: what a headless run can verify and what needs
a renderer.** M7c-1 is the clock wired into the session, the wet-surface term, the overcast, and
the view-space `NORMAL` question settled. **M7c-2 is the rain itself** — instanced billboards, the
sky-height occlusion texture, splashes — and it is screenshots only. M7-PLAN says "headless cannot
verify any of this", which is true of the particles and not of the half below: the zero-remesh
assertion and the clock are both headless facts.

Suite **797 → 804**. Streaming is untouched to the digit: **1521 viewed / 165 drawn / 1926 jobs at
404 quads per drawn chunk**, M2d's recorded figures, which is the contract every part of this
project has to keep.

### The headline: a storm costs zero remeshes, and that is now printed rather than argued

```
weather   0 edit remesh(es) / 0 relight remesh(es) during the measured window
          — wet ranged 0.00..0.67 over 1380 s of world time
```

**This is where M5's bill gets collected.** Wetness is `recent rainfall × skylight`; rainfall is one
global number and skylight is already `COLOR.r` per vertex, so a rainstorm changes **one uniform**
and nothing enters the merge key. DESIGN's stated reason for keeping the two light channels
separate rather than pre-multiplying them was this exact term, and it is the first thing to spend
what M5a paid for in vertex bytes.

**It is a difference rather than a total, and it is printed with its denominator.** The fill is
still relighting through the warm-up, so a session total would read in the hundreds and say nothing
about the storm; and a zero from a run that stayed dry is a detector that never fired, which this
project has now shipped twice. The wetness *range* over the window is what says the weather
happened. `--clockscale` is what makes fifteen seconds contain a storm — the weather is a pure
function of time, so scaling the clock is the one knob that shows a whole episode without touching
the weather at all. It is deliberately not M7d's `rainfallScale`, which leaves the sky honest and
speeds the water up.

### The clock, and the claim that was true by construction until something advanced it

`WorldClock` is advanced from `_Process`'s `delta` and from nowhere else, restored from header v3
at open and written back on save. **The demonstration TODO said was still owed is a pair of
sessions**: one ends at t ≈ 6 s, the next resumes at t = 11 s five minutes of wall clock later. The
world moved on by five seconds because five seconds were played, not because five minutes passed.
That is *time advances only while the world is open*, observed rather than asserted — Core could
never test it, because `WorldClock` only moves when something calls `Advance`.

### Wetness and overcast are box filters, and the reuse is the design

Both are `Weather.DepthNanometresOver` and a divide — **the one primitive whose exactness the whole
milestone rests on is also the only arithmetic in either**, so there is no second model of "recent
rainfall" to drift from the first. Three things fell out:

- **The soak window is exactly one episode, and that makes the answer statable.** A window ending on
  an episode boundary covers exactly one episode, so wetness there *is* `rate / maxRate` — a
  rational number a test asserts rather than approximates, and the tightest available assertion
  about the window's length. Widen it by a millisecond and it fails everywhere two neighbouring
  episodes differ, which is most of them.
- **The overcast window straddles now** — back one soak window, forward half an episode — so the sky
  gathers before the first drop and clears at about the rate the ground dries. *Storm → dark → rain*
  is most of what makes weather legible, and a sky that darkens on the same frame as the first drop
  reads as a glitch. Two tests separate the halves: one asserts the ground is **exactly** dry while
  the cloud is already up, the other that the cloud is still there after the rain has stopped.
- **A new world reads dry in a downpour for its first two minutes, and that is correct.** The window
  clamps at the start of time and the denominator deliberately does not: thirty seconds of rain has
  genuinely only wet the ground for thirty seconds. Normalising by the clamped span — the obvious
  "fix" — reports saturated ground one second after a world is created, and one test exists for it.

**This is also where the integer rule stops, deliberately.** Everything above these two returns
integers because it feeds a volume asserted to the litre. These feed a shader uniform, are never
stored, summed or compared for equality, and an `int` here would be exactness cargo-culted onto a
look term. Said in the source, because the file's own ethos argues the other way.

**Eight break-recipes, eight caught.**

### The view-space `NORMAL` question, settled — and it was a real bug

`face_tint` asked "is this face pointing up?" of `NORMAL` inside `fragment()`, **which in Godot 4 is
view space**. So the fake directional shading rotated with the player: the top of a block dimmed as
you looked down at it. It read as a plausible lighting model right up until you turned, which is why
five milestones went past without anybody filing it.

**It stopped being cosmetic the moment the sheen arrived**, exactly as M7-PLAN predicted, because a
sheen is *genuinely* view-dependent — with both terms sliding there is no way to tell the one that
is supposed to move from the one that is not. The fix is a `varying` set from `vertex()`'s `NORMAL`,
which for a chunk instance **is** the world normal, because the transform is a pure translation. It
costs no matrix multiply.

Measured, at yaw 0 and yaw 40, `--viewnormal=1` against the fix:

```
                 yaw 0                    yaw 40
             world      view          world      view
riser face  (69,130,64) (69,130,64)  (59,128,54) (53,116,50)
```

**Identical facing the default direction and diverging once you turn** — which is the bug stated as
a measurement. `--viewnormal=1` keeps the old arm, because *which* look is preferred is Matthew's
call and the old one is what shipped and was liked; `--yaw=` exists because a view-dependent
artefact is invisible in one picture by definition, and `screenshot.gd` has never been able to turn
the camera.

### The sky did not dim, and three plausible levers all silently did nothing

The storm looked convincing by eye — dark ground, hazy distance. **Sampling the two screenshots said
the sky pixels were bit-identical to the clear arm: (200, 210, 225) in both.**

`Environment.BackgroundEnergyMultiplier` does nothing to the drawn dome. Nor does
`ProceduralSkyMaterial.EnergyMultiplier`. Nor does scaling the dome's four colours. All three were
confirmed to be *set* — the material resolves, the property takes the value — and all three left
the sky unchanged to the byte.

**The cause is a note already in CLAUDE.md, one milestone old, read as a detail:** M5d turned the
environment's fog off for the terrain and left it on for the *sky*, so the procedural sky's dark
ground hemisphere does not show as a black band along the horizon. The consequence nobody had cause
to notice is that **most of the sky you can see is the fog**, at a fixed colour. Dimming
`Environment.FogLightColor` moves it: (200, 210, 225) → (83, 90, 101).

Two things worth keeping from that:

- **Eyeballing a screenshot is a measurement too, and this is the second time it has caught
  something.** M6d-3's was a false positive — a yellow outline misread as a defect. This is the
  false negative of the same shape: a picture that looks right while half the intended change did
  nothing. The pair is the argument for sampling named points rather than admiring the image.
- **A "why we keep this on" comment turned out to also be a "this is what paints the sky" comment**,
  and nobody was going to read it that way until it mattered.

Also recorded: the overcast dims the terrain through `sky_brightness` by **multiplying**
`--skybrightness` rather than replacing it, which is what keeps M5c-2's A/B alive. Verified rather
than assumed — `--skybrightness=0` still renders the terrain **pure black against a sky that is
still there**, which is the whole point of that seam.

### Still open, and handed to M7c-2

- The rain itself: billboards, the sky-height occlusion texture at 0.5 m, splashes.
- **Which face tint Matthew prefers.** The correctness argument is settled and world space shipped;
  the look is his, and `--viewnormal=1` is how the other arm is seen.
- The sheen is barely visible on a hillside seen from above, because the grazing term is small
  there. Whether it reads at all wants a wall and a play-test, not another screenshot.

---

## 2026-09-02 — M7b-2: water that outlives the window it was analysed in

Header **v3** carries the world clock and the watershed lattice; a `basins` table carries the
water; `BasinLedger` is the thing in the middle that knows about basins nobody is currently
looking at. Suite **778 → 797**. Nothing is wired into the game yet — that is M7c and M7d.

**The structural point, and it is why a ledger exists at all: a `BasinWater` only ever holds what
is inside the analysis window.** Walk a kilometre and the watershed is redone somewhere else; the
lake you left has no representation in memory at all. So the persistent thing cannot be the
window's arrays — it has to be a map from *pit coordinate* to litres that outlives every analysis,
and **that is the second time M7a-1's "identity is a world coordinate, not an array index"
decision has paid for itself.**

### Capture is exact, and the reason is a property rather than a mechanism

`BasinWater.CaptureByBasin` attributes every node's water to a basin, and **pouring the result back
into a fresh water over the same tree reproduces the state node for node** — slabs, free counts and
levels. That works because fill-and-spill is **order-independent**: where water comes to rest is
determined by how much entered at each basin, not by the order it arrived in. So a composite's slab
— water standing above two basins' rims, belonging to neither — can be credited to either of them
and poured back through the same cascade it came out of.

**The battery proves the arbitrariness rather than the comment claiming it**: attributing
composites to the *rightmost* basin instead of the leftmost leaves the whole suite green, while
dropping composite slabs entirely fails two tests. One of those is a real difference and the other
is not, and now the code says which is which.

### Three decisions in the format, all of them about what happens when something is wrong

- **Header v3 is additive, so v1 and v2 both migrate.** A v2 header is a v3 one without its clock
  and lattice, and both defaults are true statements about such a world: it has never run for any
  length of time, and it has no stored basins to be keyed on any lattice at all. Same policy M6c-2
  wrote down, now used twice.
- **A changed watershed lattice discards the volumes rather than refusing the world or
  reinterpreting them.** A pit is a sample on the lattice, so changing it renames every basin in
  the world; keeping the coordinates would land stored water on whatever pit happened to be
  nearest, which is a lake appearing in the wrong valley with nothing failing anywhere. Refusing to
  open is worse than losing rain that refills in minutes, because the chunks, the inventory and the
  player's position are all still exactly right.
- **`WriteBasins` replaces the table rather than merging into it, and the cost is stated.** The
  ledger in memory is the truth, so writing it whole is the shape that cannot desynchronise — at
  the price of rewriting rows that did not change. At 1,376 basins per square kilometre explored,
  a well-travelled world is tens of thousands of rows. **Revisit trigger: the basin write becomes
  visible next to M6b-3's 13 ms autosave**, and the fix is dirty-tracking in the ledger, which is
  why the ledger and not the store owns identity.

### Two smaller things worth keeping

- **Absorb replaces; it does not add.** Getting that backwards would double a lake every time the
  player crossed the same ground twice — a defect that only appears in a long session and looks
  like the weather being generous.
- **A basin that empties leaves no row behind**, because an absent pit already means "no water
  here" and a zero row is a second way to say the same thing that the store would carry forever.

**Ten break-recipes, nine caught**, the tenth being the attribution above. Adding the trailing
twelve bytes also moved two existing corruption tests that count offsets back from the end of the
payload — both now step over a named `ClockAndLatticeBytes` constant instead of a literal, so the
next format change is one edit rather than a hunt.

**What is left before M7 can be played: nothing in the game reads any of this yet.** The clock is
not advanced by a frame, the watershed is not analysed around the player, and no rain falls. That
wiring is M7c and M7d, and it is the first point at which a person can see whether any of it works.


## 2026-09-01 — M7b-1: the clock, the weather, and rain that is too slow to watch

`WorldClock`, `Weather` and `BasinRainfall` — the world gains time, the sky gains a forecast that
is a pure function of the seed, and a basin's catchment collects what falls on it. Suite
**764 → 778**. No persistence yet; that is M7b-2.

**The oracle passes with no tolerance at all: an hour integrated in one call equals 3,600 calls of
one second**, basin for basin, including the sub-litre remainder each one is carrying, and
including what left the world. That is the property "flew away mid-fill and came back" is made of,
and it is the cash value of *slower than realtime is accuracy, not approximation* — a tick is only
allowed to be late because arriving late and arriving on time compute the same number.

### The unit chain is the design, and it was chosen to make one multiplication exact

- A **rate** is nanometres of rain per millisecond of world time. That is also micrometres per
  second, and 1 of it is 3.6 mm/hour.
- **Depth over an interval is rate × milliseconds**, an exact integer, summed over the episodes the
  interval spans — so splitting an interval splits the sum, exactly, which is the property
  everything else rests on.
- **A nanometre of rain over a square metre is exactly one microlitre.** So the volume arriving in
  a basin is `depth × catchment`, integer, with nothing rounded away.

Nothing in that chain rounds, which is what lets the oracle assert equality rather than closeness.
**The one place a remainder appears is handed a carry rather than a rounding**: a catchment
collects microlitres and only whole litres are given to the water. Drop the remainder instead and a
drizzle rounds to zero litres *every step forever*, so a basin never fills while the same hour
integrated in one call fills it properly — and the break-recipe battery confirms the oracle catches
exactly that.

### The pacing finding, and it is the one M7d has to react to

**At real rainfall, the median basin in a 1 km window fills in 35 minutes of the heaviest weather
this world can produce** — 43 mm/hour, already a downpour — and since 55% of episodes are dry and
most of the rest are lighter, the honest expectation is *several hours*. A filling pond's surface
then rises well under a millimetre a minute. **Nobody can judge that**, and M7's whole visible
payoff is watching one fill.

So `BasinRainfall` takes a **`rainfallScale`**, and the reason it is a scale rather than a fudged
rate is worth keeping: `Weather` goes on stating real intensities, so M7c's wet-surface term and
the overcast dimming still read a real storm, while the world receives more of it. **M7d is where a
person picks the number**, and the watershed bench now prints a **`fill min`** column to pick it
against. Matthew's *"a few minutes of rain to fill the lower levels of a large cave"* implies
something like 10–30× — or it was about caves, which are M8 and far smaller than a basin's whole
capacity. Recorded rather than guessed at.

### The machine control validated itself the first time it was used in anger

Same binary, hours apart: the control read **2.48x slower** and the 1 km window cost 66.4 ms; it now
reads **1.08x** and the same window costs 29.9 ms. Normalising gives 26.8 and 27.7 — **the two
agree to within 3%**, which is much better evidence that the instrument is right than either
reading alone. A figure taken today can now be compared with one taken at M2d-2 without anybody
having to remember what the machine was doing.

### Ten break-recipes, ten caught — after the green one exposed a fixture that could not fail

Making the accumulator report only its last call's spill left the whole suite green. **The reason
is that at real rainfall none of the fixtures ever overflows**, so every assertion any of them made
about spilled water was comparing zero with zero — including the oracle's. That is the
degenerate-fixture category again, and the fix is a fixture that drowns on purpose: rainfall scaled
500x for one test, which asserts it really overflowed before asserting anything else.

Two of the caught ones are worth naming because they fail in the direction that hides: **the
accumulator forgetting to advance its own clock** re-rains the same interval forever, and **a dry
stretch returning before the clock moves** silently banks the dry time and delivers it as rain
later.


## 2026-09-01 — M7a-2: the merge tree, and a control that says the machine was 2.5x faster this morning

`MergeTree` builds the join tree of the terrain — every crossing sorted, union-find upward, so a
basin that fills past its own rim becomes half of a larger lake rather than pouring sideways
forever. `BasinWater` holds the water in it and routes overflow. Suite **756 → 764**.

**The two-cycle test flipped, which is what this part was for.** M7a-1 recorded that the leaf spill
graph cycles by construction — a crossing costs the higher of the two samples it joins, so it is
symmetric, and two basins with no cheaper exit are each other's lowest crossing. The same terrain
now fills, overflows into its sibling, rises over the ridge as one lake and finally leaves the
world, in a routine that walks strictly upward and therefore cannot loop.

### The measurement was wrong, and the thing that found it was a control rather than a mechanism

**M7a-1 published a 1 km window at 19.9 ms. The same binary, unchanged, now reports 43 ms.**

Two mechanisms were proposed and implemented before either was tested: a garbage collection landing
inside the timed region, and a cold large-object heap after warming at a smaller window. **Neither
was it.** The answer came from running the *worldgen* bench — whose Release figure has been in the
worklog since M2d-2 — and finding it equally slower: **1.16 ms/chunk against 0.47 recorded**, a
2.48x factor, which is exactly the factor every watershed column had moved.

**So the machine was 2.5x faster this morning than it is this evening, and nothing in six
milestones of published Release figures would have said so.** The bench now prints a control line
above its table:

```
  machine control: worldgen 1.16 ms/chunk against 0.47 recorded at M2d-2 — this run is 2.48x
  SLOWER than that reference. Divide the times below by that factor to compare them with any
  figure in the worklog.
```

That is *print the denominator* arriving somewhere new: not the sample size this time but the
speed of the machine the sample was taken on. **The lesson is the order of operations** — a control
that already exists settles in one run what two plausible mechanisms could not, and both mechanisms
were changes to the harness made on a hypothesis.

**Corrected figures for M7a, stated both ways.** At 1 km, measured today: sample 8.08 ms, flood
35.22, tree 23.11, **total 66.4 ms**; divided by the control's 2.48, **26.8 ms** on the machine
M2d-2 and M7a-1 measured. **The decision stands and its margin is now honest**: the analysis runs
on a worker once per window move, and even the slow figure is well inside the plan's 200 ms
rethink line — but it is a 3x margin, not the 10x that 19.9 ms against 50 implied.

### Two defects, and the second one was found by a test written to plug a hole in the first battery

- **Two components that both already drain to the window edge met at a crossing, and one of them
  was re-closed at the higher height.** Every pair of components meets somewhere eventually, so
  this was not an edge case; it silently overwrote a spill height that had been settled long
  before, and the symptom would have been a lake that stops filling at a height nothing explains.
  **Caught by the test that says a leaf's spill height is the saddle the watershed already
  computed** — two definitions of one number, the `IsCaveAt`-against-`GenerateTerrain` shape.
- **The rolled-up free capacity went stale after a drop that fit in its own basin.** `Pour`
  refreshes what it touches, which for a small add is one leaf, leaving every ancestor's subtree
  total unchanged — and `LevelAt` asks a composite how much its subtree holds, so a merged lake
  would have reported a level computed from a volume last updated at the previous overflow.
  **A new variety for the break-recipe habit: the green recipe was about the roll-up, the test
  written to plug it was about the roll-up, and the defect it actually found was somewhere else.**
  A green recipe means *no test here*, and what the missing test catches need not be the mutation
  that revealed it was missing.

### Three things about the model that are easy to undo

- **Water is held in slabs, not piles.** A leaf holds up to its own rim; a composite holds only the
  volume between its children's rims and its own. So a subtree's water is the sum of its nodes and
  "how much is in this lake" is one subtraction. It is also why `OwnCapacity` can never be negative
  and why the invariant is checkable.
- **Pouring fills the children before the parent's own slab, and that is physics rather than an
  optimisation.** Water crossing a ridge runs downhill into whatever is on the other side. Fill the
  parent first and a brimming basin's overflow stands on the ground between two lakes while one of
  them is still half empty.
- **Brim-full is not merged.** Two siblings are separate lakes until the water stands *above* the
  ridge, which is exactly when the parent's slab starts to hold something. Climb on brim-full alone
  and a full basin reports the combined lake's level while its neighbour is still filling.

### The lazy-composite-curve question is answered by measurement, not deferred

M7a-2's plan named lazy composite curves as the alternative to building them eagerly, on the
grounds that the total is O(n log n) elevations. Measured: **0.8 MB at a 1 km window** and 5.9 MB
at 2 km, for 2,204 and 9,589 nodes. **Eager, and the alternative is retired rather than deferred**
— the sixth named fallback in this project dissolved by measuring the thing it was afraid of.

**Eleven break-recipes, ten caught.** The one green is a documentation correction: setting a
composite's children's parent before closing them is belt and braces, because the `drained` flag is
only ever read through `Find`, which returns roots, and a node that has just been given a parent is
never a root again.


## 2026-09-01 — M7a-1: the watershed, and an estimate that was right for the wrong reason

`MinerCraft.Core/Hydrology/` holds `HeightField`, `Watershed`, `Basin` and `VolumeCurve` —
priority-flood over the analytic surface, one basin per depression with its pit, saddle, spill
target and catchment, and a volume→level curve that inverts. Suite **739 → 756**. No Godot, no
chunks, no streaming: the analysis takes `ISurfaceHeights` and returns plain data.

**The measurement the plan called its first job, taken first: a 1,024 m window at 4 m costs
19.9 ms** — 3.64 ms sampling, 16.30 ms flooding — on one thread in Release. The plan's threshold
was *under ~50 ms settles it forever*, so **no incremental watershed is ever built**: the window is
re-analysed wholesale on a worker when the player leaves the centre box, and a whole category of
complexity is deleted before anything was written against it.

### The estimate was inside its range and wrong about which half

M7-PLAN guessed 10–30 ms, arrived at as *65,536 samples at 0.1–0.2 µs each, plus the flood*.
Measured, **sampling is 55 ns/sample** — two to four times cheaper than assumed — and **the flood
is 82% of the total**. So the range was right for a reason that was not.

That matters more than being wrong by a factor would, because the *lever* moved: if this ever
needs to be faster, `SurfaceHeightAt` is not where the time is, and the plan implied it was. Same
shape as M5-PLAN costing propagation and saying nothing about the derive, which turned out to be
the larger half.

| window | samples | sample ms | flood ms | total | ns/sample | basins | held | spilling |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 256 m | 4,096 | 0.43 | 2.33 | 2.76 | 675 | 69 | 2.9 ML | 61 |
| 512 m | 16,384 | 1.11 | 4.09 | 5.20 | 318 | 325 | 11.4 ML | 303 |
| **1,024 m** | **65,536** | **3.64** | **16.30** | **19.94** | **304** | **1,376** | **54.7 ML** | **1,336** |
| 2,048 m | 262,144 | 14.59 | 70.82 | 85.41 | 326 | 5,668 | 211.4 ML | 5,601 |

The 256 m row is still an outlier at 675 ns/sample and is left standing rather than explained
away: at 4,096 samples the per-basin work and the allocations are a larger share, and 2.3 ms is
not a number any decision turns on.

### The trap, and it produced a fake finding before it was caught

The first run reported the 1 km window at **47.2 ms** and a per-sample cost that fell from 731 ns
at 256 m to 337 ns at 2 km — which reads as a cache or a memory-locality effect and is a
completely believable thing to write down. **It was the JIT.** One warm-up pass leaves a 2 ms
flood in tier-0 code, while the 1 km flood is promoted mid-run by on-stack replacement; the
bench was measuring which rows had been compiled. Warming up by **call count** — 32 calls or
250 ms, whichever comes first — moved the 1 km window from 47.2 ms to 19.9 ms and the 512 m one
from 10.1 to 4.1.

**This is the headless-frame-time family again**: a measurement artefact that arrives looking like
a finding, with a plausible mechanism already attached. The tell was that the discontinuity sat
between two adjacent rows rather than spreading across them.

### Flat ground was the defect that mattered, and a fixture found it rather than theory

The first design labelled cells in one sweep, taking each cell's label from its lowest neighbour.
Correct on a slope, and wrong the moment two neighbours are equal: **the corner of a flat shelf has
no strictly lower neighbour at all**, so it is declared a pit. Voxel heights are integers sampled
every 4 m, so ties are ordinary rather than exotic — real terrain would have filled with basins
that hold nothing, each stealing catchment from the real one.

The fix is Barnes' flat resolution in the one place this needs it: sweep a **tier** at a time — one
run of equal (filled, height) — seed it from whatever lower ground already touches it, and spread
the label across the flat. Only what the spread cannot reach is a pit. It is one extra queue and
the same O(n log n).

**And it was found by writing the fixture, not by reasoning about the algorithm.** The stepped tank
exists to check arithmetic; it happens to have four shelf corners.

### Two more things about the shape, both worth keeping

- **The sweep needs a global sort; the flood's own pop order is not enough.** The flood enters a
  depression from the rim and works inward, so the first cell of a descending corridor is popped
  while the deeper ones are not yet in the heap — label as you flood and that first cell becomes
  the pit, and the real one never does.
- **The leaf spill graph has two-cycles by construction.** A crossing costs the higher of the two
  samples it joins, so it is symmetric: two basins with no cheaper exit are each other's lowest
  crossing, and surplus routed around the leaves would ping-pong forever. That is not a defect to
  fix here — it is exactly what a merge tree resolves, and it is now a test
  (`TwoSiblingBasinsSpillIntoEachOtherAndThatIsWhyTheMergeTreeExists`) so that building the tree
  has something to change.

### Ten break-recipes, eight caught, and the two green ones are documentation corrections

Caught: edge as a wall; the curve not capped at the saddle; a pit keyed by sample index rather than
world column; pits tie-broken by index rather than depth; no flat resolution; volume forgetting the
cell area; the curve sorted descending; the flood pushing the neighbour's own height.

Green, and neither is a hole:

- **The saddle's explicit tie-break is belt and braces.** Replacing it with `crossing <= saddle`
  leaves the suite green, because the scan is row-major and row-major (z, x) order already survives
  translation — both rules are stable, they simply keep a different one of two equal crossings.
  Kept because it states the property as a rule rather than as a consequence of the loop's shape,
  and a tiled or parallel scan would make it the only thing holding that property up.
- **The `key < own` guard in the seeding pass is unreachable**, because every neighbour labelled at
  that moment already has a lower key. **The battery corrected a comment written an hour earlier**,
  which had claimed the guard became load-bearing once flats were handled. It did not.

Both are M4a's zeroable-epsilon category, and this is the fourth and fifth time it has come up.

### Two numbers that are for M7b rather than for M7a

- **1,376 basins in a 1 km window, and 1,336 of them spill into another basin rather than out of
  the world.** The merge tree is the common case, not an edge case — and M7b has fourteen hundred
  accumulators in view, not ten. Still trivial against SCALE.md's yardstick (a float each), but the
  plan's mental image of "a few lakes" is wrong and the tuning follows from the real number.
- **Every basin in that window full to its own saddle is 54.7 ML, which is 5.2 cm of water spread
  flat over the square kilometre.** Basins are shallow relative to rain, and the mean is 40 m³ —
  **most of them are puddles**. That is the number M7b's rainfall rate should be set against, and
  it says ponds ought to appear within minutes, which is what Matthew asked for out loud.
  **A minimum capacity below which a basin is not tracked is the obvious knob**, named here and
  deliberately not built.


## 2026-09-01 — M7 planned: the first system with no bound, and the world gets a clock

[docs/M7-PLAN.md](docs/M7-PLAN.md), split M7a–M7d, nothing written yet. Three decisions were put
to Matthew before any code and all three came back as the recommendation: **M7 renders standing
water**, **rainfall is a seeded weather cycle**, and **the watershed grid is 4 m**.

**The structural point, and it is a harder one than M5's.** Every milestone so far has had a bound
that made a local computation exact — worldgen is per chunk, meshing is a chunk plus its padding, a
carve is bounded by the tool radius, and light was saved by arithmetic: 15 m of reach against a
16 m margin, so light computed over the loaded region is exact inside the drawn one. **A watershed
has no such bound.** Where water goes from a column depends on terrain arbitrarily far away, and
there is no attenuation distance and no margin that makes a window exact. This is the first system
here that cannot be made correct by choosing a big enough neighbourhood, and every decision in M7a
is downstream of accepting that.

**What makes it tractable is that the input is a pure function rather than the world.**
`ISurfaceHeights.SurfaceHeightAt` is analytic, seeded, needs no chunk loaded, and already has an
interface with a test double — M5b built it so a `SkyColumn` test could state a flat world in one
line. So the analysis needs **no streaming, no margin, no barrier, no stage**, runs at any
resolution over any window on a worker, and is deterministic, so **only the water volume ever
needs saving**. Written down because the instinct will be to make the watershed a chunk stage like
everything else, and it is not one.

### Four things the pass found that were not in the four-bullet sketch

- **The world has no clock, and M7 needs one.** `WorldHeader` carries settings, the ID table, the
  inventory and the player. Nothing in five milestones has needed time: worldgen is timeless,
  light is a fixpoint, physics takes `dt` as an argument and remembers nothing. The accumulator's
  integrate-forward needs it, "recent rainfall" needs it, and so do M8's fill-in-progress and M9's
  collapse delay. **Additive, so v2 → v3 migrates** under M6c-2's policy.
- **A basin's identity must be world-space.** The analysis window is player-centred, so every
  array index renumbers when it moves — and persisted volume keyed on an index **silently
  reattaches to a different basin**: the lake drains, the valley next door floods, and nothing
  fails anywhere. Priority-flood already yields each depression's **pit**, which is a property of
  the terrain. That is non-negotiable 2's argument — *identity is a name the world owns, not a
  number the process assigned* — arriving somewhere nobody expected to need it. The tie-break
  between two equal pits has to be a total order on the coordinate, or the ID moves between runs.
- **The weather is analytic too, and that is what makes the deferred fill defensible.** Rainfall is
  a pure function of (seed, world time) — episodes hashed through `splitmix64` — so rain over any
  interval is a closed-form sum rather than something that has to be stepped. **Integrate-forward
  then equals the stepped version exactly**, which is the difference between a seam and a cheat.
  It is also server-authoritative for free, and testable without a clock.
- **The wet term is free, and it is where M5's bill gets collected.** Wetness is
  `recent rainfall × skylight`; skylight is already `COLOR.r` per vertex and rainfall is global, so
  it is **one uniform, zero remeshes, zero vertex bytes**. DESIGN's stated reason for keeping the
  two light channels separate rather than pre-multiplying them was this exact term, one milestone
  ahead of it existing. `sky_brightness` — built at M5c-2 with nothing behind it — gets its first
  consumer as overcast dimming, also with no repropagation.

### The oracle, and why it is the same category as M5's

**Integrating 600 s in one call must equal 600 calls of one second, to the litre.** Volumes are
integers and the weather is closed form, so the two paths are either identical or one is wrong —
no tolerance, no epsilon. **The assertion and the feature are the same statement**, because that
property *is* "flew away mid-fill and came back", the same way M5b's *incremental == from-scratch*
was both the test and the claim. It is also the cash value of *slower than realtime is accuracy,
not approximation*, which **graduated to a locked decision in DESIGN.md in this pass**, as its
note asked.

M7a gets one genuinely independent oracle as well: a conic bowl stated through `ISurfaceHeights`
in three lines, whose volume at a level has a closed form sharing no code with the subject.
Everything else in the part checks the code against itself.

### Two things deliberately accepted rather than solved

- **The window edge is an outlet, not a wall.** A basin larger than the window cannot be modelled,
  and the choice is between water pooling against nothing and water leaving the world. Outlet,
  because under-filling means a lake that should exist does not, while over-filling means water
  arriving where the player built — and in a game whose antagonist is water, the honest failure is
  the one that does not drown a base for a reason nobody can see.
- **Edits do not change the watershed at M7.** A pit you dug does not fill with rain. That looks
  like a hole in the core loop and is not: **the mechanism that carries water into an excavation is
  Tier B, which is M8 by design**, and shipping half of it here would produce water teleporting
  into a hole rather than running into it. The structure the follow-up needs is `SkyColumn`, which
  holds edited height per voxel column and has been persisted since M6a.

### One thing this changes about a decision filed as cosmetic this morning

The face tint reads `NORMAL` inside `fragment()`, which in Godot 4 is view space — left alone
because Matthew likes it. **M7c adds a wet sheen, which is also view-dependent**, and a sheen
computed off a camera-relative normal slides across surfaces as the player turns. So M7c is where
that stops being an A/B and needs an answer.


## 2026-09-01 — The lamp lights the sealed room, and turning your head changes the shade

Two screenshots of the sealed room with a lamp on the wall, a few degrees of yaw apart. Both
carry something.

**The lamp closes M6's last play item, and only half of what that item claimed.** The room was
confirmed black on 2026-09-01 and it is now lit, with falloff into the corners — so **`COLOR.g`
reaches the screen**, since the sky channel is zero in a sealed room by construction and something
is lighting it. **What the frame cannot show is the warm half**, because the room is dirt:
`block_tint` is `(1.0, 0.86, 0.66)`, and warm light on brown rock looks like white light on brown
rock. **The fixture is degenerate in exactly the way the assertion cannot see** — the same
category as M5c-1's one-voxel bore and M6a's carved-chunk `Compact` measurement. The sharp version
is a room in stone, and 2.1 million litres of it are carried. Also worth noting so a later reader
does not over-read the picture: **the lamp on that wall is M5b's `L` debug bind, not a placement
from the hotbar** — slot 3 still reads 16 L.

### The brightness that moves when you turn, and why it is not filed as a bug

*"if i turn slightly left it gets brighter... its a minor cosmetic and i kind like it now
anyways."* Not chased, at Matthew's instruction. But it is **not the artefact already recorded**,
and the recorded one's candidate list is missing what is probably the cause of both.

Two explanations fit the frames:

- **Benign composition.** `face_tint` gives ±X walls 0.65 and ±Z walls 0.8 — two adjacent walls of
  a room differ by 23% *by design*. Turning changes how much of each fills the frame, so the
  average brightness of the picture moves while every face keeps its own shade.
- **A view-space normal, which would be a one-line defect.** In a Godot 4 spatial shader `NORMAL`
  inside `fragment()` is in **view space** — the convention `Voxel.gdshader` already notes for
  `VERTEX`, two comments below the one in question. `face_tint(NORMAL)` would then be grading a
  face by its orientation *relative to the camera*, and yaw would carry a wall across the
  `abs(n.x) > 0.5` threshold, stepping the wall itself between 0.65 and 0.8.

**The discriminating test takes two seconds and needs no instrument: point at one wall and pitch
up and down.** Composition cannot change one wall's own brightness. A view-space normal, pitched
far enough, gives a vertical wall `n.y > 0.5` and renders it at the **top-face** value 1.0 — a
wall lighting up like a floor.

**If it is the view-space normal, it is a better candidate for M5d-2's rotation flicker than any
of the three recorded against it.** That list is coincident faces, frustum culling and staleness;
this is none of them, and it is **reachable by rotation alone**, which is the one property that
repro turns on — the entry itself says *"what that leaves is render-side, since neither the light
grid nor the camera position changes when you rotate"*, and then lists three things that are
harder to reach than the one sitting in the fragment shader.

**Deliberately not fixed.** The fix is `face_tint((INV_VIEW_MATRIX * vec4(NORMAL, 0.0)).xyz)`, and
it is **a look change as much as a correctness one** — the shader's stated intent is that *a box
reads as a box*, and under a camera-relative tint two opposite walls can take the same shade at
some yaws, which is the case that intent exists to prevent. Matthew likes the current behaviour,
so this is an A/B for a person rather than a defect to repair quietly.


## 2026-09-01 — Bricked in, and it goes actually black

Matthew sealed himself into the room he had just built — *"I will actually brick myself in so I
can see it go black"* — and it went black. Not dark grey: a frame containing the HUD, the brush
outline, and nothing else.

**This is the strongest confirmation M5's lighting has had, and it is a different test from the
one M5c-2 ran.** Those screenshots used `--skybrightness=0`, which scales the sky channel to zero
globally — it proves the sky channel is what lights the world, but it proves it by turning a
uniform down. **Sealing a room proves light runs out**: the sky is at full strength and simply
cannot reach, which is the mechanism the whole grid exists to model and the thing a mining game
is about.

**It is only possible because of M5d-1's fog fix, and that is worth restating.** Before it the
environment fog blended the *final* colour toward one constant, so against correctly-black terrain
the fog was 100% of what you saw and a lightless room rendered as a legible grey-blue box. A test
this sharp would have silently reported the opposite of the truth.

**Still not done: the lamp.** 16 L of lamp — one voxel — is sitting on slot 3. Placing it in a
sealed room is **the only test in the milestone that proves the two light channels stay
independent all the way to the screen**; every other test passes identically with `shadeSky` and
`shadeBlock` packed into one byte. A warm pool rather than a grey one is the whole assertion.

### The hotbar's future is an inventory screen, and that changes what a slot is

Asked whether the ID-order slot shift actually bothered him: *"Didn't care but do want to adjust
it so slots stay put, when we do the inventory screen etc, I was going to allow you to carry more
than what is on the hotbar maybe?"*

**So the fix is scheduled rather than declined, and the framing changes the design.** Today the
hotbar is a *projection*: nine slots showing the first nine materials you carry, in ID order, and
the row is fully determined by the inventory. The moment you can carry more than the row shows,
**the hotbar becomes an assignment** — which slot holds which material — and that is a different
object with different requirements:

- It is **state the player authors**, so it has to survive a quit. That is a world-header field
  and a header format version bump, v2 → v3, under M6c-2's recorded policy: *an additive version
  migrates, a version that changes what a field means is refused.* Adding a slot map is additive.
- **It makes slots stay put by construction**, which is the ask, rather than by a cleverer sort.
  `MaterialInSlot`'s revisit trigger is therefore **answered by scheduling rather than by
  reversal**: ID order was the right rule for a row that is a projection, and it stops being the
  question the moment the row is an assignment.
- It is also where **inventory capacity finally gets somewhere to go**. `VolumetricInventory` is
  unbounded at M6 deliberately, with the recorded cost that *M6 cannot answer whether volume is a
  real constraint*, and the recorded trigger was M10's containers or M11's crafting. **An
  inventory screen is a third candidate and an earlier one.**

Not built, not scheduled to a milestone yet, and recorded here so the next person planning one
starts from the four sentences above rather than from the hotbar.


## 2026-09-01 — M6's headline question is answered by a person: the work is still there

*"Quit and reopen works so does flying away."* Two of the three play items, and they are the two
the milestone exists for.

**This is the thing every previous milestone's play kept running into.** M5d-2 dug a chamber and
lost it; the recorded reason M6 was scheduled at all is that *an edited chunk which unloads loses
its edits*, so every hour of play before persistence landed was an hour thrown away — including
the play that would judge placement. That is why M6-PLAN put persistence before the more enjoyable
half. **The bet was that building second is building on a world that keeps it, and the bet is
now paid.**

Both halves were verified by proxy before today and neither proxy was the claim:

- **Unload and return** was covered by tests and by M6d-2's arms — 71 chunks loaded, 44 columns
  restored, `first draw` indistinguishable from generating. All of that says the *machinery*
  works. **None of it says a person flew away from their own tunnel and found it when they came
  back**, because a measurement re-flies a scripted path and does not care what is there.
- **Quit and reopen** was verified at M6b-3 headlessly — dig, `--quit-after`, reopen, 9 chunks
  loaded and 414 quads against a pristine 404 — and the worklog recorded that **the windowed close
  was verified only by proxy**, `--quit-after` being the same `SceneTree::quit()` teardown. That
  caveat has stood since M6b-3 and is now closed by somebody actually closing the window.

**So the failure model M6 inverted has been checked in the direction that matters.** A persistence
bug destroys work that cannot be recreated and surfaces a session later — the whole reason M6-PLAN
said the tests were the only thing between a defect and permanent data loss. The tests held, and
the confirmation is a person finding their own chamber where they left it.

### Addendum, later the same day — the better verdict

*"I keep forgetting I can just quit now and come back to my save."*

**That is a stronger statement than any of the three play items, and it is the one a persistence
milestone is actually aiming at.** The three items each ask *does it work* and get a yes. This one
says the feature has stopped being a feature: it has receded into the floor, and the habit it
replaced — do not stop, you will lose the tunnel — is now the thing that feels out of date.
**Nobody notices a save system that works**, which is why the evidence for one is almost always a
test rather than a sentence. This is the sentence.

**What is left of M6 is the walls-and-floor half of "build a room".** The stairs half is already
answered: the ramp brush is the right tool and the fast path.


## 2026-09-01 — The ramp brush earns its place, and the screenshot lied about how

Matthew built a staircase down into the excavated chamber and the play answers M6d-1's open
question: **the ramp brush is the right tool for stairs, and it is the fast path.** In his words —
*"definitely using the ramp mode, honestly using the dig tool to get those kind of stairs would
take me a lot longer."*

**That validates building the fifth shape before the play rather than after.** M6c's play found
cube stairs unwalkable — a 1 m riser against M4b's 0.5 m step height — M6d-1 went first in the
split so the play would judge a finished tool, and the play now says the tool it added is the one
people reach for. **DESIGN's carve-for-detail / place-for-bulk split stands unamended, with stairs
on the *place* side**, which is where it always put them.

### The screenshot gesture perturbs the thing the screenshot is evidence of

**Every screenshot taken with `Alt`+PrintScreen shows `ONE VOXEL (Alt)` in the status line,
whatever the player was actually doing**, because the HUD reports a held modifier and the
screenshot gesture holds it. The behaviour is correct and is deliberately left alone at Matthew's
instruction — *"don't change it"* — the HUD is answering the keyboard truthfully.

**It was believed, and a wrong conclusion was built on it.** Two shots of a half-built staircase
both read `ONE VOXEL (Alt)`, the inventory had gained ~48,000 voxels of stone between them, and
the reading written down here was *"you're cutting the stairs, not placing them"* — complete with
a proposed amendment to DESIGN that turns out not to be needed. The stone was the chamber being
dug; the stairs were placed.

**A new member of a family this project keeps rediscovering, and the first one where the
instrument was a person.** The headless frame-time trap is a measurement that reports something
adjacent to what you asked; M5c-1's shaft fixture is a scenario that passes for the wrong reason;
this is **an observation whose method changes the observed state**. The tell was available and
ignored: the status line is *live input state*, so it says what is true at the instant of capture
rather than what was true while the work was done.

**The practical consequence, worth knowing before reading any old screenshot from this project:**
the status line's modifier reading is only trustworthy in a capture that did not use a modifier —
`screenshot.gd`, or PrintScreen alone. Every other HUD element in the frame is honest, because
none of the others are keyed off a key being down.

## 2026-09-01 — The entangled miner goes to 20 a second, and faster is cheaper again

Raised at Matthew's request — *"bump the quantum miner to 20x a second"* — from 0.125 s to
**0.05 s**, the second raise in two days. Re-measured rather than assumed, which the constant's own
doc comment demanded, and the measurement said the same surprising thing it has said twice before.

```
60 s, r4h/2v, 6 m/s, entangled            8/s              20/s
swings                                     485             1131   (~18.9/s effective)
swing ms  mean / max                 0.100 / 1.198    0.070 / 0.944
voxels removed / already air per swing    19 / 13          19 / 14
relight remeshes per swing / total       1.4 / 697       1.2 / 1325
edit remeshes per second                  13.9             32.3
update ms mean / max                 3.245 / 11.725   3.651 / 10.651
```

**Faster is cheaper per swing for the third rate running** — 0.139 ms at four a second, 0.072 at
eight, 0.070 at twenty. The mechanism is the same each time and it is worth restating because it
is counter-intuitive: **consecutive swings chew the previous bite**, so at a high rate most of the
sphere is air that `Carve` skips before it ever reaches `SetVoxel`. Voxels *removed* per swing is
flat at 19 while voxels *already air* climbs, which is that mechanism visible in one line of the
report.

**What actually rises is the remesh load, and it rises because it is per swing rather than per
voxel.** 32.3 edit remeshes a second against 13.9 — a 2.3× rise tracking the swing count exactly,
not the volume dug. That is the number to watch if this is ever raised again, and it is the one
the swing-cost figure hides. `update ms` mean moved 3.245 → 3.651, about 12%, and its **maximum
went down**, which is a reminder that with 45 samples of a bursty series the max is a sample and
not a bound.

**The ceiling has a name now, which it did not before: one swing per frame, at 0.0167 s.** Below
that the cooldown stops being what paces the tool and the frame rate becomes the balance, so the
dig rate would depend on the machine — a debug bind that digs twice as fast on a better computer
is not a comparable test volume, which is the whole reason the rate is fixed rather than the
tier's. 0.05 s leaves a factor of three.

**And that ceiling is already showing, harmlessly: a 60 s run lands at 1131 swings, ~18.9/s rather
than 20**, because a swing can only fire on a frame boundary and 0.05 s is three frames at 60 Hz
with jitter either side. Matthew's own note — *"it does not need be exact"* — settles that; it is
recorded because the next person to divide 1131 by 60 and get 18.9 should find the reason rather
than a bug.


## 2026-09-01 — M6d-3: the number row goes where the hand expects it, and the game gets a face

The buildable half of M6d-3. `MinerCraft.Game/Ui/Hud.cs` is a hotbar, a crosshair and a status
line; **1–9 select a material and T cycles the tool tier**, which is the two axes swapping places.
Suite **734 → 739**. **The three play items are Matthew's and are not done** — they are the point
of the part and no amount of code closes them.

### The number row was on the wrong axis, and the argument is four days old

M6d's own TODO named the collision and did not settle it: *"the number keys pick tool tiers today,
so material selection is a second axis."* Both want 1–9, and only one of them is what a hand
expects to find there — Minecraft's number row is the hotbar and it holds **what you build with**.
**This is the same argument that swapped Ctrl and Shift back on 2026-08-31**, decades of muscle
memory against this project's few days, and it was Matthew's call again.

The tiers lost almost nothing by moving: **two picks ship**, so a cycle key on `T` is one press
where the number row was one press. **If a mod ever ships eight picks, that trade inverts** — the
tiers want the row back and the materials want somewhere else to go, and that is the shape of the
decision when it arrives rather than a problem now.

`SelectTier` was polled every frame from `UpdateMining` and is now an event on the key. That is
not tidying: the poll compared against `ReferenceEquals(_mining.Tool, _tiers[i])` to avoid
re-announcing sixty times a second, which is a guard that exists only because the input was being
read in the wrong place.

### A hotbar slot must not move under the player's fingers, and one rule buys that at a price

`VolumetricInventory.MaterialInSlot` is the row: **the carried materials in ascending ID order.**
Three properties, and the third is why it won:

- **The hotbar is what you are carrying, not what exists.** Same argument `NextMaterial` already
  made — a slot offering a material you have none of is a selection that cannot be acted on, and
  with five shipped materials most of the row would be that.
- **The cost is stated rather than hidden: picking up a material you did not have shifts every
  slot above it.** Mine your first dirt and the stone on 1 may become 2 while your hand is on the
  key. Accepted at M6 because the fix — a slot assignment the player arranges — is state that has
  to survive a quit, which is a header field and a format version, in the part of M6 most likely
  to be redone. **Revisit trigger: the play reports a slot moving under their fingers.**
- **ID order beat first-acquired order on the one case that separates them.** Acquisition order is
  stable *within* a session and loses across a quit: `Reset` replays the header's entries and a
  session's acquisition order is written down nowhere, so the row a player learned in one session
  would be a different row in the next. **A rule that is always the same beats one that is usually
  better and occasionally lies.** `TheRowIsUnchangedAcrossASaveAndReload` is the test that fails
  for the rejected alternative and passes for every other test in the group.

**And it gave an existing guarantee a second, louder dependant.** `Entries()` has sorted by ID
since M6c-2 *so that the same inventory always writes the same bytes* — a save-determinism
argument. The hotbar now means that sort is what a number key **means**, and where a shuffled save
is merely unanswerable, a shuffled hotbar moves the player's materials mid-build. Recorded in the
remarks, because removing the sort now breaks two things that look unrelated.

**Four break-recipes, four caught** — dropping the sort (2 tests), dropping the negative-slot
guard (1), off-by-one on the upper bound (4), and a lookup that ignores its own slot argument (3).

### One definition of what stone looks like

The HUD needs a colour per material and the obvious way to get one is a short palette in the HUD,
which is **two definitions of what stone looks like**: they agree the day they are written and
drift the first time either is retuned, and the symptom is a swatch that no longer matches the
block it places. So `VoxelMaterial.LayerColour` is now the shared array the block textures are
speckled from *and* the swatches are filled from. Same argument as `IsCaveAt` and
`GenerateTerrain` sharing one definition of the cave field.

The jitter stayed beside it rather than folded into it — the HUD wants the flat colour and the
block wants the speckle, and they are the same decision only as far as the hue.

### A material's label is derived and not authored, which is the one thing here that is expensive to get wrong

A `displayName` in the material JSON is the obvious answer and it is the costly one: **mods write
against a format the moment it exists**, and a name that can be authored is a name that wants
translating, which is a localisation system this project has no other reason to grow. The
identifier's path is already a human word — the base game ships `stone`, `dirt`, `grass`, `lamp` —
and it exists for every material including a placeholder standing in for a removed mod. **Revisit
trigger: the first material whose ID is not a sensible label, or the first request to run the game
in another language.**

This is the whole of M6d-3 that could have been an expensive mistake. The rest of the UI is
pixels, and TODO's own note is right that it is the part most likely to be redone.

### There was no crosshair, in a game whose two verbs are both "what am I pointing at"

The wireframe target box has been standing in for one since M3d. That works while you are aiming
at a surface and **vanishes the moment you point at sky**, so the player lost the centre of the
screen exactly when they were hunting for it. Two `ColorRect` bars, no binary asset for a plus
sign.

### The screenshot found both defects and the logs could not have

**Headless has no renderer, so a layout error looks identical to a correct layout in every log
this project prints.** The HUD is instantiated in a plain headless run deliberately — that is the
cheapest thing that executes the whole file and catches a script error, and a UI nobody has ever
constructed headlessly is M5c-2's shape of hole one layer out — but it proves nothing about where
anything lands. Two defects, both invisible to it:

- **The crosshair's vertical bar rendered as a line most of the screen tall.** `SetAnchorsPreset`
  writes offsets, the following assignment to `Size` writes them again, and the next layout pass
  recomputes the rect from the anchors — so the assignment survived for one bar and not the other.
  Anchors and offsets are now set directly and never through a preset plus a size.
- **The litres label was clipped off the bottom edge**, because the row reserved 92 px for
  something needing about 90 including its status line.

**And one thing that looked like a third defect and was not.** A pale vertical line at exactly
screen-centre *x* read as a stray wireframe edge; colouring the crosshair red isolated it, and
sampling the pixels gave **(238, 229, 88)** — the yellow cell outline's own back vertical edge,
spanning exactly the box's height, misread as white against green. **Worth recording because the
instinct that found the two real defects also manufactured a third**, and the pixel sample is what
separated them. Eyeballing a screenshot is a measurement too.

### The HUD is told and never asked

Every value it draws is read from the controller that owns it — the selection and brush from
`PlaceController`, the tier from `MiningController`, the litres from `VolumetricInventory`. A HUD
holding its own copy of the selection would be a second answer to *what am I holding*, and the two
would disagree exactly when it mattered: the frame after a material ran out and the controller
re-selected without being asked.

**Not created during a profile run**, because the profile reports draw calls and primitives and
M1d's deferred 2×2×2 mesh-block question turns on that counter — UI quads in a number that means
terrain. Verified: `--profile` reports **1521 viewed / 165 drawn / 1926 jobs at 404 quads**,
unchanged to the digit, and the plain headless run reports the same.

### What is left, and it is the part that matters

**The three play items are not done and cannot be done here.** Dig a tunnel and fly away until it
unloads and come back; quit and reopen; build a room with walls, a floor and a ramp down into it.
M6's whole reason for existing is the first of those, and DESIGN's claim that carving-for-detail
and placing-for-bulk divides cleanly is the third. **A sandbox cannot be judged by the person who
built it out of the report it prints.**


## 2026-09-01 — M6d-2: the worry dissolves, and the cost was somewhere nobody was looking

M6d-2 is the measurement half, and everything it measures already ran. Five questions, five
answers, and **the two that mattered were not the two the plan expected**. Suite unchanged at
**734**; the default headless run is unchanged to the digit — 1521 viewed / 165 drawn / 1926 jobs
at 404 quads — which is the thing an instrumentation pass has to prove before any of its numbers
are worth reading.

### 1. The headline: entering a dug world is not slower than generating it

M6 has carried this since its plan. Half-answered twice — deserialise 21 µs a chunk at M6a, a
SQLite point query 6.0 µs at M6b-1, crossover at 2,505 chunks — and what was missing was the
end-to-end figure that includes the serial lane's ordering against eight generating workers.

```
r4h/2v, standing start (the deterministic arm)      first draw      all settled
generate  --nosave                    rep1 / rep2   3.46 / 3.43     3.81 / 3.80
load      19 stored chunks in the box rep1 / rep2   3.48 / 3.43     3.85 / 3.80

r4h/2v, moving at 6 m/s
generate  --nosave                                  3.82 / 3.80     4.64 / 4.62
load      71 loaded + 44 columns restored           3.84 / 3.82     4.62 / 4.61
```

**Indistinguishable — the load-versus-generate gap is smaller than the rep-to-rep gap.** The
standing start is used because M5d-1 established it as the only arm where the chunk set at a fixed
radius is deterministic, so this compares two numbers rather than two samples of a moving camera.

**The limitation is stated rather than buried: 176 stored chunks is the most this world could be
dug to, against 1,521 tracked, so the 2,505-chunk crossover is confirmed in direction and not in
fact.** The scripted flythrough is a straight line along +X, so repeated passes deepen one trench
rather than covering new ground — five passes went 99 → 104 → 112 → 123 → 176 stored and were
plainly asymptotic. A world dug past the crossover is not reachable with the instruments that
exist, and building one is not M6d-2's job. **Nothing here retires the concern; it moves it from
"predicted to bite at 2,505" to "measured not to bite at 176".**

### 2. The finding nobody was looking for: the box-difference sweep costs more than the pipeline

`ChunkStreamer.MoveViewer` is called from `_Process` **before** the bracket that produces
`update ms`, so **every profile from M2d to M6d-1 measured the pipeline and not the sweep.**
Timed for the first time today:

```
                                     tracked   viewer ms mean / p95 / max    update ms mean
r4h/2v   6 m/s  no world open           1521    7.09–9.02 / 13.4–14.7 / 15.3      2.34
r4h/2v   6 m/s  world open              1521    9.52–10.0 / 14.6–15.5 / 15.6      2.33
r6h/3v   6 m/s  no world open           3179   13.21      / 19.32     / 19.61     4.05
r4h/2v  40 m/s  world open + mining     1521    4.84      /  6.55     / 13.69     5.31
```

**Against a 16.7 ms frame, and two to four times the whole pipeline update.** It fires only when
the viewer crosses a chunk boundary — 15 times in a 20 s run at 6 m/s — so it is a spike rather
than a load, which is exactly the shape `SampleSeries`' own doc comment says a mean hides.

Two consequences worth writing down:

- **`main %` understates the main thread and always has.** It is computed from `PipelineUpdate`
  alone. At r6h/3v the report says 31% of one core while the sweep is spending another 13.2 ms on
  15 frames out of ~1,200.
- **It is sub-linear in radius**: 2.09× the tracked chunks for 1.47× the sweep. So it is not
  purely per-chunk work.

**And it is not persistence**, which is the half M6 was actually worried about — see below.

### 3. `Forget` becoming a write is a non-event, and the design answer is why

M6-PLAN's headline structural risk: *"`ChunkStreamer.Forget` becomes a write … called
synchronously, on the sim thread, from inside `ChunkBox.ForEachDifference`, which at r16 hands it
